reading.relevance_to_proposal:
Eq (2) and Sec 3 (base policy): the proposal's convention (z_0 = eps ~ N(0,I), a_k = z_1, dz/dt = v_theta) matches Lipman's CNF convention exactly (eqs 1-3; App D: 't = 0 corresponds to noise and t = 1 corresponds to data').

Sec 7, eqs (11)-(12) (meta-training): eq (11) is Lipman's OT-CFM sample (eqs 20-23) with sigma_min = 0. Eq (12) is a CFM loss whose model is v_theta + r_{phi,W_k}, with theta frozen and extra inputs (c_k, W_k(H_k)). Theorem 2's gradient equivalence carries over to phi and W_0 when the FM target is taken as the full-history marginal field. This works because u_t = a* - eps does not depend on any parameter, and because W_k is a function of H_k that excludes the query's (eps, a*). The CFM objective being simulation-free is what lets the direct reader avoid unrolling the solver, the proposal's stated advantage over the whole-path variant (Sec 9).

Sec 6, eq (10) (sensitivity) and Sec 18 (early/late ablation): Lipman's eq 8 with the OT path implies structure the proposal can exploit. At t = 0, under the independent coupling, the exact marginal field is E[a*|c] - z, which depends only on the target mean. So the ideal memory residual at t = 0 is E[a*|c,W_k] - E[a*|c], a constant mean shift. Mode selection and higher-moment changes must happen at intermediate t, where the marginal Jacobian (t Cov[a*|x_t]/(1-t)^2 - I)/(1-t) becomes strongly expanding near mode boundaries. This supports the hypothesis that recall 'first redirect[s] which action mode is forming'. It also predicts that a z-independent reader evaluated only at t_0 can at best translate the base distribution.

Sec 11, eqs (21)-(22) (endpoint distillation): this is exactly Lipman's eq 23 applied to teacher samples. The 'terminal noise floor' is Lipman's sigma_min.

Sec 12, eq (24) and App A (path distillation): b* = E[V_t | Gamma_t = z, C = c] is the path analogue of Lipman's eq 8 marginalization. Lipman's Theorem 1 is density-based and needs Leibniz regularity, so it does not directly cover Dirac conditional paths. The proposal is right to use [13]'s weak continuity equation instead.

Sec 13, eqs (27)-(28) (retention bound): Lipman's FM fields bear directly on the 'globally L-Lipschitz, uniformly over generative time' assumption; see technical issues.

Sec 19, eqs (29)-(30) (analytic check): I verified that the proposal's b_t and kappa_t are exactly Lipman's eq 8 marginal field for source N(0,I), target N(mu, sigma^2 I) and the sigma_min = 0 linear path. A Monte Carlo regression with 2M samples matches b_t and kappa_t mu to about 3 decimals at t = 0.2, 0.6 and 0.9. Because sigma = 0.15 > 0, p_t > 0 everywhere, so Theorem 2's assumptions hold in the sanity check.

App C (source choice): Lipman supports a general p only at the level of the Sec 3 framework.

Reading map, Sec 8 table, Sec 10 and Sec 12 OT disclaimers: all consistent with Lipman's explicit statement that the marginal field is not OT.
novelty_threats: No substantive threat. Lipman et al. is a foundation for training generative models. It contains no fast weights, memory, test-time training, continual learning, consolidation or robot policies, so it does not pre-empt the proposal's claimed contributions: the fast/slow memory lifecycle, the centered external velocity reader, consolidation with retention and refresh gates, and fair comparisons with internal TTT.

Minor: training a velocity field with extra conditioning inputs (eq 12, memory as an input to the field) and distilling a teacher's samples with plain CFM (eqs 21-22) are routine applications of the FM/CFM framework, already shown for conditional generation in Lipman Sec 6.3 (super-resolution). The proposal correctly calls eqs 21-22 'a standard FM construction' and should keep avoiding any novelty claim for these objectives. Its contribution has to rest on the lifecycle and on the reader comparisons.
ideas_to_borrow: Make sigma_min explicit. Either adopt Lipman's eq 20-23 form, x_t = (1 - (1 - sigma_min) t) eps + t a*, u_t = a* - (1 - sigma_min) eps, and report sigma_min (the v2 PDF itself omits its value), or keep sigma_min = 0 and cite rectified flow / stochastic interpolants for that case. This also gives the 'terminal noise floor' in Sec 11 a concrete, standard form.

Solver-error protocol from Lipman Fig 7: for a fixed set of noise seeds (Lipman uses 256), compare low-NFE Euler / midpoint / RK4 endpoints with a 1000-NFE reference solution, for both the base field and the memory-adapted field. This directly implements the proposal's 'separately measure solver error and distribution quality' (Sec 6) and its 8/16/32-step sweep (Sec 16).

Report adaptive-solver NFE (dopri5, atol = rtol = 1e-5, as in Lipman Table 1 and Fig 10) for the base versus the adapted field, as a cheap proxy for how much the memory residual stiffens or curves the flow. This matters for latency and for the Lipschitz-dependent retention bound.

Use 2D multimodal toy targets such as Lipman's checkerboard (Fig 4: density evolution and trajectories at NFE = 4/8/10/20 with a 5x512 MLP) as a Stage-B visual and quantitative sanity check of mode coverage under memory adaptation.

Exact model likelihood via the instantaneous change of variables (Lipman App C, eqs 27-33; exact divergence is cheap in 2D, Hutchinson estimator otherwise). NLL of held-out expert actions under the memory-adapted policy is a proper distributional metric to report alongside the energy score and mode coverage (Sec 17, 'Distribution quality').

Exploit the OT-path structure in the early/late memory-access ablation (Sec 18). Under the independent coupling, the ideal residual at t = 0 is a pure mean shift E[a*|c,W] - E[a*|c], so a t_0-only, z-independent reader can only translate the base distribution. Stating this prediction in advance makes the 'repeated denoising interaction' test sharper.

Consider a probability-path ablation (OT/linear versus VP-diffusion path, as in Lipman Table 1). Diffusion paths commit to structure late (Fig 6), OT paths early, so when memory must act during denoising may depend on the path. This is optional and secondary to the reader comparisons.

Add coupling-preserving 'reflow'-style endpoint distillation (Liu et al. 2022, cited by Lipman as concurrent work) as an intermediate consolidation baseline between fresh-noise endpoint FM (eqs 21-22) and full path distillation (eq 23). It trains on unfiltered teacher pairs (eps, T(eps)) with x_t = (1-t) eps + t T(eps). It is valid when the pairs are not success-filtered and tends to preserve same-seed outputs and straighten the flow.

Outside Lipman's reference list but relevant to the OT discussion and to App C: minibatch-OT / multisample couplings (Tong et al. 2023, arXiv:2302.00482; Pooladian et al. 2023, arXiv:2304.14772). These are the standard way to move the marginal flow toward OT and to use non-Gaussian sources. Lipman et al. 2024 'Flow Matching Guide and Code' (arXiv:2412.06264) is a rigorous modern reference for the conditional-FM assumptions. All three arXiv ids were checked.
technical_issues_in_proposal: Eq (11) and eq (21) use the sigma_min = 0 interpolant and cite [2] as 'the usual' construction. Lipman always takes sigma_min > 0 'sufficiently small'. Theorem 2 assumes p_t(x) > 0 for all t in [0,1], and its App A proof assumes bounded u_t. For singular or discrete targets, both fail at t = 1 when sigma_min = 0, where the conditional field (x1 - x)/(1-t) diverges. This has little practical consequence (the event has measure zero, and the 16-step Euler grid stops at t = 15/16). It is still a citation/assumption mismatch: state sigma_min, or cite [13] or rectified flow for the sigma_min = 0 case.

The retention bound (27)-(28) assumes a field that is globally L-Lipschitz uniformly in t. FM marginal fields built as in Lipman (eq 8 with the OT path) can have very large or divergent spatial Lipschitz constants as t -> 1. (i) Multimodal targets, which the proposal's own Stage-B benchmark requires: for a 1D target at ±1 with N(0,1) source and sigma_min = 0, the exact marginal Jacobian at the mode boundary x = 0 is (t Var/(1-t)^2 - 1)/(1-t). I verified numerically that it is 44 at t = 0.75, 890 at t = 0.9 and 3824 at t = 15/16. A student fitting such a field needs a huge L, and C_L = (e^{2L}-1)/(2L) then makes the bound vacuous. (ii) Even the proposal's own unimodal sanity-check field (sigma = 0.15, eqs 29-30) has L = max|b_t| ≈ 3.41 at t ≈ 0.83, so C_L ≈ 134. For a pure mean change Δmu, R_old = ∫kappa_t^2 dt ||Δmu||^2 ≈ 5.236 ||Δmu||^2, and the bound gives W2^2 ≤ ~700 ||Δmu||^2, while the true value under the same-noise coupling is ||Δmu||^2. A time-dependent Gronwall bound using |b_t| lowers the factor to ~83. Using the time-dependent one-sided Lipschitz constant (log-norm, here b_t itself, negative for most t) lowers it to ~1.23, which is nearly tight. Recommendation: restate (27)-(28) with a time-dependent one-sided Lipschitz constant mu_t, giving C = ∫_0^1 exp(2∫_s^1 mu_r dr) ds; restrict to t in [0, 1-delta] or the solver grid; or use sigma_min > 0. Also note that for multimodal policies even the one-sided constant grows near mode boundaries. The proposal's remark that 'a large Lipschitz constant makes the bound loose' understates this structural issue.

Sec 7's 'identifies the marginal velocity of the interpolating distribution' leaves the conditioning implicit. Theorem 2's parameter-independent constant extends to the writer and interface parameters (phi, W_0) only if the FM target is defined with respect to the full causal history H_k, u*(x,t,c_k,H_k). It does not extend if the target is defined with respect to W_k, whose information content depends on phi. The proposal's conclusions are right, but the derivation should say this explicitly. It also shows that the no-leakage rule is required for the CFM-FM equivalence, not merely good practice.

App C cites [1, 2] for non-Gaussian (Gaussian-mixture) sources. Lipman supports this only through the generic Sec 3 framework ('e.g., the standard normal'). The paper's concrete Gaussian-path construction (Sec 4, Theorem 3) and all its experiments assume p_0 = N(0,I). Cite a work that treats general sources and couplings ([13], Tong et al. 2023, Pooladian et al. 2023).

Minor: with Lipman's sigma_min > 0, endpoint distillation (eqs 21-22) targets the teacher law convolved with N(0, sigma_min^2 I). The Sec 11 sentence 'teaches the student the teacher's conditional endpoint distribution' is exact only for sigma_min = 0, where Lipman's regularity assumptions are not stated.

Possible missing consolidation baseline: coupling-preserving (reflow-style) endpoint distillation on unfiltered teacher (noise, endpoint) pairs (Liu et al. 2022, in Lipman's reference list). The proposal's rule 'do not reuse a teacher noise sample that has been biased by success selection' is correct for filtered samples. Without filtering, however, reusing the teacher's noise is valid, and it offers a middle ground between eq (22) and eq (23) that the 'Endpoint vs path consolidation' comparison in Sec 17 currently omits.
stated_limitations: The paper has no explicit limitations section. The caveats it does state are listed below.

Marginal field is not OT: 'although the conditional flow is optimal, this by no means imply that the marginal VF is an optimal transport solution. Nevertheless, we expect the marginal vector field to remain relatively simple.' The second sentence is an expectation, not a theorem.
p_1 only approximates the data: with sigma_min > 0, 'the marginal probability p1 is a mixture distribution that closely approximates the data distribution q' (eq 7: p1 ≈ q).

Regularity assumptions in the proofs: Theorem 2 requires p_t(x) > 0 for all x and t. The App A proofs assume Leibniz-rule regularity, q and p_t(x|x1) decaying 'at a sufficient speed', and bounded u_t, v_t and ∇θ v_t. The ODE solution is unique only 'up to some mild conditions on the VF v_t' (App C).

Non-uniqueness of the generating field: 'There is an infinite number of vector fields that generate any particular probability path (e.g., by adding a divergence free component...)'. The paper chooses the simplest, affine one.
Diffusion paths 'do not actually reach a true noise distribution in finite time' (a limitation of the baselines, which the FM construction avoids).

CIFAR-10 FID is higher than in prior work, 'possibly ... explained by the fact that our used architecture was not optimized for CIFAR-10'. The main results are unconditional models, and IC-GAN is left out of the ImageNet-128 comparison.

Future work: 'we expect FM to open the door to allowing a multitude of probability paths (e.g., non-isotropic Gaussians or more general kernels altogether)'. This means only isotropic Gaussian conditional paths are treated.
Social responsibility: image generation can be misused, and training has an energy cost.
cited_works_worth_adding: Liu, Gong & Liu 2022, 'Flow Straight and Fast: Learning to Generate and Transfer Data with Rectified Flow' (arXiv:2209.03003). Cited by Lipman as concurrent work. It is the sigma_min = 0 independent-coupling interpolant that eq (11) actually uses, and its 'reflow' is a coupling-preserving distillation baseline for Secs 11-12.

Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden 2022, 'Building Normalizing Flows with Stochastic Interpolants' (arXiv:2209.15571). Cited by Lipman as concurrent work. It is the precursor of the proposal's [13] and gives a derivation of the sigma_min = 0 linear interpolant under its own assumptions.

McCann 1997, 'A Convexity Principle for Interacting Gases' (Adv. Math. 128). This is the source of Lipman's displacement-interpolation (OT) claim. Useful if the proposal wants to state precisely which OT property holds (conditional only).

Peluchetti 2021, 'Non-denoising Forward-time Diffusions'. Lipman notes that Theorem 1 'can also be derived from the Diffusion Mixture Representation Theorem', the same marginalization identity behind the proposal's path-distillation target eq (24).

Chen et al. 2018, 'Neural Ordinary Differential Equations'. CNF definition and adjoint sensitivity, relevant to the proposal's sensitivity eq (10) and to differentiating through the solver in the whole-path variant (Sec 9).
Grathwohl et al. 2018, 'FFJORD'. The Hutchinson trace estimator for likelihoods (Lipman App C), usable for an NLL metric of adapted action distributions.

Finlay et al. 2020, 'How to Train Your Neural ODE: the World of Jacobian and Kinetic Regularization', and Kelly et al. 2020, 'Learning Differential Equations that Are Easy to Solve'. Both are cited by Lipman. They regularize the Jacobian and solver cost, which could keep the adapted field's Lipschitz constant (the retention bound, eqs 27-28) and its latency under control.
Song et al. 2020b, 'Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations'. The probability-flow ODE and diffusion-path alternative, for a path-choice ablation.

errors_found.reader_claim: Relevance section: "It also predicts that a z-independent reader evaluated only at t_0 can at best translate the base distribution" and "Mode selection and higher-moment changes must happen at intermediate t". This is repeated in ideas_to_borrow: "a t_0-only, z-independent reader can only translate the base distribution".
errors_found.problem: The inference is false. It is true that the ideal FM residual at t=0 is a constant, E[a*|c,W]-E[a*|c]. But a constant push applied to the early state is carried through the nonlinear, multimodal base flow, and the result is a change in how much mass goes to each mode, not a translation. The reader has also misidentified the proposal's baseline: the proposal describes "A reader evaluated only at t = 1" (Sec 6, rendered pg-08), not t_0. The only related items are Sec 18's "Ablate memory access early, late, and throughout denoising" and its context/time-only reader.
errors_found.evidence: My own check (script ref02_t0shift.py in the scratchpad) uses the exact Lipman eq-8 marginal field for 0.5N(-1,0.15^2)+0.5N(1,0.15^2) and the proposal's 16-step Euler grid, with a z-independent correction delta added only at step 0 (t=0). P(+mode) goes 0.499 -> 0.552 (delta=2), 0.703 (delta=8), 0.857 (delta=16). The modes stay at ±1 throughout (mean|z| 0.977-1.055). The output is re-weighted, not translated.
errors_found.corrected: The ideal residual at t=0 is a constant mean shift. Pushed through the base flow, that shift already acts as a mode-selection lever, in the same way as steering in noise space. What an early-only, z-independent reader cannot easily do is change the shape within a mode. The prediction to register in advance is therefore 'early-only access can reweight modes but not reshape them', not 'early-only access can only translate'.

errors_found.reader_claim: Claim check 1 (eq 11 cited to [1, 2]) is judged 'partially_accurate'. Correction (b) says to 'keep sigma_min = 0 and cite rectified flow (Liu et al. 2022) or stochastic interpolants'.
errors_found.problem: The proposal cites [1, 2] together, and [1] (the Holderrieth & Erives MIT notes) gives eq (11) exactly, with sigma_min = 0. The mismatch exists only if [2] is read in isolation, so an extra citation is not needed.
errors_found.evidence: ref01.txt, Algorithm 3: 'Flow Matching Training Procedure (for Gaussian CondOT path pt(x|z) = N(tz, (1 − t)^2))... Set x = tz + (1 − t)ϵ ... L(θ) = ∥uθt(x) − (z − ϵ)∥^2'. Lipman eq 23: 'LCFM(θ) = Et,q(x1),p(x0) ‖vt(ψt(x0)) − (x1 − (1 − σmin)x0)‖^2', whose sigma_min -> 0 limit is eq (11), with x0 ~ p(x0) independent of x1.
errors_found.corrected: The verdict should be 'accurate'. The only nuance worth a footnote is that [2] itself uses sigma_min > 0.

errors_found.reader_claim: Technical issue 1 / claim check 1: '...its App A proof assumes bounded u_t. For singular or discrete targets, both fail at t = 1 when sigma_min = 0'.
errors_found.problem: This presents the boundedness failure as specific to sigma_min = 0, and it is not. Lipman's own OT conditional field (eq 21) and the marginal fields built from it are affine, or grow linearly, in x, so they are unbounded on R^d for every sigma_min. App A's boundedness is a convenience assumption that Lipman's own Gaussian paths do not literally satisfy. What is genuinely specific to sigma_min = 0 is that p_1 is no longer a positive density and that the field blows up like 1/(1-t) as t -> 1.
errors_found.evidence: App A: 'we assume that q(x) and pt(x|x1) are decreasing to zero at a sufficient speed as ‖x‖ → ∞, and that ut, vt, ∇θvt are bounded'. Eq 21: ut(x|x1) = (x1 − (1 − σmin)x)/(1 − (1 − σmin)t), which is affine in x. Sec 2: 'the probability density path p : [0, 1] × R^d → R>0'. After eq 21: 'which ... is defined for all t ∈ [0, 1]', a statement that relies on σmin > 0.
errors_found.corrected: The sigma_min = 0 mismatch consists of the positivity of p_1 (Sec 2 and Theorem 2) and the time singularity at t=1. Unbounded fields are a looseness already present in Lipman's own setting.

errors_found.reader_claim: Technical issue 2 (retention bound) proposes these remedies: 'restate (27)-(28) with a time-dependent one-sided Lipschitz constant ...; restrict to t in [0, 1-delta] or the solver grid; or use sigma_min > 0'.
errors_found.problem: The numbers the reader gives are correct: I reproduced max|b_t| = 3.408 at t ≈ 0.831, C_L ≈ 134, ∫kappa^2 = 5.236, a bound of ≈ 700, ≈ 83 for the |b_t|-Gronwall version, ≈ 1.23 for the one-sided version, and marginal Jacobians of 44, 890 and 3824. The remedies, however, only rescue the unimodal case. For multimodal targets, sigma_min > 0 or component noise makes L finite but still huge, and the Jacobian at the mode boundary is positive, so the one-sided constant is equally large. With the proposal's uniform L the problem is structural: Lip(φ_1) ≤ e^L, and any continuous flow that splits N(0,I) into well-separated modes needs a large endpoint Lipschitz constant. The reader half-concedes this ('even the one-sided constant grows'), but still lists sigma_min > 0 as a fix.
errors_found.evidence: My exact computation of the Lipman eq-8 marginal field (OT path, independent coupling) for 0.5N(-1,s^2)+0.5N(1,s^2) gives a peak Jacobian at x=0 of ≈112 at t≈0.91 for s=0.15, ≈2745 at t≈0.97 for s=0.05, and ≈16 at t≈0.83 for s=0.3 (script ref02_mix.py). With L≈112, C_L = (e^{2L}-1)/(2L) is about e^{224}.
errors_found.corrected: For the proposal's multimodal Stage-B targets, the uniform-L bound (27)-(28) is vacuous whatever sigma_min or reformulation is chosen. A time-dependent constant C = ∫exp(2∫_s^1 L_r dr)ds helps only if most of the expansion happens early, and the independent-coupling FM field places it late. The bound should be presented as applying to unimodal or near-affine fields only, or replaced by empirical retention metrics.

errors_found.reader_claim: Key result: 'Training efficiency on ImageNet-128: FM used 500k iterations at batch size 1.5k ... 33% less image throughput. The adaptive-solver NFE stays roughly constant during FM training but varies during score-matching training (Fig 10).'
errors_found.problem: Fig 10 comes from CIFAR-10 training, not ImageNet-128. The bullet also leaves out that the ImageNet-128 FM model was 25% larger.
errors_found.evidence: 'while FM (with 25% larger model) used 500k iterations with batch size 1.5k, i.e., 33% less image throughput'. Fig 10 caption: 'Function evaluations for sampling during training, for models trained on CIFAR-10 using dopri5 solver with tolerance 1e−5.'
errors_found.corrected: ImageNet-128 used 33% less image throughput with a 25% larger model. Separately, on CIFAR-10 (Fig 10) the NFE stays constant during FM training and varies during score-matching training.

errors_found.reader_claim: Key result, 2D checkerboard: 'the OT path "introduces the checkerboard pattern much earlier" along the path and gives more stable training (Fig 4)'.
errors_found.problem: The paper credits stability to the FM objective, as opposed to score matching, and not to the OT path.
errors_found.evidence: Fig 4 caption: 'The OT path introduces the checkerboard pattern much earlier, while FM results in more stable training.'
errors_found.corrected: The OT path produces structure earlier. FM, with either path, trains more stably than score matching.

errors_found.reader_claim: Relevance: 'A Monte Carlo regression with 2M samples matches b_t and kappa_t mu to about 3 decimals at t = 0.2, 0.6 and 0.9. Because sigma = 0.15 > 0, p_t > 0 everywhere, so Theorem 2's assumptions hold in the sanity check.'
errors_found.problem: Both points are minor overstatements. At t=0.9 with 2M samples, the standard error of the slope is ≈0.004; my rerun gave -2.817 against the analytic -2.826, so agreement is about 2 decimals there. Separately, Sec 19 never trains by CFM regression: it uses analytic fields, gradient writes on reconstruction error, and least-squares consolidation. Whether Theorem 2's assumptions hold is therefore moot, and bounded u_t fails in any case.
errors_found.evidence: Derivation: E[a-eps|x_t=x] = mu + (tσ^2-(1-t))/s_t^2 (x - t mu) = b_t x + kappa_t mu, which is exact. Proposal pg-21: 'Gradient writes learn from noisy demonstration actions using half squared reconstruction error ... consolidated by minimum-change least squares'.
errors_found.corrected: Eqs (29)-(30) are exactly Lipman's eq-8 marginal field for a Gaussian target with sigma_min = 0. This is an analytic identity; the Monte Carlo check is only a loose confirmation, and Theorem 2 plays no role in the executed check.

claim_check_overrides.claim: Sec 7: 'construct the usual independent-endpoint conditional FM training sample [1, 2]: x_t = (1-t) eps + t a*_k, u_t = a*_k - eps (11)'.
claim_check_overrides.reason: The claim cites [1] and [2] together. [1] (Algorithm 3, 'Gaussian CondOT path') gives exactly x = tz + (1-t)ε with target z - ε. [2] eqs 20-23 give the same construction with sigma_min > 0, t ~ U[0,1], and x0 ~ p(x0) drawn independently of x1. Calling it 'the usual' construction is justified. The sigma_min > 0 point applies to [2] taken alone and deserves a footnote, not a downgrade.

missed_points: Sec 2 of Lipman defines a probability density path as 'p : [0, 1] × R^d → R>0', and the text after eq 21 says the OT conditional field 'is defined for all t ∈ [0, 1]'. Both statements hold only because sigma_min > 0. They are the most direct textual support for the reader's sigma_min concern, and the reader quotes neither.

Non-uniqueness of the generating field ('There is an infinite number of vector fields that generate any particular probability path (e.g., by adding a divergence free component ...)', Sec 4) has direct consequences for the proposal, which the reader does not draw. (a) Sec 18's 'integrated velocity correction' can be nonzero while the action distribution does not change at all, so it is not evidence that memory is being used. (b) The retention penalty R_old (eq 25) penalizes field differences that may leave pi_old unchanged, so it is sufficient for retention but not necessary. It over-constrains consolidation and could be contrasted with distribution-level replay (old endpoints plus fresh noise), which the proposal mentions only in passing. (c) Endpoint distillation and path distillation can reach the same marginals through different fields.

The Gronwall-type retention bound is inherently vacuous for well-separated multimodal policies (this is my inference, not a statement in Lipman). With a uniform L, Lip(φ_1) ≤ e^L, and any continuous flow that maps N(0,I) to modes separated by a low-density gap needs a large endpoint Lipschitz constant. For the Lipman eq-8 field with 0.15-std bimodal components, the boundary Jacobian peaks at ≈112. The proposal's own Stage-B includes 'a multimodal target family', so the bound (27)-(28) cannot certify retention there.

The co-cited reference [1] already supplies the exact sigma_min = 0 form of eq (11), so the reader's recommendation to add rectified flow or stochastic interpolants for that case is unnecessary. Those works may still be worth adding for reflow and couplings.

Some empirical caveats are left out: the ImageNet-128 efficiency comparison used a 25% larger FM model; Table 1 baselines 'are allowed more iterations'; and FM-OT's NLL advantage on ImageNet is 0.01-0.02 bpd (Table 4: at K=1 on ImageNet-32, FM-OT ties DDPM at 3.62). On super-resolution, FM-OT is worse than SR3 on PSNR/SSIM (24.7 vs 26.4 and 0.747 vs 0.762), even though Lipman calls them 'similar'. None of this affects the proposal, because it does not rest on OT-path superiority.

In Theorem 2, the parameter-independent constant is the irreducible conditional variance of the target. Because the proposal's meta-loss (12) cannot go below E Var[a*-eps | x_t, t, c_k, H_k], raw L_meta values are not comparable across readers or history lengths unless this floor is estimated or the loss is reported relative to it. This matters for the Sec 18 'fair comparisons'. The reader's point about H_k versus W_k targets is correct and related.
verification.novelty_threat_assessment: None. Lipman et al. is a foundational paper on generative-model training. It introduces the FM and CFM objectives, Gaussian conditional paths and the OT conditional path, and it has image experiments plus one conditional (super-resolution) experiment. It contains nothing on fast weights, test-time training, memory, continual learning, consolidation, retention or robot policies. The proposal uses it only as the standard training objective (eqs 11-12, 21-22) and makes no novelty claim for those objectives: Sec 11 explicitly calls endpoint distillation 'a standard FM construction'. Two things stay routine applications of Lipman plus conditional FM rather than contributions: training a residual velocity field with extra conditioning inputs by CFM, and distilling teacher samples with fresh-noise CFM. The proposal's contribution has to rest on the fast/slow memory lifecycle, the centered external reader, and the factorial reader comparisons. The paper matters more for technical soundness than for novelty. Its eq-8 marginal field, analysed for the proposal's multimodal targets, shows that the uniform-L retention bound (27)-(28) is vacuous. The reader's numbers on this are correct, but its suggested fixes (sigma_min > 0, a one-sided Lipschitz constant) do not rescue the multimodal case.

ref.title: Sun et al., Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States (2024)
ref.role: Primary internal-TTT baseline: gradient-written fast models (TTT-Linear, TTT-MLP) as recurrent states. The proposal's writer (eq 7-8) is essentially a TTT inner loop.
ref.focus: Exact inner-loop loss (multi-view reconstruction with theta_K, theta_V, theta_Q), mini-batch TTT, dual form, learnable init W_0, learnable inner LR, outer loop training, relation to linear attention, results & compute. Precisely compare with the proposal's writer/reader: what is actually different? Is the proposal's "external velocity readout" meaningfully distinct?

reading.summary:
Problem. Self-attention keeps every past token in a growing KV cache, so its cost per token grows over time. RNN layers compress the context into a fixed-size state, but "their performance in long context is limited by the expressive power of their hidden states". The paper shows Mamba's perplexity by token index flattening after 16k tokens, while a Transformer's keeps falling.

Method. The hidden state is itself a model f with weights W. The update rule is a gradient step on a self-supervised loss, and the output rule is a prediction by f. Because the state is trained even on test sequences, the layers are called Test-Time Training (TTT) layers. The self-supervised task is a multi-view reconstruction, ||f(theta_K x_t; W) - theta_V x_t||^2, with a separate test view theta_Q x_t used for output. The views are learned in an outer loop (next-token prediction) by differentiating through the inner gradient steps ("gradients of gradients"). The initial state W_0 (theta_init) and a token-dependent inner learning rate eta(x) = eta_base * sigmoid(theta_lr . x) are also learned in the outer loop.

Two instantiations are given. TTT-Linear uses f_res(x) = Wx. TTT-MLP uses a two-layer MLP with 4x hidden width and GELU. Both wrap the model as f(x) = x + LN(f_res(x)). Efficiency comes from two techniques. Mini-batch TTT (b = 16) takes each gradient with respect to the W at the end of the previous mini-batch. A "dual form" computes W_b and the outputs z_1..z_b with matmuls and a causal mask, without materializing the per-token gradients or weights; it trains more than 5x faster in JAX. Theorem 1: a linear f with batch GD, eta = 1/2 and W_0 = 0 is exactly linear attention. Theorem 2: a Nadaraya-Watson learner with an exponential kernel is exactly softmax self-attention. This motivates a general "learner" abstraction (train/predict) that covers parametric and nonparametric learners.

Results. The paper reports language-modeling perplexity at 125M-1.3B parameters on the Pile (2k and 8k context) and on Books3 (1k-32k), following the Mamba paper's Chinchilla protocol. At 2k context, TTT-Linear with the Mamba backbone, Mamba and the Transformer are comparable. At 8k and 32k, both TTT variants beat Mamba, and TTT keeps reducing perplexity with token index up to 32k, as the Transformer does. An ablation ladder (Table 1) goes from linear attention (15.91 perplexity) to TTT-Linear (11.09). The largest gains come from mini-batch TTT (-1.70) and from LN plus residual inside f (-1.22). A learnable W_0 costs +0.04 but is needed for stable training. Wall clock: on TPU, TTT-Linear trains 10% faster per iteration than the Transformer at 2k. On an A100, inference latency per token stays roughly constant for the TTT variants, but TTT-MLP carries a memory-I/O overhead.

What the paper does not address. It frames TTT as learning to learn at "the same level" as regular training, and as a special case of fast-weight programmers (W fast, theta slow). It has no robotics, generative or denoising experiments. It has no continual learning or consolidation: W restarts from the shared W_0 for every sequence and is discarded afterwards.
reading.core_mechanism:
Generic layer (Fig. 3): hidden state W_t, update rule W_t = W_{t-1} - eta * grad_W l(W_{t-1}; x_t) (eq 2), output rule z_t = f(x_t; W_t) (eq 1). Write happens before read for the same token: Fig. 5 code runs state.train(tok) and then state.predict(tok).

Naive loss (eq 3): l(W; x_t) = ||f(x~_t; W) - x_t||^2, where x~_t is a corrupted input, "similar to denoising autoencoders".

Learned multi-view loss (eq 4): l(W; x_t) = ||f(theta_K x_t; W) - theta_V x_t||^2. theta_K x_t is the training view, theta_V x_t the label view. Output rule (eq 5): z_t = f(theta_Q x_t; W_t), with theta_Q x_t the test view. theta_K, theta_V and theta_Q are low-rank linear projections learned in the outer loop. In the Mamba-style backbone, theta_K and theta_Q are merged into one projection (Fig. 13 caption).

Inner and outer loops. The inner loop updates only W. The outer loop trains theta_rest, theta_K, theta_Q, theta_V, theta_init (= W_0) and theta_lr on next-token prediction, backpropagating through the inner gradient steps (Table 2, Sec 2.2).

Inner model: f(x) = x + LN(f_res(x)). f_res is W x (square W) for TTT-Linear, or a 2-layer MLP with 4x hidden width and GELU for TTT-MLP. The layers are multi-head (Table 3 lists heads), so W sits at head dimension; this is my inference from the head counts, not stated explicitly.

Learnable learning rate: eta(x) = eta_base * sigmoid(theta_lr . x). eta_base = 1 for TTT-Linear and 0.1 for TTT-MLP, chosen as the largest stable value from {0.01, 0.1, 1, 10}. TTT-MLP uses a 10% warmup of eta_base. The paper notes eta(x) "can also be interpreted as a gate for grad l".

Mini-batch GD (eq 6): W_t = W_{t-1} - eta G_t = W_0 - eta * sum_{s<=t} G_s, with G_t = grad l(W_{t'}; x_t) and t' = t - mod(t, b). b = 1 is online GD, b = T is batch GD, and the paper uses b = 16.

Dual form (linear case, theta = I): W_b = W_0 - 2 eta (W_0 X - X) X^T and Z = W_0 X - 2 eta Delta, where Delta = (W_0 X - X) mask(X^T X) and mask is upper-triangular with zeros. Cost is O(b d^2 + b^2 d). Appendix A extends this to K-layer MLPs with element-wise nonlinearities, and to other functions via vector-Jacobian products.

Theorem 1: with f(x) = Wx, batch GD, eta = 1/2 and W_0 = 0, W_t = sum_s (theta_V x_s)(theta_K x_s)^T, so z_t = sum_s (theta_V x_s)(theta_K x_s)^T (theta_Q x_t). This is linear attention.

Theorem 2: with the Nadaraya-Watson estimator f(x; x_1..x_t) = sum_s kappa(x, x_s) y_s / sum_s kappa(x, x_s), y_s = theta_V x_s and kappa proportional to exp((theta_K x)^T theta_Q x'), the layer is exactly self-attention.

Training memory: gradient checkpointing through time; only the T/b end-of-mini-batch W's are stored.

Mapping onto the proposal:
- write cue q_e (proposal eq 7) = training view theta_K x_t
- content sg(y_e) = label view theta_V x_t
- read query q_t = Q_phi(z_t, t, c_k, h_theta) (eq 3) = test view theta_Q x_t
- slowly learned W_0 = theta_init
- eta_f = eta, but fixed in the proposal and learned per token in [3]
- the step W_{k+1} = W_k - eta_f grad l_assoc (eq 8) = online GD with b = 1, one step per experience
- differentiating L_meta (eq 12) through the writes to train phi and W_0 = the outer loop of [3]
key_results: Fig. 2 left (Pile, 8k context, 350M-1.3B): TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP have perplexity similar to Mamba at matched FLOPs. Fig. 2 right (Books, 1.3B, training FLOPs matched to Mamba 1.4B): 'TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP can keep reducing perplexity by conditioning on more tokens, while Mamba cannot after 16k context.'

Pile 2k: 'TTT-Linear (M), Mamba, and Transformer have comparable performance'; TTT-MLP (M) is slightly worse at large FLOP budgets. Pile 8k: 'both TTT-Linear (M) and TTT-MLP (M) perform significantly better than Mamba'. 'as context length grows longer, the advantage of TTT layers over Mamba widens.' The Transformer 'still has good (if not the best) perplexity at every model size' but costs more FLOPs.

Books 2k: Mamba is slightly better than TTT-Linear. Books 32k: both TTT variants beat Mamba, and TTT-MLP (T) is slightly better than Mamba. With the Mamba backbone TTT-MLP is at best comparable to TTT-Linear; with the Transformer backbone TTT-MLP is clearly better.

Table 1 ablation (125M, perplexity): linear attention 15.91; improved linear attention 15.23; TTT equivalence 15.23; +learnable W_0 15.27 (+0.04, but 'the rows below cannot train stably without it'); +LN and residual in f 14.05 (-1.22); +mini-batch TTT (b=2048 to b=16) 12.35 (-1.70); +learnable eta 11.99 (-0.36); +Mamba backbone 11.09 (-0.90).

Fig. 7: smaller inner mini-batch b gives better perplexity (b=1 is online GD and best; batch GD is worst). b=16 trades speed against quality. Batch GD 'has a smaller effective search space' because W_t is only one step from W_0.
Dual form: 'training with the dual form is more than 5x faster than with primal' in JAX. On a TPU v5e-256 at 2k context, the Transformer takes 0.30 s/iteration and TTT-Linear 0.27 s.

Fig. 12 (A100, 1.3B): prefill and decode time per token stays roughly constant for TTT and Mamba and grows linearly for the Transformer. TTT-MLP is slower: 'the additional complexity of the MLP structure increases wall-clock time much more relative to FLOPs'.
Figs. 4/14: one inner step lowers the loss from l(W_{t-1}; x_t) to l(W_t; x_t), and l(W_t; x_t) pulls further below l(W_0; x_t) as t grows. Gradient descent 'cannot reduce it to zero'.
Theorem 1 (linear f + batch GD + eta=1/2 + W_0=0 equals linear attention) and Theorem 2 (Nadaraya-Watson with exponential kernel equals self-attention).
Fig. 16: models trained from scratch get worse perplexity once context becomes too long for their size; the best context length grows with model size.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 21 table: 'TTT layers [3] — Gradient-written fast models, including linear and MLP variants.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Abstract: 'The key idea is to make the hidden state a machine learning model itself, and the update rule a step of self-supervised learning... We consider two instantiations: TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP, whose hidden state is a linear model and a two-layer MLP respectively.' Eq 2: W_t = W_{t-1} - eta grad l(W_{t-1}; x_t).
proposal_claim_checks.correction: Optional precision: both variants wrap the model as f(x) = x + LN(f_res(x)), and the MLP uses 4x hidden width with GELU. The proposal's f_W (eq 6) has neither LN nor a residual.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Reference list: '[3] Sun, Y., et al. ... 2024; arXiv:2407.04620. Fast linear and MLP models as recurrent states.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: arXiv v1 is 5 Jul 2024. Fig. 9 caption: 'TTT layers with parametric learners are also RNN layers, since their hidden state is also fixed in size.'
proposal_claim_checks.correction: Cite v4 (31 Aug 2025) if relying on the updated related work and limitations text.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 21 distinction: 'External velocity readout with the same writing and lifecycle budgets.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: [3] has no generative, velocity or robot setting, and no lifecycle: 'The TTT initialization W0 is shared between all sequences, even though subsequent weights W1,...,WT are different for each input sequence.' Its TTT layers replace self-attention inside the backbone (Sec 2.7, Fig. 13). Its related work notes Clark et al. [15] 'give a Transformer a final layer of fast weights, whose initialization is trained as slow weights.'
proposal_claim_checks.correction: The distinction exists but is narrower than the table implies. The writing (eqs 7-8, meta-learned views and W_0, outer loop through inner gradients) is [3]'s own framework and is not a distinction. An additive readout after the backbone is a restricted special case of the TTT/FWP design space: a fast-weight layer at the output, cf. Clark et al. [15]. The lifecycle is absent from [3], so 'same lifecycle budget' describes a modified TTT baseline, not [3]'s layer.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 8 table: 'Internal TTT layer — Fast memory changes transformer features; strong established comparison [3, 5, 6]. Its effects on sampling are less directly isolated, but it may be the most effective option.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: [3] is evaluated only on language-model perplexity: 'We evaluate our instantiations at the scale of 125M to 1.3B parameters'. At short context: 'At 2k context, TTT-Linear (M), Mamba, and Transformer have comparable performance'. The advantage appears only at long context: 'as context length grows longer, the advantage of TTT layers over Mamba widens.'
proposal_claim_checks.correction: [3] establishes TTT as strong for long-context language modeling (8k-32k tokens), not for few-shot (1-16 experience) adaptation or for denoising and flow-matching policies. In the short-context regime, [3] shows parity with Mamba and the Transformer, not superiority. Evidence of strength in the proposal's regime must come from [5]/[6] or from the planned experiments.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 6: 'An internal TTT layer changes hidden features that determine the velocity. It therefore also changes the denoising path. Our proposed interface exposes the velocity correction directly, allowing explicit reset centering, departure measurements, and reader swaps. The difference is the intervention location and lifecycle, not whether denoising is affected at all.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: In [3] a TTT layer's output z_t = f(theta_Q x_t; W_t) feeds into later layers (Sec 2.3: the test view 'is mapped to the current output token z_t and propagated forward through network layers'). With W = W_0 the layer gives the network's no-history behavior as trained, because W_0 = theta_init is shared across sequences.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: The first and last sentences are correct. Explicit reset centering is not unique to an external readout. An internal TTT layer can be centered the same way: add O(f_{W_k}(theta_Q h) - f_{W_0}(theta_Q h)) to the hidden stream, which vanishes exactly at W = W_0. Departure can be measured internally by comparing v with W_k against v with W_0, at the cost of an extra backbone pass. The external readout makes these cheaper and more modular, but a fair comparison must include a centered internal TTT layer, or location will be confounded with centering.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 17: 'Internal TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP — Same writer data, meta-training targets, and lifecycle; compare both parameter and latency budgets.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: [3] defines TTT layers as causal sequence layers ('We define a sequence modeling layer as an autoregressive mapping from one sequence to another'). Every processed token is written before it is read (Fig. 5: state.train(tok) then state.predict(tok)), and weights restart at W_0 for each sequence.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: [3]'s layer cannot be used unchanged with 'the same writer data and lifecycle'. The proposal must specify: (a) only experience records write, and the current candidate's tokens do not, since Sec 15 says to 'Hold fast weights fixed during this solve'; (b) how experience records reach the internal layer's key/value space (the backbone must be run on the records to get hidden states at the insertion layer); (c) persistence across decisions instead of per-sequence reset; (d) how a causal TTT scan treats bidirectionally attended action-chunk tokens. The latency comparison is sensible; [3] reports that TTT-MLP carries a large wall-clock overhead relative to FLOPs.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 2: 'An internal TTT module can also implement useful association.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Eq 4 is a key-to-value reconstruction, and footnote 4 says 'The subscript K hints at a connection to self-attention'. theta_K and theta_V are 'analogous to the Key and Value parameters of self-attention'. Theorem 1 gives exact equivalence to linear attention in the linear/batch-GD case.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 5: 'A nonlinear MLP does not by itself prove an expressive separation from attention-based formulations [4].'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: [3] proves equivalence only for linear f with batch GD (Theorem 1) and argues for greater MLP expressivity empirically: 'The larger capacity of a more expressive hidden state is well-utilized in long context'. It offers no separation theorem.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: Also cite [3] here. Its Theorem 1 and Table 1 ladder show exactly which ingredients (online or mini-batch GD, LN plus residual, learnable eta) move a TTT layer away from linear attention.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Implicit (Sec 5 and Sec 7): the association writer (eqs 7-8) with slow encoders, a learned W_0 and meta-gradients 'through the earlier gradient writes' is presented as the proposal's own design; [3] is not cited in Sec 5 or Sec 7.
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: [3] Sec 2.3: 'we learn the self-supervised task as part of the outer loop'. The training view is theta_K x_t and the label view theta_V x_t. Sec 2.7: 'Learnable W0... we can learn it as part of the outer loop'. Sec 2.2: 'calling backward on grad l means taking gradients of gradients'.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: Attribute the writer to [3]'s learned multi-view reconstruction inner loop, and to FWP and meta-learning precedents cited there (Clark et al. 2022; Schlag et al. 2021; Irie et al. 2021). Describe the proposal's changes as deviations: nonlinear view encoders, a frozen pretrained label view, a tanh MLP without LN/residual, and a fixed eta_f.

reading.relevance_to_proposal:
Section 5, eqs 6-8 (writer). The writer is almost exactly [3]'s TTT inner loop. The proposal's l_assoc(W, e) = 1/2 ||f_W(q_e) - sg(y_e)||^2 maps onto [3]'s eq 4, l(W; x) = ||f(theta_K x; W) - theta_V x||^2: the masked cue q_e is the training view and y_e is the label view. The read query q_t = Q_phi(...) in eq 3 is the test view theta_Q x (eq 5 of [3]). The proposal's slowly learned W_0 is [3]'s theta_init. The step in eq 8 is [3]'s online GD with b = 1, one step per experience. The outer loop that trains phi and W_0 through the writes (Sec 7, eq 12) is [3]'s outer loop (Sec 2.2, Table 2), with an FM velocity loss in place of next-token prediction.

The real deviations in the writer:
(i) The views are general encoders, not linear projections. [3] explicitly invites this: 'Future work might experiment with more flexible transformations'.
(ii) The label view is a frozen pretrained encoder under stop-gradient. [3] instead learns theta_V through the outer loss, with no collapse problem, because the outer loss (not l) trains theta_V.
(iii) f_W = tanh(qA+b)B + d_0 without the LN plus residual that [3] found worth -1.22 perplexity.
(iv) A fixed eta_f, with no learned, input-dependent write gate.
(v) The write stream differs. It is past experience records, not the tokens currently being processed, and the read query comes from a different object: the noisy candidate z_t at time t. In [3], theta_K and theta_Q act on the same token, and the Mamba backbone even merges them.

Section 6 ('What is different from internal TTT?') and Section 8 (reader table). [3] backs the proposal's candid statement that the difference is 'intervention location and lifecycle'. Is the external velocity readout meaningfully distinct? Only partly.
- Distinct, for engineering reasons: (a) it bolts onto a frozen pretrained FM backbone, and at W_0 it reproduces the pretrained base exactly; (b) the reader and query modules can be swapped; (c) departure ||r|| costs one extra reader call, not a second backbone pass.
- Not distinct: the write rule, the meta-learning, persistence (shared with RoboTTT [6]), or 'querying with the evolving candidate'. Any TTT layer inside the FM transformer is re-queried with features of z_t at every solver step.
- Centering is not exclusive either: an internal TTT layer can be centered and reset exactly.

Architecturally, the external readout is a fast-weight layer placed at the network output, with additive, centered injection into velocity space (cf. Clark et al. 2022, cited in [3]). It is a restriction of the internal-TTT design space. The likely cost is expressivity: the correction cannot reshape internal features within a solver step and sees the backbone only through pooled h_theta. The honest framing is therefore 'modularity and measurability of a frozen-backbone adapter', to be tested against a centered internal TTT layer at several insertion depths. The final-layer position is the limiting case, and it should not be framed as a distinct mechanism.

Section 7 and Sec 20, step 2 (higher-order differentiation). [3] shows that differentiating through inner gradient steps is routine at LM scale ('taking gradients of gradients'), with gradient checkpointing through time. With a frozen theta, the direct reader's meta-gradient never passes back through the backbone: h_theta is an input feature and phi sits downstream. The worry about attention backends and double-backward therefore applies mainly to the internal-TTT baseline.

Section 17 (baselines). This is the primary source for the internal TTT-Linear/MLP baseline. Theorem 2 provides a principled 'history tokens / retrieval' baseline: a Nadaraya-Watson / softmax learner over the same views. Table 1 provides the ablation ladder from linear attention to the full writer. With only 1-16 experiences, [3]'s core motivation (compressing very long context into a fixed state) does not apply. Attention over the stored experiences is cheap, and in [3] the short-context regime shows parity, not superiority.

Section 18 (falsifiable outcomes). The 'internal TTT >= external reader' criterion needs the specification fixes listed under technical issues, or the comparison will not be interpretable.

Sections 11-14 (consolidation, retention, refresh). [3] provides nothing here: its fast weights are per-sequence and discarded, so it does not pre-empt the lifecycle contribution. It also gives no evidence about long-lived persistent fast weights (Stage D, 10 or more task arrivals). That is a regime [3] never tests: no decay, no forgetting gate, no capacity study.

Sec 19 (sanity check). This is unaffected, since it uses no TTT-style learned writer.
novelty_threats: The fast-memory writer (eqs 7-8) with meta-learned views and W_0, trained by differentiating a downstream loss through the gradient writes, is [3]'s framework: a learned multi-view reconstruction as the inner loop, next-token prediction as the outer loop, theta_init and theta_lr learned. The proposal cannot claim novelty for 'gradient-written associative memory whose interfaces are meta-trained for future performance'.

[3] already frames the two parameter sets as slow and fast: 'Our inner-loop weights W can be viewed as "fast" and outer-loop weights theta as "slow"', and it presents networks with TTT layers as fast-weight programmers. The slow/fast vocabulary and the parametric-memory framing are therefore not new.

An output-side fast-weight readout already exists. [3] cites Clark et al. 2022, which 'give a Transformer a final layer of fast weights, whose initialization is trained as slow weights'. The 'external readout' is a special case (final layer, additive) of TTT/FWP layer placement. What remains new is velocity-space injection with explicit centering inside an FM sampler, plus the lifecycle.

'Memory queried by the evolving candidate at every denoising step' happens automatically when any TTT layer sits inside an FM/diffusion transformer, because the layer is re-evaluated on features of z_t at every solver step. This is not a differentiator against [3]-style internal TTT.

[3]'s discussion already motivates TTT with human-like learning on non-i.i.d. streams: 'any piece of data can be used for both training and testing'. The biological and continual framing overlaps rhetorically, though not technically.
Low threat: [3] has no consolidation, replay, reset gate, retention bound or persistent cross-sequence state. These lifecycle contributions are not pre-empted by [3].
ideas_to_borrow: Learnable, experience-dependent write rate or gate: eta(e) = eta_base * sigmoid(theta_lr . e). It gave -0.36 perplexity in [3] and acts as a relevance gate for which experiences get stored. Sweep eta_base over {0.01, 0.1, 1, 10}, keep the largest stable value, and warm it up for MLP fast nets, as [3] does.

Wrap the fast net as f(q) = q + LN(f_res(q)) (possible because the proposal's net is 16 to 16). [3] found this gave -1.22 perplexity and improved inner-loop stability. The proposal's centering still makes reset exact, because it subtracts the W_0 output.

Build a Table-1-style ablation ladder from the linear-attention-equivalent writer (linear f, batch GD, W_0 = 0) up to the proposed writer (tanh MLP, online writes, learned W_0, learned eta), adding one ingredient per row. This answers the [4]/'secretly linear attention' question empirically and shows what the nonlinear fast net actually buys.

Use Theorem 2 as a matched nonparametric baseline: softmax or Nadaraya-Watson attention over the stored experience keys K(q_e) and values y_e, queried by the same Q_phi(z_t, t, c_k, h_theta). Only the learner changes (parametric vs nonparametric); the views stay fixed. With 16 or fewer experiences it is cheap, so it should be the default 'history retrieval' control.

Add an insertion-depth sweep for the internal-TTT comparison: centered TTT layers at blocks 1..L of the FM transformer, plus the external velocity readout as the output-layer limit. Match fast-parameter count (e.g., in a width-128, 4-head backbone, per-head 32x32 TTT-Linear has 1,024 fast params versus the proposal's 1,072) and latency. This isolates 'intervention location' from centering and lifecycle.

Add writer-health diagnostics modeled on Figs. 4/14: track l(W_0; e_t), l(W_{t-1}; e_t) and l(W_t; e_t) along the experience stream. The first gap shows whether writes generalize to new experiences; the second shows how much each write stores.

Report the write-batching choice. [3] shows that online or small-mini-batch GD strongly beats batch GD. When several records arrive together, declare the order and batch size b, and compare against a one-step batch write.

Consider learning the label view through the outer loss, as [3] does with theta_V, as a planned variant. [3] shows this works without a separate anti-collapse objective, because the downstream loss, not l, trains the view.
Adopt [3]'s cost reporting: training FLOPs matched between methods, and latency split into write cost (per experience) and read cost (per solver step), analogous to prefill vs decode in Fig. 12.
technical_issues_in_proposal: Attribution gap. Sections 5 and 7 present the association writer and 'differentiating future-query loss through the earlier gradient writes' without citing [3]. [3] is cited only in the Sec 8 and Sec 21 tables. Eqs 7-8 plus a learned W_0 are [3]'s eq 4 / eq 2 / Sec 2.7 with nonlinear views.

The internal-TTT baseline is under-specified and incompatible with [3] as written. In [3], a TTT layer writes every token it processes (write then read, causal), and W restarts at W_0 for each sequence. The proposal's memory writes only experience records, is read-only during the denoising solve (Sec 15: 'Hold fast weights fixed during this solve'), and persists across decisions. For 'same writer data and lifecycle', the proposal must state: which tokens write; whether candidate tokens write at each solver step; how experience records are encoded into the insertion layer's hidden space (running the backbone on the records); and how a causal TTT scan handles bidirectional action-chunk tokens.

The claimed advantages of the external interface (exact reset centering, departure measurements) are not exclusive to it. A centered internal TTT layer, h <- h + O(f_{W_k}(theta_Q h) - f_{W_0}(theta_Q h)), also resets exactly at W = W_0, and departure can be measured by running the backbone with W_k and with W_0. Unless the internal baseline is also centered, the comparison confounds location with centering. The real, defensible advantage is modularity with a frozen pretrained backbone, plus cheaper measurement.

Kernel / linear-attention equivalence of the proposed memory in its own regime. For f_W = tanh(qA+b)B + d_0, one write changes the recall at query q by exactly -eta_f (h(q).h(q_e) + 1) delta_e through the (B, d_0) parameters, where h = tanh(qA+b) and delta_e = f(q_e) - sg(y_e). That is a linear-attention / delta-rule readout with key h(q_e) and value -delta_e. The (A, b) update adds an NTK-weighted term. I checked numerically that this first-order expression matches the exact one-step change to 0.13% relative error at eta = 1e-3. With 1-16 small-eta writes, the 'nonlinear' memory therefore behaves close to a DeltaNet with a learned feature map, which is TTT-Linear with b = 1 and no LN/residual per [3]. The retrieval and attention baselines are consequently very strong comparators in Stage B, and [3]'s long-context compression motivation does not apply at 16 or fewer experiences.

The fast bias d_0 (counted among the 1,072 fast parameters) makes every write shift the recalled activation by -eta_f delta_e for every query, including unrelated ones. The centered residual is therefore nonzero for all states and contexts after any write. This is a built-in cross-query interference channel that R_phi must learn to suppress. Consider making d_0 slow, or adding LN as in [3].

The stop-gradient in eq 7 is described imprecisely. The inner gradient grad_W l_assoc never differentiates y_e, so sg does not change the write, and with a fixed pretrained target encoder it changes nothing at all. It matters only for the meta-gradient to a learnable target encoder. The caveat that a learned target 'requires ... anti-collapse checks; reconstruction alone is not enough' holds only if the target is trained on l itself. [3] trains its label view theta_V through the outer loss with no collapse issue.

Evidence regime. [3]'s advantages appear only at long context (8k-32k tokens). At 2k context, TTT-Linear is comparable to Mamba and the Transformer, and on Books 2k Mamba is slightly better. Citing [3] as a 'strong established comparison' for few-shot robot adaptation (1-16 experiences) extrapolates beyond its evidence. [3] also has no generative or denoising experiments.

The fixed eta_f with no write gate ignores [3]'s finding that an input-dependent learning rate helps. More importantly, [3] offers no evidence for persistent fast weights over a long lifetime: W is discarded after each sequence, with no decay or forgetting gate. Stage D (10 or more task arrivals with persistent writes) is untested territory for TTT-style memories, and capacity and interference controls are essential there.

Missing baseline, suggested by [3]'s related work on dynamic evaluation [47, 48] and on TTT [72] / PAD [28]. Directly fine-tune the FM backbone, or a LoRA/adapter, on the available demonstrations or corrections with the FM loss at test time, optionally from a meta-learned (MAML-style) initialization. When the experience protocol supplies expert actions, this is the obvious strong test-time-training comparator, and it is distinct from both internal TTT layers and the external reader.

Meta-gradient cost. For the direct reader with frozen theta, no backpropagation through the backbone is needed: h_theta enters only as an input feature and phi is downstream of it. The concern in Sec 20 step 2 about higher-order differentiation through the attention backend therefore applies mainly to the internal-TTT baseline, and should be labeled that way when budgets are compared.
stated_limitations: Abstract: 'TTT-MLP still faces challenges in memory I/O, but shows larger potential in long context'.

Sec 1/4.2: 'such instantiations can still require substantial wall-clock time, even after applying our improvements in efficiency. It remains to be seen whether our framework can produce instantiations that either overcome this limitation or offer benefits outweighing it.'

Novelty is limited for linear hidden states: 'The idea of using linear models as hidden states has already been well studied in DeltaNet'. 'DeltaNet ... is equivalent to TTT-Linear with inner-loop mini-batch size 1, without the Layer Norm and residual connection.'
Batch GD is weak: 'batch GD has a smaller effective search space, which ends up hurting performance for language modeling'. Gradient descent reduces the TTT loss but 'cannot reduce it to zero'.
No clean linear fit on the scaling plots, 'not even for Transformers'. Scaling cannot be extrapolated with confidence.
Only GPU inference kernels were written: 'the training kernel would require substantial effort and cannot be used on our TPUs'.
Hybrid architectures were not evaluated. Experiments were limited to 1.3B parameters and 32k context by academic resources.
Fig. 14: in middle layers, ||x_t|| rises steadily and all three TTT losses rise with it.
Fig. 16: from-scratch models degrade when context is too long for their size. The TF-finetune baseline has 2.8x the inference FLOPs.
Sec 2.3 footnote: adding a decoder g after f 'did slightly improve results' but 'made overall training less stable and added significant computational cost'.
Views are only linear projections: 'It would be a big coincidence if the first one we have tried turns out to be the best.'
cited_works_worth_adding: Clark, Guu, Chang, Pasupat, Hinton, Norouzi, 'Meta-learning fast weight language models' (arXiv:2212.02475, 2022). A final-layer fast-weight layer updated by gradient steps, with its initialization learned as slow weights. This is the closest precedent for an output-side 'external' fast-weight readout and should be cited in Sec 6 and Sec 21.

Schlag, Irie, Schmidhuber, 'Linear transformers are secretly fast weight programmers' (ICML 2021). Introduces the delta-rule fast-weight memory (DeltaNet), equivalent to TTT-Linear with b = 1 without LN/residual. It is the cheapest principled linear fast-memory baseline and matches the first-order behavior of the proposal's one-step writes.

Irie, Schlag, Csordás, Schmidhuber, 'Going beyond linear transformers with recurrent fast weight programmers' (NeurIPS 2021). MLP fast weights that predate TTT-MLP; prior art for a nonlinear fast associative net.

Irie, Csordás, Schmidhuber, 'The dual form of neural networks revisited' (ICML 2022). Shows that gradient-updated linear layers equal attention over the training patterns. It supports the kernel/attention view of eq 8 and the [4] discussion.

Irie, Faccio, Schmidhuber, 'Neural differential equations for learning to program neural nets through continuous learning rules' (NeurIPS 2022). Continuous-time fast-weight programmers, relevant to a memory acting inside an ODE sampler.

Yang, Wang, Zhang, Shen, Kim, 'Parallelizing linear transformers with the delta rule over sequence length' (arXiv:2406.06484, 2024). An efficient DeltaNet implementation for the linear fast-memory baseline.

Hansen, Jangir, Sun, Alenyà, Abbeel, Efros, Pinto, Wang, 'Self-supervised policy adaptation during deployment' (PAD, arXiv:2007.04309, 2020). Robot-policy test-time training at deployment with a self-supervised auxiliary loss; a missing robotics-TTT baseline and related-work entry.

Wang, Sun, Gandelsman, Chen, Efros, Wang, 'Test-time training on video streams' (arXiv:2307.05014, 2023). Online TTT whose weights persist across a stream of frames, the closest TTT precedent for persistent fast weights across decisions.

Sun, Wang, Liu, Miller, Efros, Hardt, 'Test-time training with self-supervision for generalization under distribution shifts' (ICML 2020), and Gandelsman, Sun, Chen, Efros, 'Test-time training with masked autoencoders' (NeurIPS 2022). The origin of TTT and of masked-reconstruction TTT, which the proposal's 'partially masked cue view' writer mirrors.
Sun et al., 'Learning to (learn at test time)' (arXiv:2310.13807, 2023). The preliminary MTTT paper: an inner-loop reconstruction task learned in an outer loop.

Krause, Kahembwe, Murray, Renals, 'Dynamic evaluation of neural sequence models' / 'Dynamic evaluation of transformer language models'. Direct test-time fine-tuning of the whole model; the analog of the missing baseline of fine-tuning the FM backbone or an adapter on available demonstrations.

Kirsch & Schmidhuber, 'Meta learning backpropagation and improving it' (NeurIPS 2021), and Andrychowicz et al., 'Learning to learn by gradient descent by gradient descent' (NeurIPS 2016). Learned update rules, relevant to the proposal's alternative learned-loss writer [17].

errors_found.reader_claim: Technical issue 4: the one-step change through (B, d_0) is a linear-attention/delta-rule readout with key h(q_e); the (A, b) update 'adds an NTK-weighted term'; 'this first-order expression matches the exact one-step change to 0.13%'; 'the nonlinear memory therefore behaves close to a DeltaNet with a learned feature map, which is TTT-Linear with b = 1 and no LN/residual per [3].'
errors_found.problem: The conclusion drops the (A, b) term, which is also first order in eta and not small. The reader's own script (ref03_kernel_check.py) gets the 0.13% match only for the full NTK expression (B, d_0 term plus A, b term). The (B, d_0) term alone, i.e. DeltaNet over h, is a much worse fit. The linearization also holds only for small eta_f, and the proposal never specifies eta_f. [3] itself uses eta_base = 1 (TTT-Linear) and 0.1 (TTT-MLP).
errors_found.evidence: My re-run over 20 random inits (scratchpad/ref03_verify_check.py), median values. |A,b term| / |B,d_0 term| = 0.53. Relative error of the (B, d_0)-only 'DeltaNet over h' approximation = 0.36 at eta = 1e-3. The full NTK first-order error is 0.001 at eta = 1e-3, 0.14 at eta = 0.1 and 3.1 at eta = 1. [3] App. C: 'The inner-loop base learning rate eta_base is set to 1 for TTT-Linear and 0.1 for TTT-MLP.' [3] only says DeltaNet 'is equivalent to TTT-Linear with inner-loop mini-batch size 1, without the Layer Norm and residual connection' (Sec 4.2). It makes no claim about MLP fast nets.
errors_found.corrected: For small eta_f, each write acts as a kernel/linear-attention update using the (matrix-valued) empirical NTK of f_W over all 1,072 fast parameters, with delta-rule error terms. It is not a DeltaNet over the 32-d tanh features. At eta_f of the order [3] uses, the approximation degrades and fails at eta = 1. The proposal already hedges this point in Sec 5 ('A nonlinear MLP does not by itself prove an expressive separation from attention-based formulations [4]'), so this supports the proposal's caution rather than exposing an error.

errors_found.reader_claim: Technical issue 5: 'The fast bias d_0 ... makes every write shift the recalled activation by -eta_f delta_e for every query ... The centered residual is therefore nonzero for all states and contexts after any write. This is a built-in cross-query interference channel ... Consider making d_0 slow, or adding LN as in [3].'
errors_found.problem: Overstated. d_0 is only one interference channel. The tanh features are not centered, so h(q).h(q_e) is generically nonzero for unrelated queries, and the A, b term also moves f at every q. The centered residual would be nonzero after a write even with no d_0. LN over the feature dimension removes only the mean across features, not a per-feature bias shift, so 'adding LN' does not obviously fix this.
errors_found.evidence: My re-run: the d_0 shift is a median of only 24% of the total one-step change at a random query (eta = 1e-3). The reader's own script prints 0.006 for the d_0 shift against 0.036 for the total change at an unrelated query.
errors_found.corrected: Making d_0 slow removes the query-independent part of the kernel (the '+1'), but cross-query interference remains through non-centered features and the NTK term. Interference controls (unrelated-query drift after writes) are needed in any case.

errors_found.reader_claim: Ideas to borrow: 'in a width-128, 4-head backbone, per-head 32x32 TTT-Linear has 1,024 fast params versus the proposal's 1,072'.
errors_found.problem: This is a parameter-count error. A 4-head TTT-Linear layer with 32x32 per-head W has 4 x 1,024 = 4,096 fast parameters per inserted layer, and more if TTT layers are inserted at several depths. That is about 4x the proposal's budget.
errors_found.evidence: [3] Table 3 lists heads per model, and the caption notes the multi-head residual block structure applies to TTT-Linear/TTT-MLP. Proposal eq 6: 16x32 + 32 + 32x16 + 16 = 1,072.
errors_found.corrected: Matching 1,072 fast parameters needs a single-head 32-d TTT-Linear layer, or 4 heads of 16x16 (1,024 total), per inserted layer. The total must also be reported when inserting at multiple depths.

errors_found.reader_claim: Bibliographic check: 'I could not check a peer-reviewed venue ... citing it as an arXiv preprint is safe.'
errors_found.problem: The paper was published at ICML 2025.
errors_found.evidence: PMLR page https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/sun25h.html, title 'Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States', 'Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning'. ICML 2025 poster: icml.cc/virtual/2025/poster/43617.

errors_found.problem: The citation gap is real: Sec 5 cites only [4] and [17], and Sec 7 cites only [1, 2]. But the proposal never claims novelty for the writer. It calls it a 'starting decision'. Sec 21 frames the distinction from [3] as 'External velocity readout with the same writing and lifecycle budgets', which concedes that the writing is shared. It also states the 'defensible contribution' elsewhere.

The column is 'Research distinction to test', and it says 'with the same writing ... budgets', i.e. writing is held fixed across the comparison. Relative to [3], an external velocity readout does not exist in [3]: [3]'s layers replace self-attention inside the backbone (Sec 2.7, Fig. 13).
