errors_found.reader_claim: Key result: under 'Books 2k/32k' the reading states 'With the Mamba backbone TTT-MLP is at best comparable to TTT-Linear; with the Transformer backbone TTT-MLP is clearly better.' Stated limitation: 'Fig. 16: ... The TF-finetune baseline has 2.8x the inference FLOPs.'
errors_found.problem: Minor misattributions. The backbone-effect statement is in Sec 3.1 (Pile, 'Effect of backbone ... in our evaluations so far'). The 2.8x inference-FLOPs note is in Appendix C, 'Experiments in Figure 2 (right)', not Fig. 16.
errors_found.evidence: [3] Sec 3.1: 'Second, with Mamba backbone, TTT-MLP at best is only comparable to TTT-Linear; but with Transformer backbone, TTT-MLP is clearly better.' App. C: 'Transformer (TF finetune) has 2.8x the inference FLOPs, giving it an advantage as our baseline.'
errors_found.corrected: Attribute each statement to its correct section. The numbers themselves are correct.

errors_found.reader_claim: Technical issue 8: 'The fixed eta_f with no write gate ignores [3]'s finding ...'
errors_found.problem: Slightly overstated. The proposal has no learned, input-dependent gate, but it does plan rate and gate selection.
errors_found.evidence: Proposal Sec 15, offline step 5: 'Select rates, capacities, and gates using validation tasks.' Sec 5: 'start with explicit capacity and write-rate sweeps.'
errors_found.corrected: The proposal selects write rates and gates as hyperparameters. [3]'s learned token-dependent eta(x) = eta_base * sigmoid(theta_lr . x) (-0.36 ppl in Table 1) is a stronger, learned alternative worth adding.

errors_found.reader_claim: '[3] trains its label view theta_V through the outer loss with no collapse issue' (relevance and technical issue 6).
errors_found.problem: This is inference, not something [3] states. [3] never discusses collapse. It trains the whole backbone jointly on next-token prediction, whereas the proposal freezes the backbone.
errors_found.evidence: [3] Sec 2.3: 'In the outer loop, theta_K, theta_V, theta_Q are optimized alongside theta_rest'. No mention of collapse anywhere in the text.
errors_found.corrected: [3] shows that an outer-loss-trained label view works in joint LM training. Whether it avoids degenerate targets with a frozen FM backbone and few experiences is untested.

errors_found.reader_claim: Technical issue 10: the concern about higher-order differentiation through the attention backend 'applies mainly to the internal-TTT baseline'.
errors_found.problem: Partly right, but incomplete. For the direct reader trained with eq 12 on interpolants x_t and a frozen theta, no gradient through the backbone is needed. The whole-path energy reader (gradient steps on Z through v_theta, eq 15) and the value reader do need backbone input gradients, and possibly solver unrolling in meta-training. The proposal itself says 'its input gradients may be needed'.
errors_found.evidence: Proposal Sec 7: 'The backbone is frozen in the first experiment, though its input gradients may be needed.' Proposal Sec 7: 'Unlike the whole-path optimization alternative, this direct-reader objective does not require unrolling a sampling solver'.
errors_found.corrected: The concern applies to the internal-TTT baseline and to the path-energy and value readers, but not to the direct reader.

claim_check_overrides.claim: Sec 21 distinction: 'External velocity readout with the same writing and lifecycle budgets.'
claim_check_overrides.reason: As a statement about [3] it is correct: [3] has no external or velocity readout, and its layers replace self-attention inside the backbone ('directly replace self-attention in a Transformer', Sec 2.7). The phrase 'same writing ... budgets' holds the writer fixed and does not claim it as a distinction, so the reader's objection that 'the writing is not a distinction' targets a claim that was not made. The remaining caveats, the Clark et al. [15] final-layer fast-weight precedent and the fact that [3] has no lifecycle (so the baseline is a modified TTT), concern novelty relative to other work and baseline specification, not accuracy about [3].

claim_check_overrides.claim: Sec 8 table: 'Internal TTT layer — Fast memory changes transformer features; strong established comparison [3, 5, 6]. Its effects on sampling are less directly isolated, but it may be the most effective option.'
claim_check_overrides.reason: [3] is a peer-reviewed (ICML 2025), widely used method that matches strong baselines at 2k ('At 2k context, TTT-Linear (M), Mamba, and Transformer have comparable performance') and beats Mamba at long context. 'Strong established comparison' does not claim superiority in few-shot robot adaptation, and the sentence is hedged ('may be'). The reader's regime caveat is valid, but it is a caveat, not an inaccuracy.

claim_check_overrides.claim: Sec 6: 'An internal TTT layer changes hidden features that determine the velocity... Our proposed interface exposes the velocity correction directly, allowing explicit reset centering, departure measurements, and reader swaps. The difference is the intervention location and lifecycle, not whether denoising is affected at all.'
claim_check_overrides.reason: The text says the interface 'allows' centering and measurement. It does not claim these are impossible internally, and it names location plus lifecycle as the only difference. The reader's point that an internal TTT layer can be centered the same way (h + O(f_{W_k} - f_{W_0})) is a sound experimental-design recommendation: include a centered internal baseline. It does not show the statement to be wrong.

claim_check_overrides.claim: Implicit (Sec 5 and Sec 7): the association writer with slow encoders, learned W_0 and meta-gradients through writes is presented as the proposal's own design; [3] is not cited in Sec 5 or Sec 7.
claim_check_overrides.reason: Verified: Sec 5 cites only [4] and [17], and Sec 7 cites only [1, 2]. So the attribution gap is real, and the writer is essentially [3]'s eq 4, eq 2 and Sec 2.7 (learned views, learned theta_init, 'gradients of gradients'). But the proposal makes no novelty claim for the writer. It calls it a 'starting decision', its Sec 21 distinction explicitly holds 'the same writing' fixed, and its stated 'defensible contribution' is the continual-FM algorithm, the transfer account and the reader experiments. 'Inaccurate' overstates this; it is a citation or attribution fix.

missed_points: Venue: [3] is published at ICML 2025 (PMLR vol. 267, sun25h), not only as an arXiv preprint. The reader said the venue could not be checked.

[3] directly questions an MLP fast net in a short-context regime. Sec 3.2: 'Compared to TTT-Linear, TTT-MLP with matched FLOPs performs worse at short context but better at long context ... The larger capacity of a more expressive hidden state is well-utilized in long context (therefore an advantage), but redundant in short context (therefore a disadvantage in our setting with matched FLOPs).' With only 1-16 experiences, [3]'s evidence favors the linear fast state. The proposal's choice of a nonlinear 16-32-16 tanh MLP needs a matched-compute TTT-Linear-style (linear f) writer as a first-class ablation. The reader noted short-context parity with Mamba/Transformer but missed this MLP-vs-linear point.

[3] Sec 4.3 and Table 2 contrast its outer loop, which is 'at the same level' as regular training and uses naturally occurring sequences, with meta-learning where 'the outer loop needs a collection of datasets or tasks ... Since it is hard to collect millions of datasets, this outer loop is hard to scale.' The proposal's meta-training depends on curated history-dependent episodes (10k synthetic delayed-association episodes, then robot episodes with expert future actions; 'Without a dependence on history, a successful policy can simply ignore memory'). That is the regime [3] flags as hard to scale, a concern for Stages D-E that the reader did not raise.

[3] Sec 2.1: 'every heuristic needs to decide which input to remember or forget. Our W remembers inputs that produce large gradients – intuitively, inputs that make W learn a lot.' Under gradient writes, high-error experiences are stored most strongly. That includes the 'wrong associations, conflicting evidence' and misleading-memory conditions the proposal trains and tests on (Secs 7 and 18). This bears on robustness and motivates a learned write gate, but the reader tied the gate only to perplexity gains.

[3] explicitly anticipates embodied use: 'For video tasks and embodied agents, whose context length can easily scale up to millions or billions, f could be a convolutional neural network' (Sec 5). It also cites robotics TTT follow-ups: manipulation [28] (PAD) and legged locomotion [71] (Sun et al. 2021, 'Online learning of unknown dynamics for model-based controllers in legged locomotion', RA-L). The reader listed PAD but missed [71], a robot online-adaptation precedent.

[3] cites Irie & Schmidhuber [40], 'Images as weight matrices: Sequential image generation through synaptic learning rules' (ICLR 2022): '[40] builds an image generator using the images as fast weights'. This is a fast-weight-programmer precedent inside a generative process, relevant to the related work on memory inside generative sampling. The reader missed it (it listed [37] and [38]).

Internal inconsistency in [3] that the reader reported without flagging. The Fig. 2 caption says TTT 'have similar perplexity in 8k context' to Mamba, while Sec 3.1 says 'At 8k context, both TTT-Linear (M) and TTT-MLP (M) perform significantly better than Mamba'. Cite the Sec 3.1 wording cautiously.

Figure 7 (verified from the rendered page) shows perplexity rising monotonically from about 10.9 at b = 1 to about 11.7 at b = 2048, with 11.09 at b = 16. The gap between the proposal's online b = 1 writes and [3]'s b = 16 is small (about 0.2 ppl). The large Table 1 gain (-1.70) is from b = 2048 to b = 16 in a different configuration. This matters for the reader's suggestion to compare against a one-step batch write.

On the proposal's technical side, the reader's own NTK check shows that the (A, b) hidden-layer update is about half as large as the (B, d_0) readout term at first order (median ratio 0.53 in my re-run). The proposal's fast MLP therefore does adapt its features, not only a linear readout, even in the lazy regime. Any 'secretly linear attention' reduction must use the full 1,072-d tangent features.
verification.novelty_threat_assessment:
Medium overall, unevenly distributed across components.
(1) The fast-memory writer (eqs 6-8, a learned W_0, and meta-gradients through the writes in Sec 7) is high overlap. It is [3]'s learned multi-view reconstruction inner loop (eq 4: ||f(theta_K x; W) - theta_V x||^2), the output rule on a separate test view (eq 5), a learned theta_init, and an outer loop that takes 'gradients of gradients', with prior FWP precedents cited in [3] ([15], [38], [62]). The proposal does not explicitly claim this as new: Sec 21 holds 'the same writing' fixed and places its contribution elsewhere. So [3] exposes a local attribution gap in Secs 5 and 7 rather than negating a stated contribution.
(2) The external, centered velocity-space readout inside an FM sampler is low-to-medium. [3] has no such readout and no generative or robot experiments. It does cite Clark et al. [15] ('a final layer of fast weights, whose initialization is trained as slow weights') as an output-side placement precedent. The proposal already frames reader superiority as a falsifiable empirical question.
(3) Consolidation, replay, reset gates, retention bounds and persistent cross-decision state are low: [3] resets W to W_0 for every sequence ('The TTT initialization W0 is shared between all sequences') and has no lifecycle.
[3]'s strongest threat is evidential, not priority. Its Theorem 1/2 equivalences, the DeltaNet equivalence and the finding that MLP hidden states are 'redundant in short context' imply that with 1-16 experiences, linear fast weights, DeltaNet and softmax-attention/retrieval baselines are likely to be very competitive. The proposal's nonlinear writer and external reader must beat these under matched compute.

ref.title: Liu et al., Test-Time Training with KV Binding Is Secretly Linear Attention (2026, arXiv 2602.21204)
ref.role: Theory threat: TTT with KV-binding may reduce to (linear) attention. Proposal says: "attention-like representation under stated final-layer assumptions, allowing update-dependent features"; "No blanket claim that nonlinear fast memory escapes all attention equivalences."
ref.focus: State the exact theorem(s) and assumptions (which layers linear? single step? multi-step? MLP fast net?). Does the equivalence apply to the proposal's 16-32-16 tanh MLP fast net with gradient writes (eq 6-8)? What empirical claims do they make? Is the proposal's characterization accurate?

reading.summary:
PROBLEM. The paper looks at test-time training used as a sequence-modeling layer, where the inner loop fits a self-supervised key-value binding objective. Prior work calls this TTT-KVB (examples: TTT-Linear/MLP, LaCT, ViT^3/ViTTT, Titans). The usual reading is that the inner loop "memorizes" a key-to-value map in fast weights and the query "retrieves" from it. The authors argue this reading is empirically wrong. Their alternative: TTT-KVB is a learned linear attention operator. They restrict scope explicitly: "This paper focuses on the first variant" (KV-binding loss) and not TTT-E2E (Tandon et al., 2025).

EMPIRICAL "MEMORIZATION PARADOX" (Sec 4). The tests use pretrained or retrained LaCT-LLM (760M), LaCT-NVS (114M) and ViTTT-B (90M). (i) Fig. 1: more inner-loop steps at inference lowers the inner loss but makes perplexity and PSNR worse. (ii) Table 1: flipping the inner loop to gradient ascent and retraining from scratch keeps or slightly improves performance: ppl 16.43->16.19, PSNR 25.94->25.85, top-1 79.34->79.61. (iii) Fig. 2: t-SNE shows Q and K clearly mismatched in distribution in every LaCT-NVS block, so the fast function is evaluated out of distribution. (iv) Table 1: replacing Q with K barely changes results (16.18 ppl, 25.95 dB, 79.18%). Their conclusion: "these failures suggest that in practice TTT does not operate as test-time memorization."

THEORY (Sec 5, App B-G). Theorem 5.1 assumes an inner-loop function with a "linear, bias-free final layer" f(x) = phi(x;Theta) W, and one gradient step on any loss L(f_t(k)) that updates all parameters. After that step, the output at any query has linear-attention form. The query feature phi_{t+1}(q) is taken at the updated Theta. The key feature phi_t(k) and the value g_t(k) = -eta dL/df_t(k) are taken at the pre-update state. Theorem 5.2 unrolls this over a sequence with one GD step per token. Theorem 5.3 adds momentum, which only reweights the values. They rewrite LaCT (SwiGLU, Frobenius-inner-product loss, momentum, Muon, weight norm) and ViTTT (GLU plus depthwise conv, the conv being sliding-window linear attention) in this form. Sec 5.2 uses the view to explain the anomalies. More inner steps at test time create a different attention operator (train-test mismatch). Gradient ascent flips the sign of the value, which the learned projections absorb. Q/K asymmetry is expected because q and k feed different slots, phi_{t+1}(q) versus phi_t(k).

PRACTICE (Sec 6, App H-I). They simplify LaCT/ViTTT step by step down to plain linear attention (Table 2). Updating only the last layer (Variant 1) gives the best performance on all three tasks. The full reduction to vanilla linear attention (Variant 6) costs +0.4 ppl and -0.2 dB relative to the original baseline, or +0.87 ppl and -0.24 dB relative to Variant 1. When the kernel is static (only the last layer updated) and there is no weight normalization, the state update is associative. That gives a parallel prefix-scan form: up to 4.0x TTT-layer throughput and a 1.19x end-to-end training speedup. Updating the kernel parameters or applying weight normalization breaks associativity (App I). Stated limitation: the "analysis ... is limited to settings where the inner-loop final layer is linear and bias-free". Titans and Atlas are said to satisfy the assumptions but were not tested.
reading.core_mechanism:
Setting (Sec 3). Tokens are projected to q, k, v. Fast weights f_theta are updated online by GD on L = ||f(k) - v||^2 or on a dot-product loss (LaCT/ViTTT use L = -<f(k), v>). The output is f_updated(q).

Thm 5.1 (one step, all parameters updated). Assume f_t(x) = phi(x; Theta_t) W_t with W in R^{Dh x Dout}. "Linear, bias-free final layer" is the only structural assumption. One GD step (W_{t+1}, Theta_{t+1}) = (W_t, Theta_t) - eta grad L(f_t(k)) gives, for any query q:
  o = phi_{t+1}(q) (W_t + phi_t(k)^T g_t(k)),   g_t(k) := -eta dL/df_t(k)
so q_hat = phi_{t+1}(q), k_hat = phi_t(k), v_hat = g_t(k), S_0 = W_t. The proof (App B) only uses grad_W L = phi_t(k)^T dL/df_t(k). The same proof covers MSE, dot-product, or any loss that depends on W only through f_t(k).

Thm 5.2 (sequence, one GD step per input): o_t = phi_{t+1}(q_t) (W_0 + sum_{i=0..t} phi_i(k_i)^T g_i(k_i)). The kernel phi_i is taken at the parameters in force when token i was written. The query kernel phi_{t+1} is taken at the latest parameters.

Thm 5.3 (momentum dW_t = grad + alpha_t dW_{t-1}): same form, with v_hat_i = m_i = g_i * sum_{j=i..t} beta_i^j and beta_i^j = prod_{s=i+1..j} alpha_s.

LaCT (Eq. 1, App E): o_t = phi_{t+1}(q_t)(W_{1,0} + sum_i M(phi_i(k_i)^T m_i)) with m_i = v_i sum_j eta_j beta_i^j. Caveat I found: App E.3 moves the nonlinear Muon operator M inside the sum ("M(.) is applied element-wise to each key-value outer product before accumulation"). The stated update actually applies M to the accumulated momentum W_{t+1} = W_t - eta M(dW_t). The LaCT-with-Muon rewrite is therefore not an exact identity. Weight normalization turns the state into S_{t+1} = Norm(S_t + phi^T m), still a linear read of a state but no longer a sum over history (App E.4).

Reduction (Sec 6.1). With only the last layer updated, phi is static and becomes a learned kernel. A single linear layer removes phi. With the Frobenius loss g_t = -v, so v_hat = v. The end point is o = q(W + sum_i k_i^T v_i). Parallel form (App H): O = Phi(Q)W_{1,0} + (Phi(Q)Phi(K)^T ⊙ C^{↑L}) V, with C_ti = sum_{j=i..t} eta_j prod_{s=i+1..j} alpha_s.

APPLICATION TO THE PROPOSAL'S FAST NET, eq (6)-(8): f_W(q) = tanh(qA+b)B + d_0, 16-32-16, all 1,072 parameters written by one plain-SGD step per experience on l_assoc = 1/2||f_W(q_e) - sg(y_e)||^2. Fold the fast bias d_0 into the state with a constant feature: phi_{A,b}(q) = [tanh(qA+b), 1] in R^33 and S = [B; d_0] in R^{33x16}. The net then has exactly the Thm 5.1 form, so Thms 5.1-5.2 apply. With g_i = eta_f (y_{e_i} - f_{W_i}(q_{e_i})), which is a delta-rule, state-dependent value because the loss is MSE:
  m_t = f_{W_k}(q_t) = phi_{A_k,b_k}(q_t) [S_0 + sum_{i<k} phi_{A_i,b_i}(q_{e_i})^T g_i].
I checked this numerically with random weights and 8 sequential writes: max error 4.4e-16. The query kernel has to be the updated one. Substituting the initial (A_0, b_0) gives an error of 0.58, against an output norm of 4.76.

Centered memory in eq (4): m_t - f_{W_0}(q_t) = [phi_{A_k,b_k}(q_t) - phi_{A_0,b_0}(q_t)] S_0 + phi_{A_k,b_k}(q_t) sum_i phi_i(q_{e_i})^T g_i. If only (B, d_0) are written, the first term vanishes and m_t - f_{W_0}(q_t) = sum_i <phi(q_t), phi(q_{e_i})> g_i. That is exactly unnormalized linear cross-attention from the denoising-state query q_t = Q_phi(z_t, t, c_k, h) to the written experience keys, with delta-rule (DeltaNet-like) values. No writes happen during the ODE, so S_k is fixed for all 16 solver steps and only the query features change with (z_t, t).

Not covered by the theorems:
- A nonlinear final layer (explicitly excluded).
- Adaptive per-parameter optimizers such as Adam: the update is no longer rank-1 in the (key, value) outer product. This is my inference; the paper does not discuss it.
- Weight normalization: the state is not a sum.
- Iterated retrieval (proposal eq 13), whose output is a composition of several reads.
- The proposal's downstream nonlinear readers R_phi, s_phi, V_W. These act on the attention-like output m_t in the same way a post-attention MLP does.
key_results: Fig. 1 (LaCT-LLM and LaCT-NVS): at inference, 1->64 inner-loop iterations lower the inner loss, but 'downstream performance degrades consistently as the number of inner-loop steps increases'. The trend is only shown as a plot; the text gives no exact numbers.

Table 1, gradient ascent (retrained from scratch with the sign-flipped update): LaCT-LLM ppl 16.43 -> 16.19, LaCT-NVS PSNR 25.94 -> 25.85, ViTTT top-1 79.34 -> 79.61. The ascent 'consistently increases the inner-loop loss'.
Table 1, replacing Q with K: ppl 16.18, PSNR 25.95, top-1 79.18, i.e. 'little to no degradation'.
Fig. 2: t-SNE of LaCT-NVS blocks 1, 4 and 7 shows 'a pronounced and consistent mismatch' between the Q and K distributions (and between V and O).

Table 2 reduction trajectory (ppl / PSNR / top-1): Baseline 16.43 / 25.94 / 79.34; V1 last-layer-only 15.93 / 25.97 / 79.63 (best on all three tasks); V2 no weight norm 16.31 / 25.93 / 79.63; V3 single linear layer 16.23 / 25.71 / 79.39; V4 no per-token lr 16.12 / 25.70 / 79.39; V5 no momentum 15.97 / 25.70 / 79.39; V6 no orthogonalization, i.e. plain linear attention, 16.80 / 25.73 / 79.54. For ViTTT, V6 removes gradient normalization instead.
Deeper inner MLPs help NVS (25.93 -> 25.71 when collapsed to a linear layer). Gradient orthogonalization helps the LLM (15.97 -> 16.80 when removed). Other components are marginal.

Headline gaps: the intro says full TTT beats the reduced linear attention 'only marginally (+0.87 perplexity on LLM, +0.24 dB on NVS)', which is V1 vs V6. Sec 6.1 reports '+0.4 perplexity on LLM and -0.2 dB on NVS', which is Baseline vs V6. Both agree with Table 2 but use different reference points.

Efficiency, TTT-layer tokens/s: recurrent 4.30M (Baseline) -> 14.40M (V5) -> 89.67M (V6); parallel 30.18M (V2) -> 57.28M (V5) -> 124.6M (V6). 'Up to 4.0x' corresponds to V5, parallel vs recurrent. End-to-end training speedup is 1.19x (parallel V2) and 1.06x (recurrent V2) vs original LaCT (Fig. 4).

Setups (App A): 760M LaCT-LLM on FineWeb-Edu, 20K iters on 8xA100, evaluated on 2.5B Book-3 tokens at 32k length. 114M LaCT-NVS on RealEstate10K at 128x128. ViTTT-B (90M) on ImageNet-1K for 60 epochs. No seeds, standard deviations or error bars are reported for any table, so differences of about 0.2-0.3 ppl, about 0.1 dB or about 0.3% are of unknown significance.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 21 table, [4] 'Relevant mechanism': 'An attention-like representation under stated final-layer assumptions, allowing update-dependent features.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Thm 5.1: 'Consider a TTT model whose inner-loop function has a linear, bias-free final layer, f(x) = phi(x;Theta) W ... performs one step of gradient descent ... updating all trainable parameters ... o = phi_{t+1}(q)(W_t + phi_t(k)^T g_t(k)) ... q_hat = phi_{t+1}(q), k_hat = phi_t(k), v_hat = g_t(k), S_0 = W_t.' Conclusion: the analysis 'is limited to settings where the inner-loop final layer is linear and bias-free.' Sec 6.1 on update-dependent features: 'Updating Theta_t within the inner loop makes phi_t a dynamic kernel that is difficult to unroll analytically.'
proposal_claim_checks.correction: Accurate but incomplete. (a) The paper's own label is stronger: 'learned linear attention' / 'linear attention-like operator'. (b) The exact theorems cover plain GD, one step per token, applied sequentially, plus momentum. The Muon-based LaCT rewrite (App E.3) moves a nonlinear operator inside a sum and is not exact, and weight normalization makes the state non-additive. (c) The summary leaves out the paper's second main contribution: the empirical evidence that TTT-KVB does not behave like memorization (gradient ascent, Q->K replacement, the inner-steps paradox). That evidence bears more directly on the proposal's interpretation of its writer than the representation theorem does.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 21 table, [4] 'Research distinction to test': 'No blanket claim that nonlinear fast memory escapes all attention equivalences.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Intro: 'even TTT variants with complex fast-weight parameterizations (including multi-layer MLPs and momentum) can be equivalently rewritten as a form of learned linear attention operator.' My numerical check shows the proposal's eq (6)-(8) net satisfies Thm 5.2 to 4.4e-16 once d_0 is folded into a constant-1 feature (scratchpad/ref04_check/check.py).
proposal_claim_checks.correction: The stance is consistent with the paper, but it understates the situation and is not a 'distinction to test'. The proposal's fast net (linear output layer B plus fast bias d_0, plain SGD, MSE loss) sits inside the class covered by Thms 5.1-5.2. The bias is not a loophole, because it is exactly a constant-feature row of the state. So the right statement is not 'no blanket claim of escape' but 'our fast memory is a TTT-KVB instance and hence linear-attention-like per [4]; any gain must come from reader location, lifecycle, or the dynamic kernel.' The column should name a testable item instead, for example external reader vs a linear/DeltaNet cross-attention over experience tokens with a matched state size.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 5 ('Why begin with this writer?'): 'A nonlinear MLP does not by itself prove an expressive separation from attention-based formulations [4].'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Sec 5 intro: 'We show analytically that TTT induces a linear attention-like operator in a general form, even when the inner loop consists of multi-layer non-linear mappings.' Sec 6.1 Step 3: 'increasing MLP depth simply induces a more complex kernel function phi(.) over queries and keys.'
proposal_claim_checks.correction: Correct and appropriately hedged. Note that [4] neither proves nor disproves a separation when the hidden layer is also written: the query kernel phi_{t+1} then depends on the full history, so the representation places no restriction on expressivity. [4] reports it as 'non-reducible' (App I).

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Reference list: '[4] Liu, J., et al. Test-Time Training with KV Binding Is Secretly Linear Attention. 2026; arXiv:2602.21204. Consult the stated assumptions when invoking its equivalence result.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: arXiv abs page: authors 'Junchen Liu, Sven Elflein, Or Litany, Zan Gojcic, Ruilong Li'; comment 'ICML 2026'; v1 24 Feb 2026, v4 12 May 2026.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: Add the venue: ICML 2026 (PMLR 306).

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 1 (not attributed to [4], but [4] bears on it): 'History influences the action through updated weights. This distinguishes the proposed implementation from a fixed network that only receives additional context tokens. It does not imply a universal mathematical separation between fast-weight models and in-context computation.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Thm 5.2: o_t = phi_{t+1}(q_t)(W_0 + sum_i phi_i(k_i)^T g_i(k_i)), which [4] calls 'the extended linear attention form on sequential inputs'. Sec 6.1 Step 1: with only the final layer updated, 'phi(.) then acts as a learnable kernel function with effective queries and keys given by phi(q) and phi(k).'
proposal_claim_checks.correction: The hedge is right, but 'distinguishes' is an implementation distinction (constant-size recurrent state), not a functional one. Take the last-layer-only case, which [4] found best empirically. There the memory read equals a linear cross-attention from the query to the history tokens phi(q_e) with delta-rule values. A fixed network with a linear-attention layer over experience tokens computes the same thing.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 5 (not attributed to [4], but contested by it): 'It gives an explicit answer to what fast weights store: learned associations between available cues and event content.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: [4] Sec 4 summary: 'Downstream behavior is largely insensitive to both the quality and direction of inner-loop optimization, and to the presence of a meaningful query signal. These failures suggest that in practice TTT does not operate as test-time memorization.' Conclusion: 'the inner loop does not perform meta learning in the conventional sense, but instead parameterizes a structured mixing of queries, keys, and values.'
proposal_claim_checks.correction: The write objective states what the writer is trained to fit, not what the trained system actually uses. [4] shows that for end-to-end-trained KV-binding layers the association reading can be empirically false. The proposal should present 'associations between cues and content' as a hypothesis and test it with [4]-style controls (sign-flipped writer, write-steps sweep, Q/K overlap). Caveat: [4]'s evidence comes from LLM, NVS and image classification with Frobenius-loss writers and long within-sequence contexts. It does not cover few-shot cross-decision episodic writes with an MSE loss, so it does not directly refute the proposal's claim.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 6: 'An internal TTT layer changes hidden features that determine the velocity ... The difference is the intervention location and lifecycle.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: [4] Thm 5.1-5.3 apply equally wherever the fast function is placed. The memory output is phi_{t+1}(q) S in both cases.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: Consistent with [4]. Under [4]'s view, both the internal TTT baseline and the external memory are linear-attention-like operators over the same written experiences, which supports the proposal's framing that only the injection point and lifecycle differ.

reading.relevance_to_proposal:
Sec 1, eq (1) (pi(a_k | c_k, W_k), history acts through weights). Thm 5.2 shows the fast-weight read is a linear-attention read over transformed history, so 'weights vs context tokens' is an implementation difference (constant-size recurrent state). The proposal's hedge ('does not imply a universal mathematical separation') is correct. Its baseline 'History tokens / retrieval' (Sec 17) should include a linear-attention or DeltaNet cross-attention over experience tokens, because that is the functional twin of eq (6)-(8) with last-layer writes.

Sec 3 (biological analogy, CA3 partial-cue recall; 'This does not rule out attention'). [4]'s evidence that trained KV-binding layers act as 'feature mixers' rather than retrieval weakens the claim that the fast net implements cue-dependent recall. The proposal already avoids ranking itself against attention there, which is good.

Sec 4, eq (3)-(5). The query q_t = Q_phi(z_t, t, c_k, h_theta) comes from the evolving candidate action, while the write keys q_e come from masked experience cues. That is the cross-source Q/K setting in which [4] found 'distributional asymmetry'. Under [4]'s view, eq (4) centering subtracts the S_0 (initial-state) contribution. With last-layer-only writes, r depends on memory only through sum_i <phi(q_t), phi(q_{e_i})> g_i.

Sec 5, eq (6)-(8). The fast net falls squarely inside Thms 5.1-5.2 once d_0 is folded into a constant feature (verified numerically). Because every parameter (A, b, B, d_0) is written, the kernel is dynamic, which is [4]'s hard case: no associative or parallel form (App I), and a history-dependent query feature tanh(qA_k + b_k). The MSE loss makes the values delta-rule-like, g = eta_f (y - f(q_e)), so the relevant attention-family comparator is DeltaNet / Gated DeltaNet, not vanilla linear attention. The optional 'decay or proximal penalty' for bounded memory corresponds to a forget/decay gate as in gated linear attention. The alternative learned scalar write loss [17] still gives the same form if the loss depends on W only through f_W(q_e). That is my inference from the App B proof, not something the paper states.

Sec 6 ('What is different from internal TTT?'). Consistent with [4]: both designs are linear-attention-like memories, and they differ in where the output is injected and in the lifecycle.

Sec 8. The 'Internal TTT layer' reader is, per [4], learned linear attention inside the transformer. The eq (13) recurrent Hopfield retrieval and the energy/value readers compose several attention-like reads nonlinearly. That is outside the one-read form of Thm 5.1 but gives no demonstrated expressivity separation.

Sec 14 (reset gate, refresh, meta-training over a mixture of backbone checkpoints) and Sec 16-18 (1-16 experiences in Exp. B). [4]'s finding that changing the number of inner-loop steps at inference degrades performance through train-test mismatch warns that persistent W_k accumulating more writes than seen in meta-training, or a different eta_f or write count at deployment, can hurt. The reset/refresh criteria should include a sweep over write count and write rate beyond the meta-training range.

Sec 17-18 (baselines, falsifiable outcomes). 'Internal TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP' is covered. Missing is [4]'s reduction ladder applied to the proposal's own memory: last-layer-only writes, single linear layer, and Frobenius vs MSE loss. [4] found last-layer-only writes best on all three of its tasks and full-to-linear-attention losses of only about 0.2-0.9 ppl or about 0.2 dB.

Sec 21 table. The characterization is accurate but omits [4]'s empirical anti-memorization results, and its 'distinction to test' entry is a non-claim rather than a test.
novelty_threats: The proposal's fast memory, eq (6)-(8), is structurally a TTT-KVB layer: MLP fast net, gradient writes on a key-value MSE binding loss, and slow parameters meta-learned through the writes. Thms 5.1-5.2 show it is a linear-attention-like operator over the written experience keys and values, and a numerical check on the exact 16-32-16 tanh net with bias confirms the identity to 4.4e-16. So the memory module itself adds no mechanism novelty beyond TTT, linear attention, or DeltaNet. Any novelty must come from the external velocity read-out, the centering/reset lifecycle, and consolidation. The proposal mostly acknowledges this (Sec 6, 'difference is the intervention location and lifecycle').

If only (B, d_0) are written, which is the configuration [4] found best (Variant 1 best on LLM, NVS and ImageNet), then m_t - f_{W_0}(q_t) = sum_i <phi(q_t), phi(q_{e_i})> g_i. That is exactly linear cross-attention from the denoising state to the experience set. The 'history via weights, not context tokens' framing (eq 1) would then be functionally identical to a history-token baseline that uses a linear-attention reader, which weakens the conceptual motivation for fast weights over retrieval or context methods.

[4] reports that collapsing complex TTT all the way to vanilla linear attention costs only about 0.4-0.9 ppl or about 0.2 dB. This suggests the proposal's nonlinear tanh MLP and full-parameter writes may add little over a linear fast memory. The proposal gives no justification for choosing the MLP over a linear or DeltaNet memory, and it plans no ablation of that choice.

[4]'s empirical 'memorization paradox' (gradient ascent works, queries replaceable by keys, more inner steps hurt) undercuts the proposal's interpretive and biological story that fast weights store cue-to-content associations recalled from partial cues (Sec 3, Sec 5 'explicit answer to what fast weights store'). If the proposal's trained memory behaves similarly, the CA3/complementary-learning framing becomes decorative.

Because internal TTT and the external reader are both attention-like memories, [4] makes it more plausible that internal TTT (or a plain linear-attention layer) will match the external reader. That would trigger the proposal's own falsification clause (Sec 18: 'If internal TTT matches or beats the external reader ... abandon the superiority claim').

Limits of the threat: [4]'s experiments are long-context sequence modeling (32k-token LLM, NVS, ImageNet) with Frobenius inner-product losses, single runs without error bars, and within-sequence self-attention-like Q/K. None covers few-shot, cross-decision episodic writes, MSE writers, robot policies, or flow-matching velocity readout. The anomalies might not transfer.
ideas_to_borrow: Sign-flip control ([4] Sec 4.2): meta-train a copy of the proposal with gradient ascent in eq (8), W_{k+1} = W_k + eta_f grad l_assoc, and compare adaptation curves. If performance survives, the gains do not come from association storage. With an MSE loss, ascent is not a pure value-sign flip (the +f(q_e) term makes it anti-delta), so also run a Frobenius-loss writer, L = -<f(q_e), y_e>, where [4]'s argument applies exactly.

Write-steps / write-rate sweep at deployment ([4] Fig. 1): with meta-trained slow parameters fixed, vary the number of gradient steps per experience (1..64) and eta_f. Plot inner l_assoc against downstream success. This tests the memorization interpretation and quantifies train-test mismatch for persistent W_k. Extend it to more experiences than the 1-16 used in meta-training.

Q/K overlap diagnostics ([4] Fig. 2, Sec 4.4): compare the distribution of denoising queries q_t = Q_phi(z_t, t, c_k, h) with write keys q_e (t-SNE plus a quantitative measure such as MMD or nearest-neighbour distance). Add a 'query with the cue view instead of z_t' ablation to test whether the z_t- and t-dependence of the query, central to the claim that memory acts throughout denoising, is actually used.

Reduction ladder on the proposal's own memory ([4] Table 2), with everything else fixed: (a) write only (B, d_0) with (A, b) slow, giving a static kernel and exact linear cross-attention; (b) single linear fast layer (TTT-Linear / DeltaNet); (c) MSE vs Frobenius inner-product writer; (d) remove or add decay. Report which components matter.

Explicit attention-family baselines with matched state size (about 1,072 numbers): linear-attention and DeltaNet / Gated DeltaNet cross-attention from the denoising state to experience tokens. These are the functional twins of eq (6)-(8) under Thm 5.2 and should sit next to the 'history tokens / retrieval' baseline.

If the last-layer-only variant is adopted, use [4]'s parallel prefix-scan form (App H), O = Phi(Q) S_0 + (Phi(Q)Phi(K)^T ⊙ C) V, to parallelize meta-training over the causal history H_k. This avoids sequential unrolling of writes during second-order outer updates.

Reframe eq (4) centering with the linear-attention decomposition: m_t - f_{W_0}(q_t) separates an S_0 (initial-state) term from the history term. Useful for 'departure' measurements and for designing reset (setting the state back to S_0).
Report throughput and latency of recurrent vs parallel memory forms, as [4] does (tokens/s per variant), to support the proposal's success-latency-memory tradeoff reporting.
technical_issues_in_proposal: Eq (6) has a fast output bias d_0. Strictly, that violates [4]'s 'bias-free' assumption, but the bias is trivially absorbed as a constant-1 feature, phi = [tanh(qA+b), 1], S = [B; d_0]. The proposal's wording ('under stated final-layer assumptions') could be read as leaving room for its net to fall outside the theorem. It does not: the theorem holds exactly for eq (6)-(8), verified numerically to 4.4e-16. The proposal should state this explicitly.

Eq (7) is an MSE writer, so the effective values g_i = eta_f (y_{e_i} - f_{W_i}(q_{e_i})) depend on the current memory state (delta rule). [4]'s reduction to vanilla linear attention (g_t = -v) and its explanation of the gradient-ascent anomaly hold for Frobenius inner-product losses (LaCT, ViTTT). The proposal's memory should therefore be compared with delta-rule attention (DeltaNet / Gated DeltaNet). Under MSE, sign-flipping is not a trivially absorbed value flip, so [4]'s ascent evidence does not transfer directly.

Sec 5 asserts that the association writer 'gives an explicit answer to what fast weights store'. [4]'s central empirical finding contests this for trained KV-binding layers, and the proposal does not cite [4] for it. Without sign-flip, write-steps and Q/K diagnostics, this interpretive claim, and the CA3/partial-cue analogy it supports, is unjustified.

Train-test mismatch: [4] shows that changing the number of inner-loop steps at inference changes the effective attention operator and degrades performance. The proposal's persistent W_k accumulates writes across decisions and is meta-trained on 1-16 experiences over a mixture of backbone checkpoints. The plan never tests write counts or rates beyond the meta-training range. Sec 14's 'can still adapt with the same budget' criterion does not cover this; Sec 5 mentions only 'capacity and write-rate sweeps'.

Missing baselines: no linear-attention or DeltaNet cross-attention memory with a matched state, no last-layer-only fast-memory ablation (the best variant in [4]), and no linear-vs-MLP fast-memory ablation. 'Internal TTT-Linear/MLP' tests the injection point, not the memory parameterization.

Missing connection: the optional 'decay or proximal penalty' for bounded memory (Sec 5) is, in [4]'s view, a data-independent or data-dependent forget gate on a linear-attention state (GLA, Mamba, Gated DeltaNet). That literature should be cited and used for design choices.

The Sec 21 'Research distinction to test' entry for [4] is a disclaimer, not a testable distinction. It should name a concrete test, for example external velocity reader over a TTT-KVB memory vs a matched linear/DeltaNet cross-attention memory under the same lifecycle.

Minor: if the proposal later adopts Muon, Adam or weight normalization in the writer (Sec 5 leaves the writer open), note that [4]'s exact equivalence covers plain SGD and momentum only. The LaCT/Muon rewrite in [4] App E.3 moves a nonlinear operator inside a sum and is not exact, and weight normalization makes the state non-additive (App E.4).
stated_limitations: 'Our analysis applies broadly to TTT formulations based on key-value binding, but is limited to settings where the inner-loop final layer is linear and bias-free.'

'Empirically, we focus on LaCT (Zhang et al., 2025) and ViTTT (Han et al., 2025) as case studies ... Other key-value-binding variants such as Titans ... and Atlas ... also satisfy the assumptions of our theorems, and we expect our results to extend to them; empirical validation on these models is left to future work.'

'Extending these insights to nonlinear final layers, and exploring deeper connections between TTT and modern linear attention mechanisms in both directions, remain additional avenues for future work.'
Scope: 'this paper exclusively focuses on this variant' (TTT-KVB), not end-to-end TTT (TTT-E2E).

Sec 6.1 / App I: updating kernel parameters makes phi_t 'a dynamic kernel that is difficult to unroll analytically', and together with weight normalization this 'breaks associativity, thereby preventing parallelization'. The parallel form exists only for Variants 2-6.
LaCT derivation: 'LaCT also applies weight normalization after each update, which we omit here for simplicity.'

Not stated by the authors, but evident from the text: no seeds or variance are reported; the Muon rewrite (App E.3) is not an exact identity; and the Q/K and gradient-ascent tests cover only Frobenius-loss models (LaCT, ViTTT).
cited_works_worth_adding: Schlag, Irie, Schmidhuber (2021), 'Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers', ICML. The canonical fast-weights = linear-attention equivalence. It bears directly on the eq (1) 'weights vs context tokens' framing.

Yang, Wang, Zhang, Shen, Kim (2024b), 'Parallelizing Linear Transformers with the Delta Rule over Sequence Length', NeurIPS (DeltaNet). [4] notes 'DeltaNet and its variants are equivalent to TTT with a single linear layer and MSE loss'. The proposal's MSE writer is a delta rule, so this is the natural attention-family baseline.

Yang, Wang, Shen, Panda, Kim (2024a), 'Gated Linear Attention Transformers with Hardware-Efficient Training', ICML. Data-dependent decay; the counterpart of the proposal's decay/proximal penalty for bounded memory.
Zhang et al. (2025), 'Test-Time Training Done Right' (LaCT), arXiv:2505.23884. Large-chunk TTT with an MLP fast net; [4]'s main testbed. Relevant to chunked or batched writes of multiple experiences.
Han et al. (2025), 'ViT^3: Unlocking Test-Time Training in Vision', arXiv:2512.01643. The second testbed, which uses a constant inner learning rate of 1.0.

Wang, Shi, Fox (2025), 'Test-time regression: a unifying framework for designing sequence models with associative memory', arXiv:2501.12352. Frames the proposal's writer family as test-time regression and helps position the eq (7) design choices.

Tandon et al. (2025), 'End-to-End Test-Time Training for Long Context', arXiv:2512.23675. TTT-E2E, which [4] excludes. Relevant if the proposal's learned write loss [17] moves toward end-to-end objectives.

Behrouz, Zhong, Mirrokni, 'Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time' (NeurIPS), and Behrouz et al. (2025c), 'It's All Connected' (Miras), arXiv:2504.13173. Memory-as-optimization designs with forgetting and retention gates, claimed by [4] to satisfy its assumptions. Relevant to the proposal's retention and decay choices.
Katharopoulos et al. (2020), 'Transformers are RNNs: Fast Autoregressive Transformers with Linear Attention', ICML. The base linear-attention formulation used in [4]'s equivalence.

Dalal et al. (2025), 'One-Minute Video Generation with Test-Time Training', CVPR. TTT layers inside a diffusion transformer: a close precedent for gradient-written memory inside a generative denoiser.

errors_found.reader_claim: Summary and key_results: 'more inner-loop steps at inference lowers the inner loss but makes perplexity and PSNR worse' and '1->64 inner-loop iterations lower the inner loss'.
errors_found.problem: This is false for the LLM panel. The reader repeated the caption but did not check the plot. For LaCT-LLM the inner loss falls only from 1 to 8 iterations, then rises again from 8 to 64 while perplexity keeps rising. The inverse relationship therefore holds cleanly only for NVS, and for LLM only up to 8 steps. The reader also did not report the sizes, which can be read from the plot.
errors_found.evidence: Caption: 'Increasing inner-loop iterations improves inner-loop loss but degrades task performance'. A 300-dpi render of Fig. 1 (right panel) shows the inner loss at about -0.73 (1 step), about -1.05 (2), about -1.29 (4), about -1.37 (8, the minimum), about -1.35 (16), about -1.31 (32) and about -1.28 (64). Perplexity rises from about 15.18 to about 15.74. In the left panel (NVS), the inner loss falls monotonically from 0 to -60 and PSNR drops from about 26 to about 17-18 dB.
errors_found.corrected: NVS: the inner loss decreases monotonically and PSNR drops by about 8-9 dB. LLM: the inner loss is lowest at 8 steps and then increases, while perplexity rises monotonically from about 15.2 to about 15.7. Neither panel's numbers appear in the text.

errors_found.reader_claim: Summary: 'Fig. 2: t-SNE shows Q and K clearly mismatched in distribution in every LaCT-NVS block'.
errors_found.problem: This overstates the figure. Only blocks 1, 4 and 7 are shown, and the evidence is a qualitative t-SNE with no quantitative overlap measure. The reader's own key_results entry correctly says 'blocks 1, 4 and 7'.
errors_found.evidence: Fig. 2 panels are labelled 'Block 1', 'Block 4' and 'Block 7'. The text says 'we observe a pronounced and consistent mismatch between Q/K and V/O across layers'.
errors_found.corrected: The t-SNE plots of blocks 1, 4 and 7 (qualitative only) show a Q/K and V/O mismatch.

errors_found.reader_claim: core_mechanism: 'With the Frobenius loss g_t = -v, so v_hat = v.'
errors_found.problem: The sign is inconsistent, and the error is copied from a typo in the paper. Thm 5.1 defines g_t(k) = -eta dL/df_t(k). For L = -<f(k), v> we have dL/df = -v, so g_t = +eta v. The line 'g_t = -v, so v_hat = v' contradicts v_hat = g_t.
errors_found.evidence: App E.2: 'The upstream gradient with respect to the output is dL/df_t(k_t) = -v_t'. Thm 5.1: 'g_t(k) := -eta dL/df_t(k)'. Step 5 (the typo): 'for both LaCT and ViTTT, g_t(k) = -v and removing momentum recovers v_hat = v'.
errors_found.corrected: For the Frobenius loss, dL/df = -v and g_t = eta v, so v_hat is proportional to v. The paper's Step 5 statement 'g_t(k) = -v' conflates dL/df with g.

errors_found.reader_claim: ideas_to_borrow: 'If the last-layer-only variant is adopted, use [4]'s parallel prefix-scan form (App H), O = Phi(Q) S_0 + (Phi(Q)Phi(K)^T ⊙ C) V, to parallelize meta-training over the causal history H_k.'
errors_found.problem: App H's parallel form requires a Frobenius inner-product loss, where the values are the fixed v_i and do not depend on the state. The proposal's writer is MSE (eq 7). Even with a static kernel its values are g_i = eta_f (y_i - phi(q_{e_i}) S_i), which depend on the running state S_i. That is the delta rule, and the prefix-scan formula in App H does not apply to it. Delta-rule models need the separate chunkwise algorithm of Yang et al. 2024b. With only 1-16 writes per episode, parallelizing the writes would also save little.
errors_found.evidence: App H.2: 'Since grad_{W1} L = Phi(K_t)^T dL/df_t(K_t) and using the Frobenius inner product loss, we have: dW_t = -Phi(K_t)^T V_t + alpha_t dW_{t-1}.' Sec 2.1: 'DeltaNet and its variants are equivalent to TTT with a single linear layer and MSE loss'. Proposal eq (7): l_assoc = 1/2 ||f_W(q_e) - sg(y_e)||^2.
errors_found.corrected: App H applies only if the writer is switched to a Frobenius loss. With the proposal's MSE writer, the last-layer-only variant is DeltaNet on the features phi(q_e) with a nonzero initial state S_0, and it needs DeltaNet-style chunkwise parallelization.

errors_found.reader_claim: ideas_to_borrow (sign-flip control): '...so also run a Frobenius-loss writer, L = -<f(q_e), y_e>, where [4]'s argument applies exactly.'
errors_found.problem: With a Frobenius writer, the gradient-ascent control is uninformative by construction. Ascent from (A, b, B, d_0) produces exactly the negated output of descent from (A, b, -B, -d_0). The proposal meta-learns W_0 and the reader R_phi, so a sign flip can be absorbed exactly. The result is determined in advance and says nothing about memorization. The control is informative only for the MSE writer, where ascent becomes an anti-delta rule that can diverge.
errors_found.evidence: [4] Sec 4.2: 'where the inner-loop loss is a Frobenius inner product, flipping the gradient is equivalent to negating the loss itself.' Sec 1: 'gradient ascent preserves performance because sign inversions are absorbed into the learned value projection'. My numerical check on the proposal's 16-32-16 tanh net over 8 writes (/tmp/claude-1001/-home-licho-workspace-Horsea/6362e6e4-1b6e-43f7-ba9b-09289d83a6f6/scratchpad/ref04_verify/signflip.py) gives max|f_ascent(W0) + f_descent(-W0)| = 0.0 for the Frobenius loss and 30.46 for MSE.
errors_found.corrected: Run the sign-flip control only with the MSE writer, and read the result carefully (divergence is a trivial failure mode). A Frobenius sign-flip adds no evidence.

errors_found.reader_claim: novelty_threats #1: 'Thms 5.1-5.2 show it is a linear-attention-like operator over the written experience keys and values ... So the memory module itself adds no mechanism novelty beyond TTT, linear attention, or DeltaNet.' Claim-check #2 correction: 'our fast memory is a TTT-KVB instance and hence linear-attention-like per [4]'.
errors_found.problem: This overstates what [4] establishes for the proposal's actual configuration, in which all of A, b, B and d_0 are written. Here the kernel is dynamic. The theorem's form o = phi_{k}(q)(S_0 + sum phi_i(q_{e_i})^T g_i) is then an algebraic identity for any network with a linear last layer. Its query feature tanh(qA_k + b_k) depends nonlinearly on the whole write history, so the form implies no equivalence to linear attention or DeltaNet. [4] itself calls this case hard to unroll and non-reducible. The reader contradicts itself: claim-check #3 correctly says the representation 'places no restriction on expressivity'. The module lacks novelty because it is TTT-MLP ([3]), which the proposal already acknowledges, not because of [4]'s theorem.
errors_found.evidence: Sec 6.1 Step 1: 'Updating Theta_t within the inner loop makes phi_t a dynamic kernel that is difficult to unroll analytically.' App I.1: 'This nested structure prevents expressing the output as a simple weighted sum over history'. Proposal Sec 21 row [4]: 'allowing update-dependent features'.
errors_found.corrected: [4] gives an exact equivalence to linear attention, or to DeltaNet under MSE, only when (B, d_0) alone are written. For the full-write configuration it provides a rewrite, not a reduction. The proposal's wording ('attention-like representation ... allowing update-dependent features'; 'no blanket claim') is more precise than the reader's suggested replacement.

errors_found.reader_claim: Claim-check #5 correction: 'the memory read equals a linear cross-attention ... A fixed network with a linear-attention layer over experience tokens computes the same thing.'
errors_found.problem: This holds only for last-layer-only writes, which the proposal does not use. Even then the values g_i = eta_f(y_i - f_{W_i}(q_{e_i})) are sequential and depend on the state, so the matching layer is DeltaNet (a recurrent delta-rule state), not plain linear attention over tokens. The proposal's sentence also already calls this an implementation distinction and explicitly disclaims a mathematical separation.
errors_found.evidence: Proposal Sec 1: 'This distinguishes the proposed implementation from a fixed network that only receives additional context tokens. It does not imply a universal mathematical separation between fast-weight models and in-context computation.'
errors_found.corrected: The proposal's hedge is accurate as written. The functional twin holds only in the last-layer-only, MSE case, where it is DeltaNet cross-attention with initial state S_0.

errors_found.reader_claim: relevance / technical_issues #4: '[4]'s finding that changing the number of inner-loop steps at inference degrades performance ... warns that persistent W_k accumulating more writes than seen in meta-training ... can hurt.'
errors_found.problem: This extrapolates beyond the evidence. [4] Fig. 1 varies the number of gradient iterations per update step at inference. It does not vary the number of tokens or experiences written, and [4] reports no length or write-count extrapolation experiment. Fig. 3 shows perplexity against position only up to the 32k evaluation length. The recommendation is reasonable, but it is the reader's inference and not a finding of [4].
errors_found.evidence: Sec 4.1: 'we vary the number of inner-loop gradient steps at inference time ... without changing the architecture, training data, or learned parameters.'
errors_found.corrected: Only a write-steps-per-experience sweep is directly motivated by [4]. A sweep over the number of experiences beyond 1-16 is a separate generalization test that [4] does not address.

errors_found.reader_claim: key_results: "'Up to 4.0x' corresponds to V5, parallel vs recurrent."
errors_found.problem: This is ambiguous and probably not the maximum. The largest parallel/recurrent ratio in Table 2 is Variant 4 (53.99M/13.31M = 4.06x). Variant 5 gives 57.28/14.40 = 3.98x. The paper does not say which variant it means.
errors_found.corrected: 'Up to 4.0x' matches V4 (4.06x) or V5 (3.98x). The paper does not specify.

errors_found.reader_claim: technical_issues #3: 'Without sign-flip, write-steps and Q/K diagnostics, this interpretive claim ... is unjustified'. ideas_to_borrow #3 proposes a 'query with the cue view instead of z_t' ablation.
errors_found.problem: The reader missed controls the proposal already includes. They test directly whether stored content is used: reset, shuffled and wrong-memory controls, training with wrong associations, and readers that see only context and time versus the candidate action. These test content dependence more directly than [4]'s sign flip. The proposal also fixes the targets (sg of a pretrained encoder), which removes the learned value projection that [4] uses to explain away gradient ascent.
errors_found.evidence: Proposal Sec 17: 'Adaptation: task success versus available experiences ... and reset/shuffled/wrong-memory controls.' Also Sec 17: 'Use a reader that sees only context and time, one that also sees the candidate action, and one that reads transformer features.' Sec 7: 'Include wrong associations, conflicting evidence'. Sec 5: 'use a fixed pretrained event encoder for y_e'.
errors_found.corrected: The association claim is partly covered by the planned controls. Genuinely new additions from [4] are a Q/K overlap diagnostic, a write-steps sweep, and a last-layer-only / linear-memory ablation.

errors_found.reader_claim: Summary: 'They rewrite LaCT ... and ViTTT (GLU plus depthwise conv ...) in this form.'
errors_found.problem: This is imprecise. ViTTT's GLU does not have Thm 5.1's phi(x)W form. The output is an element-wise gate on a linear branch, and App F derives a separate gated variant. The depthwise conv is handled separately in App G.
errors_found.evidence: App F.1: 'Unlike the general form where the kernel function output is followed by matrix multiplication with a final layer, here the GLU uses element-wise multiplication between the nonlinear gating phi_t(x) and the linear projection xW_{1,t}.'
errors_found.corrected: LaCT fits Thm 5.3 (up to the inexact Muon step). ViTTT is shown to be a gated linear-attention variant through separate derivations (App F-G).

claim_check_overrides.claim: Sec 21 table, [4] 'Research distinction to test': 'No blanket claim that nonlinear fast memory escapes all attention equivalences.'
claim_check_overrides.reason: The statement accurately reflects [4]. The paper proves that an attention-like rewrite exists for any network with a linear, bias-free last layer. For the dynamic-kernel case it calls the result 'difficult to unroll analytically' and 'non-reducible' (Sec 6.1, App I), so it neither establishes nor refutes an expressive separation. The reader wanted to replace this with 'our fast memory is ... hence linear-attention-like per [4]', which overstates [4] for the proposal's full-parameter writes. The legitimate criticism is about presentation: the column holds a disclaimer rather than a testable distinction. That is not an accuracy problem.

claim_check_overrides.claim: Sec 1: 'History influences the action through updated weights. This distinguishes the proposed implementation from a fixed network that only receives additional context tokens. It does not imply a universal mathematical separation between fast-weight models and in-context computation.'
claim_check_overrides.reason: The proposal already describes this as an implementation distinction and explicitly disclaims a mathematical separation, which is exactly the correction the reader offers. The reader's counter-claim that a fixed linear-attention layer 'computes the same thing' holds only for last-layer-only writes, and only with state-dependent delta-rule values (DeltaNet). The proposal writes all of A, b, B and d_0, so its kernel is dynamic.

missed_points: [4]'s memorization-paradox evidence depends on the Frobenius (dot-product) loss and transfers poorly to the proposal. (a) The Frobenius loss is linear in f and unbounded below; in NVS, Fig. 1's inner loss runs from 0 to -60. So 'lower inner loss' mostly means larger output magnitude, not better key-value fitting, and the premise of the Sec 4.1 test is weak. (b) Gradient ascent under this loss is an exact reparameterization; the paper concedes that flipping the gradient 'is equivalent to negating the loss itself' and that the sign is 'absorbed into the learned value projection'. The proposal uses an MSE writer (bounded, with a minimizer) and fixed stop-gradient targets from a pretrained encoder, so it has no learned value projection. The reader treats the anomalies as generic evidence against memorization without these caveats.

The paper's anti-memorization experiments are weaker than the reader presents. The Fig. 1 intervention is inference-only (no retraining), so the degradation is equally consistent with a memorizing layer whose downstream weights are calibrated to 1-step writes; the paper's own Sec 5.2 explanation is 'train-test mismatch'. For the Q->K replacement, the paper does not say whether the models were retrained; if they were, invariance only shows that learned projections can compensate. Fig. 2 is a qualitative t-SNE of 3 blocks with no quantitative overlap measure.

Numbers that do not line up in [4]. Fig. 1's LLM perplexity at 1 step (about 15.18) does not match the Table 1/2 baseline (16.43), and the evaluation setting is not explained. The Table 2 LLM column is non-monotone along the reduction ladder (15.93 -> 16.31 -> 16.23 -> 16.12 -> 15.97 -> 16.80), with single runs and no seeds. Variant 1's 'best on all three tasks' margins are tiny: +0.03 dB on NVS and +0.29 pp on ViTTT over the baseline. [4]'s recommendation to write only the last layer is therefore weakly supported.

Capacity and dimension argument. [4]'s Step 3 rationale is conditional: 'When q and k already have sufficient representational capacity, this added complexity is unlikely to help', and NVS shows depth helps (25.93 -> 25.71). The proposal's queries are only 16-dimensional. A linear fast layer would have a 16x16 (+16) state, versus 33x16 with the tanh kernel. [4] therefore does not support the reader's suggestion that the tanh MLP may add little for this proposal; only matched-state baselines can settle it.

Under Thm 5.3, the momentum-weighted 'value' m_i = g_i * sum_{j=i..t} beta_i^j depends on the current step t. It acts as a time-varying decay mask (the C matrix in App H), not a fixed value. This is relevant if the proposal adds the 'decay or proximal penalty' it mentions.

For the proposal's actual full-write configuration, the key features phi_{A_i,b_i}(q_{e_i}) are frozen at the kernel state at write time, while the query uses the latest (A_k, b_k). This is precisely [4]'s dynamic, non-reducible case, so [4] gives no functional reduction for the proposed memory. The closest actual comparator is TTT-MLP ([3]), which the proposal already includes as a baseline.

[4] studies self-attention-style TTT, where every token of one stream both writes and reads. The proposal is cross-stream: writes come from experience cues, and reads come from denoising states under a different encoder. [4] has no experiments in this setting, so its Q/K-asymmetry result is suggestive at most. The reader notes 'within-sequence' Q/K only in passing.

Positive support for the proposal. [4] explicitly contrasts TTT-KVB with TTT-E2E and notes that Titans and Atlas 'satisfy the assumptions ... empirical validation on these models is left to future work'. Nothing in [4] addresses external readout, memory lifecycle (reset or centering), consolidation into slow weights, or flow-matching or robot policies, which are the parts of the proposal claimed as contributions.
verification.novelty_threat_assessment:
LOW threat to the proposal's claimed contributions, MEDIUM threat to its interpretive framing and baseline design.

[4] does not pre-empt anything the proposal claims as new. The proposal's claimed contributions are the external centered velocity reader evaluated at every denoising step, the reset/refresh lifecycle, FM-specific consolidation, and continual retention. [4] studies within-sequence TTT-KVB layers for LLM, NVS and ImageNet, and says nothing about external readout, consolidation or policies. The proposal does not claim novelty for the memory module, which is a TTT-MLP / KV-binding instance already covered by [3].

[4]'s theorem is exact but uninformative for the proposal's full-parameter writes. By the paper's own account the kernel is then dynamic and 'non-reducible', so [4] does not show that the proposed memory equals linear attention. It does equal DeltaNet cross-attention (with state S_0) if only (B, d_0) are written.

The real pressure from [4] is in three places:
(1) It casts doubt on the proposal's Sec 5 and Sec 3 story that fast weights 'store associations' recalled from partial cues. This is weakened for the proposal's MSE writer with fixed targets, and the proposal already plans shuffled and wrong-memory controls.
(2) It motivates matched-state linear-attention and DeltaNet cross-attention baselines, plus a last-layer-only ablation.
(3) It makes it more plausible that internal TTT will match the external reader, which would trigger the proposal's own falsification clause.

The reading's claim that the memory module 'adds no mechanism novelty beyond TTT, linear attention, or DeltaNet' because of [4] overstates the theorem. The lack of module novelty is real, but it comes from [3].

ref.title: Feng et al., WAM-TTT: Steering World-Action Models by Watching Human Play at Test Time (2026, arXiv 2607.06988)
ref.role: Closest robot TTT prior. Proposal claims: "Residual TTT in a video expert; adaptation from human-video prediction and KV objectives; adapted weights fixed during robot rollout." Distinction claimed: "Continual causal writes from the chosen robot experience protocol."
ref.focus: Architecture (world-action model, which experts, where TTT layers sit, residual form), TTT objectives, when adaptation happens and whether weights are frozen during rollout, action generation (diffusion/FM?), experiments, results, limitations. Verify each clause of the proposal's claim. Identify anything that pre-empts the proposal's novelty (e.g., centered/residual TTT, reset, continual writes, consolidation).
