reading.summary:
Problem. Most robot foundation models, including VLAs, condition on one timestep or a few history frames. RoboTTT extends visuomotor context to 8K control timesteps ("about five minutes at 30 Hz control") while keeping inference latency constant. Its argument is that long context enables one-shot in-context imitation from human video, on-the-fly improvement from the robot's own history, robustness to perturbation, and stronger multi-stage long-horizon performance. It also claims that closed-loop performance rises steadily with pretraining context length, which the authors present as "a new scaling axis for robot foundation models".

Method. RoboTTT starts from NVIDIA GR00T N1.7: an Eagle VLM backbone plus a flow-matching Diffusion Transformer action head (538M parameters, 16 layers) that predicts H-step action chunks. A TTT layer is inserted after the self- and cross-attention in each of the 16 DiT layers. Each TTT layer adds about 10M parameters, for 690M in total.
- Division of labour: attention works within one timestep (register tokens, proprio token and noised action tokens, cross-attending to that timestep's VL tokens). The TTT layers work across time, on the per-timestep attention outputs flattened along time. VL tokens are not passed through TTT; 16 learned register tokens carry VL information across time instead.
- Fast model: a two-layer GeLU MLP updated by plain gradient descent on the key-value-binding MSE (TTT-KVB). The inner learning rate is learned, on top of a base of 0.1. RoPE supplies positions.
- Gating: each layer adds TTT output as O = tanh(α)⊙O_TTT + O_attn, with α∈R^d initialised to 0.001.
- Training: sequence flow-matching loss, with the fast weights unrolled within each training sequence. W0 and the Q/K/V projections are meta-learned through gradients of gradients. The noise level is sampled independently for each action chunk ("sequence action forcing"). TBPTT carries fast weights across segment boundaries but detaches their gradients there.
- Inference: each rollout starts from the learned W0, performs one fast-weight mini-batch update per inference/action chunk, and propagates the weights forward.
- Pure-context segments: masking the FM loss on selected timesteps turns them into context that only writes fast weights. This yields two protocols. (i) One-shot imitation: a human video with masked loss is followed by a robot trajectory with FM loss. (ii) DAgger Distillation: a DAgger rollout in which all executed actions, both suboptimal robot actions and human corrections, update the fast weights, while the FM loss is computed only on human corrections. The paper calls this an instance of Algorithm Distillation.

Training scale. Pretraining uses 30K steps on 16 GB200 GPUs over tabletop bimanual robot data plus egocentric human data. Context length is increased gradually to the target, and only the new sequence layers are trained while the rest of GR00T is frozen. Post-training is done separately for each task: 20K steps, 1K context, all parameters fine-tuned.

Results. Evaluation is on three real bimanual YAM assembly tasks (Pup Go Car, Circuit with 60 unseen configurations, and the 10-stage, 5-minute Gear Bot), with 20 trials per task (10 for Gear Bot).
- Average task completion: RoboTTT 79%, GR00T N1.7 42%, GR00T N1.7 Hist. 49%, GDN (Gated DeltaNet in the same placement) 56%. RoboTTT is the only method with full successes on Gear Bot (2/10).
- Context scaling: performance rises monotonically from 128 to 8K pretraining context (71.5% at 8K); GDN shows no trend.
- One-shot imitation on Circuit, with the same prompt for every configuration: 6/10 successes vs 0/10 for GDN.
- Perturbation recovery: roof 15/20 vs 13/20 (GDN); tire 18/20 vs 18/20.
- DAgger Distillation on Pup Go Car: +36% for RoboTTT and +29% for GDN, vs about +9% for standard DAgger on average across the four models.
- Ablations: an MLP fast model beats a linear one by 27%; removing sequence action forcing collapses performance.

The paper does not study consolidation into a memory-free policy, fast-weight reset beyond the start of a rollout, continual or multi-task learning, or forgetting.
reading.core_mechanism:
1) Generic TTT (Sec. 2). Tokens X have projections Q_t=θ_Q x_t, K_t=θ_K x_t, V_t=θ_V x_t.
- Update: W_t ← W_{t-1} − η ∇_W L_FW(f_{W_{t-1}}(K_t), V_t), with L_FW(v̂,v)=||v̂ − v||² (Eq. 1).
- Apply: O_t = f_{W_t}(Q_t) (Eq. 2). "This 'update then apply' operation occurs during both training and inference."
- θ_Q, θ_K, θ_V and W0 are learned with the outer task loss.
- The project page confirms: "RoboTTT uses the key–value binding loss (TTT-KVB)", as opposed to TTT-E2E.

2) Architecture (Sec. 3.1, App. A.1).
- DiT input over T timesteps: [R_1, Φ_1, q_1, Ã_1, …, R_T, Φ_T, q_T, Ã_T]. R_t are N=16 learned register tokens, Φ_t the VLM tokens, q_t the proprio token, Ã_t the noised action tokens.
- Attention operates on R_t, q_t, Ã_t of a single timestep and cross-attends to Φ_t.
- The attention outputs are flattened over time into X=[R_1,q_1,Ã_1,…] and passed to the TTT layer, which performs Eq. 1 and Eq. 2.
- Gate (Eq. 3): O = tanh(α)⊙O_TTT + O_attn, with α∈R^d per layer, initialised to 0.001.
- There is one TTT layer in each of the 16 DiT layers. Fast model: "a two-layer MLP with GeLU activation … updated by standard gradient descent". Inner learning rate is learned on top of a base of 0.1. RoPE with θ=10000.
- Fig. 2 shows one mini-batch per action-chunk decision (W_0→W_1→…→W_{T/H}; timesteps t=1, 1+H, …). The inference panel is labelled "One Mini Batch per Inference", and the tokens in its update mini-batch include noised action tokens.
- Not specified in the paper: the chunk length H, the number of denoising steps k ("k-step denoising"), and which of the k per-denoising-step fast-weight updates is propagated to the next decision.

3) Sequence training (Sec. 3.2).
- Loss: L_fm(ξ;W0) = 1/T Σ_t E_{τ_t,ε} || v_θ(Φ_t, A_t^{τ_t}, q_t; W_{t−1}) − (A_t − ε) ||² (Eq. 5).
- Interpolant: A^τ = τA + (1−τ)ε, so τ=0 is noise and τ=1 is data, the same convention as the proposal's Eq. 11.
- Sequence action forcing: each τ_t is sampled independently as τ_t = s(1−u), u~Beta(1.5,1), s=0.999.
- W0 is "meta-learned through gradients of gradients".
- TBPTT: fast weights are carried across segment boundaries with gradients detached there; W0 receives gradient only through the first segment.

4) Learning from context (Sec. 3.3).
- The FM loss is masked on selected timesteps, which then "serve as pure context, updating the fast weights without providing an imitation target".
- Video-to-robot pairs: the human video updates fast weights only; the robot trajectory carries the loss.
- DAgger Distillation: ξ^DAgger = {(l,o_t,q_t,A_t)}, where each A_t is either a robot action A^R_t or a human correction A^H_t. "The fast weights are updated on the full interaction history, not only the executed corrections but also the suboptimal robot actions themselves, while the flow-matching loss is masked to the human corrections only." At test time, "its own corrections then enter the history and are absorbed into the fast weights".

5) Inference. "RoboTTT starts each rollout from the learned initialization W0, updates the fast weights on the current observation, and propagates them to the next timestep. At each timestep, action chunks are generated with k-step denoising."

In the proposal's notation: RoboTTT is an internal-TTT reader at every DiT layer. The write happens once per decision k, using KVB on internal tokens that include the noised candidate. W_k persists within the rollout, and W0 is meta-learned. There is no centering, no external velocity residual, and no consolidation or reset lifecycle.
key_results: Main evaluation (Fig. 7, Table 1; project page gives exact numbers). Average task completion: RoboTTT 79%, GR00T N1.7 42%, GR00T N1.7 Hist. 49%, GDN 56%. The paper summarises this as "87% higher than the single-step context baseline … and 41% higher than the best baseline GDN".

Per-task completion (RoboTTT / GR00T / Hist / GDN): Pup Go Car 89/57/40/57; Circuit on unseen configurations 78/23/54/53; Gear Bot 71/47/54/59. The Pup Go Car numbers are after DAgger training (Fig. 8 caption: "All evaluations in this figure predate the DAgger training used for Pup Go Car in the main results").
Full successes (Table 1): Pup Go Car 9/20 vs 3/20, 0/20, 3/20. Circuit 13/20 vs 3/20, 8/20, 8/20. Gear Bot 2/10 vs 0/10 for every baseline.

Context scaling (Fig. 8; average over the three tasks; pretraining context varied, post-training always at 1K). RoboTTT reaches 71.5% at 8K vs 43.9% at 1K; the best short-context baseline (GR00T Hist.) is 45.6%. Approximate curve values: RoboTTT ≈0.31, 0.29, 0.39, 0.44, 0.54, 0.60, 0.715 for 128→8K. GDN ≈0.02, 0.18, 0.40, 0.35, 0.43, 0.36, 0.44 (no trend). Single-step baseline ≈0.375.

Below 1K context, RoboTTT falls short of its longer-context variants. The authors attribute this to rollouts exceeding the training window: "the fast weights are updated far beyond the window seen in training, and positional embeddings extend to unseen positions."

One-shot imitation from one in-context human video on Circuit, unseen configurations, prompt always "assemble circuit" (Table 2): RoboTTT 65% completion and 6/10 successes; GDN 33% and 0/10. GR00T variants were not evaluated because they cannot condition on the video.

Perturbation recovery on Pup Go Car (Table 3). Roof removed: RoboTTT 15/20, GR00T 10/20, Hist 3/20, GDN 13/20. Tire removed: 18/20, 11/20, 5/20, 18/20. This used 30 minutes of perturbation data co-trained with the task data.

DAgger on Pup Go Car (Fig. 10), with 100 DAgger trajectories pooled (50 from RoboTTT, 50 from GR00T). Standard DAgger on corrections only gives "+9% on average across the four methods, and by 13% on the two sequence models". DAgger Distillation gives "33% average improvement: 36% for RoboTTT and 29% for GDN". Approximate bar values: RoboTTT 0.655 before → 0.73 human-only → 0.89 DAgger Distillation; GDN 0.44 → 0.51 → 0.57; GR00T 0.53 → 0.57 human-only = 0.57 full-trajectory; Hist 0.39 → 0.40.

Ablations on Pup Go Car (Fig. 12, approximate). No sequence action forcing ≈0.02 (a collapse). TTT-Linear ≈0.48, which is "27% worse than the MLP fast model" (≈0.655). TTT on state tokens only ≈0.45; adding action tokens ≈0.555 (+23%); adding register tokens ≈0.655 (+18%). GR00T N1.7 with the same register tokens ≈0.44; the paper says "register tokens do not help GR00T N1.7".

Two statements in the paper do not match its own figures. (i) The Fig. 8 caption says RoboTTT surpasses the best short-context baseline "from 1K onward", but the text gives 43.9% at 1K vs 45.6% for the baseline. (ii) The paper says TTT-Linear "outperforms the GR00T N1.7 baseline", but its ≈0.48 in Fig. 12 is below GR00T N1.7's ≈0.53 before DAgger in Fig. 10; it is above only the register-token GR00T (≈0.44). Also, at 512 context GDN (≈0.40) roughly equals RoboTTT (≈0.39), despite "still outperforming GDN at matched lengths".

Scale and compute. DiT 538M plus TTT, 690M total. Pretraining: 30K steps on 16 GB200 GPUs; global batch 64 for context ≤4K and 16 above; AdamW with weight decay 1e-5; WSD schedule with peak learning rate 2e-5. Post-training: 20K steps on 8 GPUs, 1K context, cosine schedule with peak learning rate 5e-5. Deployment: RTX 5090 at 30 Hz with four RealSense D405 cameras at 480p. No absolute latency numbers, training seeds or confidence intervals are reported.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 21 table, [6]: "Internal gated TTT in a diffusion transformer"
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Sec. 3.1: "RoboTTT consists of a vision-language model (VLM) backbone and a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) (52) action head with TTT layers… We add TTT layers after the self- and cross-attention layers." App. A.1: "We add a TTT layer to each of its 16 DiT layers." Eq. 3: "O = tanh(α) ⊙ O_TTT + O_attn", with α∈R^d "initialized to near zero (0.001)".
proposal_claim_checks.correction: The claim is accurate but undersells how close RoboTTT is to the proposal. The DiT is GR00T N1.7's flow-matching action head predicting action chunks, the same policy class as the proposal (Eq. 5 of RoboTTT is a flow-matching velocity loss with target A_t − ε). Suggested wording: "internal, tanh-gated TTT-MLP (KV-binding inner loss) in every layer of a flow-matching DiT action head of a VLA (GR00T N1.7), meta-trained over sequences of up to 8K timesteps".

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 21 table, [6]: "fast weights persist across decisions"
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Sec. 3.2 Inference: "RoboTTT starts each rollout from the learned initialization W0, updates the fast weights on the current observation, and propagates them to the next timestep." Fig. 2 caption: "Inference starts from the learned initialization W0, updating fast weights on each observation and propagating them forward" (inference panel: "One Mini Batch per Inference").
proposal_claim_checks.correction: Add the scope. Fast weights persist within one rollout (training context up to 8K timesteps; deployed episodes of 1–5 minutes at 30 Hz) and are reset to the meta-learned W0 at the start of every rollout. The one exception is one-shot imitation, where the state persists from the human-video segment across a scene reset into robot execution ("beyond conditioning across episodes"). Nothing persists across rollouts or tasks.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 21: "RoboTTT's DAgger Distillation teaches failure-to-correction adaptation into fast weights"
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Sec. 1: "Through DAgger Distillation, a training procedure that distills DAgger-style (57) failure-to-correction mappings into fast weights, it learns to improve on the fly." Sec. 3.3: "This asymmetry, failures as context and corrections as targets, is precisely how the human's failure-to-correction mapping is distilled into the fast weights." Sec. 3 intro: "a meta-learning method that teaches the policy to improve on-the-fly".
proposal_claim_checks.correction: This is a faithful paraphrase of the paper's own wording, but mechanically it is the slow parameters (W0, the TTT projections and the fine-tuned DiT) that are trained offline on human-correction targets. Fast weights still reset to W0 every rollout; the learned object is the fast-weight update dynamics. A precise version: "offline meta-training (on DAgger data) of slow parameters so that in-episode fast-weight updates implement failure-to-correction."

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 21: DAgger Distillation "should not be conflated with the proposed deployment-time transfer into the slow backbone"
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Sec. 4: "We collect 50 DAgger trajectories each with RoboTTT and GR00T N1.7 as the base policy, and use the pooled 100 trajectories to train all methods." Fig. 10 caption: "Task completion after fine-tuning on a pool of 100 DAgger trajectories." App. A.2: "post-training fine-tunes all parameters." There is no memory-off evaluation, reset gate, retention measurement or repeated cycle anywhere in the paper.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: The distinction holds on substance. RoboTTT never distils the fast-adapted behaviour of a teacher snapshot into a memory-free slow policy, never tests with memory removed, never refreshes fast memory after transfer, and never measures retention. The framing "fast weights vs slow backbone" is imprecise, though: DAgger Distillation, and the standard DAgger baseline it is compared with, are themselves slow-weight updates made between deployment rounds on deployment-collected data, as is the proposal's periodic consolidation. The real differences are the supervision source (human corrections vs samples from an accepted adapted teacher), the objective (meta-learning in-context correction vs making the adapted behaviour memory-free), and the lifecycle (one round, no retention or reset gate vs repeated gated cycles with replay).

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 8 reader table: Internal TTT layer — "Fast memory changes transformer features; strong established comparison [3, 5, 6]"; "Its effects on sampling are less directly isolated, but it may be the most effective option."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: TTT output is added into the hidden stream of every DiT layer (Eq. 3). RoboTTT reports 79% vs 56% average over GDN and one-shot imitation of 6/10 vs 0/10. Evaluations use 20 or 10 real-robot trials, with no seeds or confidence intervals reported; the paper is a July 2026 v1 preprint.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: "Changes transformer features" is correct. "Established" overstates the evidence: RoboTTT is a single recent preprint on 3 tasks in one lab with small trial counts. It is, however, the strongest robot-scale evidence that internal TTT works in a flow-matching policy, so it should be treated as the default internal-TTT baseline, not merely a comparison.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 6: "An internal TTT layer changes hidden features that determine the velocity. It therefore also changes the denoising path… The difference is the intervention location and lifecycle, not whether denoising is affected at all."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: The TTT layers sit inside the DiT, which is evaluated at each of the k denoising steps, and their tokens include the noised action tokens Ã_t (Sec. 3.1). Eqs. 1–2 are "update then apply": W_t is computed from W_{t−1} using the current timestep's tokens before O_t = f_{W_t}(Q_t). The Fig. 2 inference panel shows noised-action tokens in the update mini-batch.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: The statement that RoboTTT also affects every denoising step is correct. It omits a third difference: the write rule and when it happens. RoboTTT writes self-supervised KV bindings of all internal tokens (register, proprio, noised action) at every decision, and because of update-then-apply the fast state used within a denoising step also depends on the current noisy candidate. The proposal writes explicit cue→content associations from selected experience records and holds W_k fixed during the solve (Sec. 3, Sec. 15 step 2). The difference is therefore location plus writer plus lifecycle.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 21 table, research distinction vs [6]: "Explicit external reader and repeated slow consolidation/reset."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: RoboTTT has no external velocity reader; TTT output enters the hidden stream through the tanh gate. There is no consolidation step, and the only reset is to W0 at rollout start. Post-training is per task ("We then post-train on each downstream task at 1K context length for 20K steps"). Limitations (Sec. 6) mention training cost, TTT objectives and RL, but not continual learning.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: This is a valid distinction and RoboTTT does not pre-empt it. Note that RoboTTT's tanh gate addresses a problem similar to the proposal's centering (preserving the pretrained model when memory is added), but only at the start of training. Nothing makes the TTT contribution zero at W=W0, and a learned W0 plus update-then-apply means the empty-memory policy is not the base GR00T policy.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 17 baseline row: "Internal TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP — Same writer data, meta-training targets, and lifecycle; compare both parameter and latency budgets."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: RoboTTT's own ablation compares TTT-MLP and TTT-Linear ("27% worse than the MLP fast model"). Its writer is KVB on all internal tokens every decision, supported by register tokens (+18%), action tokens (+23%) and sequence action forcing (removing it gives ≈0.02).
proposal_claim_checks.correction: Forcing "same writer data" produces a hybrid that is not RoboTTT: stripping KVB on internal tokens, register tokens and sequence action forcing would weaken the internal-TTT baseline. The proposal should add RoboTTT-as-published as a separate baseline, alongside the matched-writer internal-TTT variant.

reading.relevance_to_proposal:
RoboTTT is the closest prior work to Sections 1, 4–8 and 16–18, and it is essentially the "internal TTT" arm of the proposal's reader factorial, already built at robot scale on a flow-matching VLA.

- Sec. 1 requirements. RoboTTT meets Requirement 1 (immediate usefulness from causal experience: one-shot imitation, perturbation recovery, DAgger-learned recovery) and Requirement 2 (interaction during generation: TTT layers in every DiT layer process the noised action tokens at each denoising step, so recall depends on the current candidate). It does not address Requirement 3 (durable transfer surviving memory removal) or Requirement 4 (renewed plasticity after transfer). The proposal's defensible space is 3 and 4 plus the external centered reader.

- Sec. 3 / Sec. 15, what changes when. RoboTTT writes once per decision, which matches the proposal's "update between decisions". It differs in two ways: (i) the write is update-then-apply on the current tokens, including the noisy candidate, so the effective state inside a solve is not frozen; (ii) state resets to a meta-learned W0 at every rollout. The proposal's online loop (Sec. 15, "Do not reset between action chunks") is consistent with RoboTTT's within-episode persistence.

- Sec. 4, Eqs. 3–5. RoboTTT replaces the external residual r = R(m) − R(f_{W0}(q)) with O = tanh(α)⊙f_{W_t}(Q) + O_attn inside each DiT layer. It has no centering, so resetting W does not recover the base sampler. The proposal's exact-reset property (App. B.2) is a real structural difference from RoboTTT.

- Sec. 5, Eqs. 6–8. RoboTTT's inner loss ||f_W(K_t) − V_t||² with learned projections is the robot-scale analogue of l_assoc (Eq. 7). Differences: K and V are learned through the outer FM loss rather than coming from a fixed pretrained target encoder with stop-gradient; writes cover all internal tokens rather than curated cue/content views; the fast net is a 2-layer GeLU MLP in each of 16 layers. The proposal's 16-32-16 tanh MLP (1,072 parameters) is far smaller.
  - The proposal worries that a jointly learned target "requires … anti-collapse checks". RoboTTT's learned V, trained only via the downstream task loss, did not collapse, which is a useful data point.
  - RoboTTT's "Limitations: future work might explore robotics-oriented objectives for the TTT layers" is exactly the proposal's association writer and learned-loss writer [17]. That is an open niche.

- Sec. 6, Eqs. 9–10. Confirms that internal TTT also changes the denoising path. The sensitivity argument applies equally to RoboTTT, so "memory influences every denoising step" is not a differentiator.

- Sec. 7, Eqs. 11–12. RoboTTT's Eq. 5, L = 1/T Σ E||v_θ(Φ_t, A_t^{τ_t}, q_t; W_{t−1}) − (A_t − ε)||², is the proposal's Eq. 12 instantiated at scale. It uses the same interpolant convention and target, a causal prefix W_{t−1}, and loss masking to make pure-context writes, which corresponds to the proposal's "experience prefix + later queries". Differences: RoboTTT samples τ from a shifted Beta rather than uniformly; it truncates meta-gradients with TBPTT; and its post-training unfreezes θ, whereas the proposal freezes θ initially. RoboTTT's pretraining phase (only the new sequence layers trained, GR00T frozen) is exactly the proposal's first-experiment regime.

- Sec. 8 and Sec. 17, reader factorial and baselines. RoboTTT is the concrete internal TTT-MLP baseline. Its ablation already answers MLP vs Linear for a robot FM policy (MLP about 27% better). It also shows that a GDN (delta-rule linear memory) baseline with matched placement, gating and parameter count is informative, and that naive history concatenation can hurt through spurious correlations (Hist. 39.5% vs 57% on Pup Go Car). All three belong in the Sec. 17 baseline list.

- Sec. 11–14, consolidation, retention and refresh. RoboTTT has no counterpart; this is where the proposal's contribution lies. Its results also sharpen the proposal's App. B.4 point. RoboTTT's gains come mostly from history-dependent, non-context-identifiable information: stage tracking under state aliasing, occluded objects, the goal specified only by a video, and recovery after one's own failure. Such information cannot be consolidated into a memory-free student. The consolidable "reusable skill" family must therefore be constructed deliberately (Sec. 16), and reset must not occur mid-episode.

- Sec. 16, stages. RoboTTT's one-shot imitation protocol (same prompt, goal identifiable only from the in-context video) is the real-robot version of Stage B ("hold the current query context fixed while changing the prefix"). Its tasks and protocol (rubric-based completion scores, identical initial placements, perturbation tests) are a ready template for Stage E, where RoboTTT would be the internal-TTT competitor.

- Sec. 18, falsifiable outcomes. "If internal TTT matches or beats the external reader, … abandon the superiority claim." RoboTTT is the specific system that test must be run against, and the proposal should expect it to be strong.

- Sec. 21. The table entry is accurate but too thin. It should note that RoboTTT uses the same flow-matching action-chunk policy class, reads with the noisy candidate at every denoising step, has a meta-learned W0 and KVB writer, resets per rollout, and does per-task post-training without continual evaluation.
novelty_threats: Using memory during generation is not new. RoboTTT already puts gradient-written, persistent fast weights inside a flow-matching VLA action head, where they are used at every denoising step and queried with the evolving noisy action candidate (TTT tokens include Ã_t). The proposal's Requirement 2 ("memory is queried while the action candidate evolves") and its Sec. 6 sensitivity argument therefore cannot be claimed as novel. Only the external, centered location of the correction differs.

Persistence of W_k across decisions and meta-learning of W0 are both pre-empted. RoboTTT persists fast weights across decisions within a rollout, meta-learns W0 and the write projections through the outer FM loss ("W0 is meta-learned through gradients of gradients"), and trains with a causal sequence FM loss with masked pure-context writes. The proposal's Eqs. 1, 8 and 12 and its Sec. 7 meta-training recipe are thus largely pre-empted in their internal-TTT form.

The delayed-cue benchmark idea is already shown on a real robot. RoboTTT demonstrates adaptation from context where the current prompt is uninformative (one-shot imitation, same prompt across configurations: 6/10 vs 0/10 for GDN). This is the real-robot version of the proposal's Stage B, so the proposal's "recall" and "immediate usefulness" claims are not new in robotics; only the lifecycle around them would be.

Corrections as memory writes are pre-empted in the fast-only regime. DAgger Distillation already uses executed failures plus corrections as fast-weight context, meta-trained so that later actions correct earlier failures, and at test time the model absorbs its own corrections. The proposal's writer records ("executed action, correction, outcome", Sec. 5) are covered by this, including on-the-fly recovery without online human feedback.

The "deployment data → slow backbone" loop has precedents. RoboTTT's DAgger rounds are slow-weight fine-tuning on deployment-collected data. Works RoboTTT cites (EVOLVE-VLA 2512.14666, on-the-fly VLA adaptation via test-time RL 2601.06748, TTT-Parkour 2602.02331) "collect extra data on test tasks to fine-tune the entire model". The proposal's slow-update component is therefore not new by itself. Its novelty must rest on distilling fast-adapted behaviour into a memory-free student, with retention and reset gates, over repeated task arrivals.

The case for a nonlinear, gradient-written fast model over a delta-rule memory already has robot evidence. RoboTTT shows TTT-MLP beats TTT-Linear by 27% and beats GDN at matched parameters (79% vs 56%), and GDN fails to benefit from longer context. The proposal hedges on attention equivalence ([4]) but cannot claim the robot-side comparison as new.

The proposal's own falsification criterion is at real risk. RoboTTT's strong internal-TTT results make it plausible that internal TTT will match or beat the external centered reader. If so, the proposal's surviving contributions would be the lifecycle (consolidation, retention, reset/refresh, meta-training across backbone checkpoints) and endpoint vs path distillation.
ideas_to_borrow: Loss masking to separate pure-context writes from supervised queries ("by masking the flow-matching loss on selected timesteps, those timesteps serve as pure context"). This is a clean implementation of the causal prefix / later-query split in the proposal's Eq. 12, and the DAgger Distillation masking pattern (failures as context, corrections as targets) gives a concrete format for the writer's records.

Sequence action forcing. When training on sequences of decisions whose earlier actions are also written into memory, sample the FM noise level independently for each chunk. RoboTTT reports that training without it is unstable and closed-loop performance collapses (≈0.02). Adopt it for any internal-TTT baseline and for any variant that writes action tokens.

TBPTT with carried fast weights and gradients detached at segment boundaries, so that W0 receives gradient only through the first segment. Use it for long-history meta-training in Stages D and E, and label it as a first-order truncation, as the proposal's Sec. 7 requires.

Two-phase training. First train only the new memory layers with the pretrained FM backbone frozen (RoboTTT pretraining), then optionally fine-tune everything. The first phase matches the proposal's "θ frozen initially" regime. Also borrow the gradual context-length curriculum.

Learned per-dimension tanh gate initialised near zero (α=0.001) for adding a memory pathway to a pretrained FM policy. The proposal could combine it with its centering, or at least give the internal-TTT baseline this gate for fairness.

Register tokens (N=16) as a compact carrier of vision-language information into memory, instead of writing all VL tokens. These are candidate cue/query features for Q_φ and the content encoder. The matched-register control (GR00T with registers ≈0.44 vs RoboTTT ≈0.655) is a good template for separating capacity from mechanism.

Baselines to add to Sec. 17: RoboTTT-as-published (internal gated TTT-MLP with KVB writer in all DiT layers); GDN in the same placement with matched gating and parameters; a history-frame policy (which can be worse than no history); a register-token-matched base; and, for correction data, DAgger human-only vs full-trajectory vs DAgger Distillation.

Evaluation protocols: one-shot imitation with an identical prompt, so the target is identifiable only from context; perturbation recovery (remove an installed part mid-episode); rubric-based completion scores plus full-success counts; recorded and reproduced initial object placements across methods; and a plot of performance against history or context length.

Test fast-weight update dynamics beyond the meta-training horizon. RoboTTT attributes weak short-context results to rollouts that exceed the training window, where fast weights update "far beyond the window seen in training" and positional embeddings extrapolate. The proposal meta-trains on 1–16 experiences but deploys continual writes over long lifetimes, so it should run explicit write-count extrapolation sweeps.

GR00T N1.7 is a candidate Stage E backbone. Its flow-matching convention (x=τA+(1−τ)ε, target A−ε, τ=s(1−u), u~Beta(1.5,1), s=0.999) should be matched when meta-training the residual reader, so the reader is trained on the same time distribution as the base.
technical_issues_in_proposal: The Sec. 21 table understates RoboTTT. "Internal gated TTT in a diffusion transformer" omits that it is the GR00T N1.7 flow-matching action-chunk head, the same policy class the proposal targets, and that its fast weights act at every denoising step with the noisy candidate in the query. Without this, readers may think "memory used throughout action generation" (Central question, Requirement 2) is a novel element.

Sec. 6 and Sec. 17 frame the internal-TTT difference as "intervention location and lifecycle" only. RoboTTT also differs in the write rule: self-supervised KV binding of all internal tokens every decision, and update-then-apply on current tokens, so the fast state inside a solve depends on the noisy candidate. The proposal holds W fixed during the solve and writes curated cue→content pairs. Since the proposal's factorial design says to change one axis at a time, it must decide which writer the internal-TTT arm uses and report both variants.

The "same writer data" fairness control (Sec. 17) can inadvertently weaken the internal-TTT baseline. RoboTTT's performance depends on writing action tokens (+23%), register tokens (+18%) and sequence action forcing (collapse without it). A retrofitted TTT-Linear/MLP fed only the proposal's experience records is not RoboTTT. RoboTTT-as-published, and GDN, are missing baselines.

The capacity gap is unaddressed. The proposal's 1,072 fast parameters per episode are orders of magnitude below RoboTTT's per-layer two-layer MLP fast models across 16 DiT layers (each TTT layer adds about 10M slow parameters; the exact fast-weight count is not reported). RoboTTT argues that capacity ("a fast model … offers greater capacity than the vector-valued states of recurrent neural networks") and nonlinearity (Linear is 27% worse) matter for robot histories. The proposal needs a capacity-scaling plan for Stages D and E, and must match fast-state size and latency when comparing readers.

Where fast memory helps in RoboTTT has consequences for consolidation. Most of RoboTTT's gains come from episodic, non-context-identifiable information: stage tracking under visual aliasing, occlusion, a goal given only by video, and recovery after one's own miss. By the proposal's own App. B.4 argument, these cannot be moved into a memory-free slow policy, and a reset mid-episode would destroy them. The proposal should state that consolidation and reset apply only between episodes and only to a deliberately built reusable-skill family, and should expect that much of the value of fast memory on real robot tasks stays episodic.

The proposal's sequence meta-training (Eq. 12 over several later queries per write) does not mention noise-level coupling across queries. RoboTTT found that sharing one noise level across a sequence makes training unstable. If queries in an episode are trained jointly, and especially if executed or noised actions are also written, per-query independent τ should be specified.

Meta-training horizon vs deployment horizon. Stage B uses 1–16 experiences, but the lifecycle envisions continual writes over many decisions and task arrivals. RoboTTT shows degradation when fast-weight updates run beyond the trained window and attributes part of it to positional extrapolation. The proposal lacks an explicit test of write-count and length extrapolation and a policy for positional or time encoding in the writer.

Eq. 11 samples t uniformly. A GR00T or π0-style backbone is trained with a shifted-Beta τ that emphasises the noisy end. A residual meta-trained under uniform t is evaluated on a solver grid whose base field was fit under a different weighting. This is minor, but it should be matched or justified when moving to Stage E.

Sec. 21 says RoboTTT's DAgger Distillation "should not be conflated with the proposed deployment-time transfer into the slow backbone". The proposal's consolidation is also periodic and offline, and RoboTTT's DAgger fine-tuning is also a slow update from deployment data. The distinction should rest on the supervision source and objective (human corrections to meta-train in-context correction, vs adapted-teacher samples to make behaviour memory-free, with retention and reset gates), not on deployment time or fast vs slow weights.

Evidence-strength caution. RoboTTT reports 10–20 real-robot trials per condition, with no seeds or confidence intervals, and some text claims do not match its own figures (1K vs short-context baseline; TTT-Linear vs GR00T; abstract 62% vs body 63%). The proposal should not cite RoboTTT numbers as established effect sizes or as power-analysis inputs, and its own statistical plan (multiple training seeds, paired orders) is appropriately stricter.
stated_limitations: "First, scaling training context length increases training cost; future work could adopt more recent TTT training techniques such as TNT (42)."

"Second, while we develop a principled way of integrating TTT into robot foundation models, future work might explore robotics-oriented objectives for the TTT layers (as explored for vision (24))." The current inner loss is generic KV binding.

"Finally, although RoboTTT improves task performance substantially, it does not handle every failure mode encountered in deployment; combining it with reinforcement learning to optimize task success directly is a natural next step."

Implicit: below 1K pretraining context, performance suffers because "the fast weights are updated far beyond the window seen in training, and positional embeddings extend to unseen positions". Post-training at 1K is shorter than every task episode.
Implicit: "more sophisticated test-time optimizers such as Muon (33; 78) are left to future work". The fast model uses plain gradient descent.

Not acknowledged as limitations but absent from the paper: consolidation of fast-weight knowledge into slow weights, persistence across rollouts (fast weights reset to W0 each rollout), multi-task or continual learning (separate post-training per task), forgetting or retention measurement, latency numbers, seeds and confidence intervals, and the values of the chunk length H and denoising steps k.
cited_works_worth_adding: Laskin et al., 'In-context Reinforcement Learning with Algorithm Distillation', ICLR 2023 (arXiv 2210.14215). RoboTTT frames DAgger Distillation as an instance of it; it is the template for meta-learning an improvement process into in-context or fast-weight dynamics, and a direct alternative to the proposal's consolidation for 'learning to improve'.

Zhang et al., 'Test-Time Training Done Right' (LaCT), arXiv 2505.23884, 2025. The large-chunk, nonlinear TTT that RoboTTT follows, with Muon. Relevant to the internal-TTT baseline design and the capacity arguments.

Tandon et al., 'End-to-End Test-Time Training for Long Context' (TTT-E2E), arXiv 2512.23675, 2025. The inner loop is trained end-to-end from the task loss, the contrast to KVB named on the project page. Relevant to the proposal's learned-loss writer ([17]) and its second-order meta-gradients.

Behrouz et al., 'Nested Learning: The Illusion of Deep Learning Architectures', arXiv 2512.24695, 2025. Cited on RoboTTT's project page, not in the paper. It frames multi-timescale (fast/slow) memories and continual learning in one framework and is a potential novelty threat to the proposal's fast/slow lifecycle that should be checked.

Behrouz et al., 'Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time' (arXiv 2501.00663) and 'It's All Connected … retention, and online optimization' (arXiv 2504.13173). Test-time memorization with explicit retention and forgetting gates. Relevant to the proposal's Sec. 5 decay and proximal-penalty discussion and to the reset/refresh design.

Yang, Kautz, Hatamizadeh, 'Gated Delta Networks: Improving Mamba2 with Delta Rule', ICLR 2025 (arXiv 2412.06464). RoboTTT's main recurrent-memory baseline; a delta-rule fast-weight memory without test-time gradient descent that the proposal should include.
Chen et al., 'Diffusion Forcing', arXiv 2407.01392, 2024. The basis for per-chunk independent noise levels (sequence action forcing), needed for sequence meta-training with written actions.

Ross, Gordon, Bagnell, 'A Reduction of Imitation Learning … No-Regret Online Learning' (DAgger), AISTATS 2011. The correction-data protocol behind DAgger Distillation and the natural source of 'correction' experience records.

Ziakas & Russo, 'VITA: Zero-shot value functions via test-time adaptation of vision–language models', ICLR 2026. Which RoboTTT calls 'the closest setting to ours': fast weights used to adapt value functions for robotics. Directly relevant to the proposal's value/control reader (Sec. 10).

Bai et al., 'EVOLVE-VLA: Test-time training from environment feedback for VLA models' (arXiv 2512.14666); Liu et al., 'On-the-fly VLA adaptation via test-time reinforcement learning' (arXiv 2601.06748); Zhu et al., 'TTT-Parkour' (arXiv 2602.02331). Deployment-time full-model updates in robotics and prior art for the proposal's slow-update-from-deployment component.

Bousmalis et al., 'RoboCat: A self-improving generalist agent for robotic manipulation', TMLR 2024. Iterative self-improvement by fine-tuning on self-generated data across task arrivals; prior art for the proposal's repeated consolidation lifecycle.
Dai et al., 'RoboMME: Benchmarking and understanding memory for robotic generalist policies', arXiv 2603.04639, 2026. A memory benchmark usable in Stage E.

Sridhar et al., 'MemER: Scaling up memory for robot control via experience retrieval' (arXiv 2510.20328); Torne et al., 'MEM: Multi-scale embodied memory for VLA models' (arXiv 2603.03596); Gao et al., 'Gated Memory Policy' (arXiv 2604.18933); Mark et al., 'BPP: Long-context robot imitation learning by focusing on key history frames' (arXiv 2602.15010). Retrieval and keyframe memory baselines for the proposal's 'history tokens / retrieval context' row.

Torne et al., 'Learning long-context diffusion policies via past-token prediction', arXiv 2505.09561, 2025; de Haan et al., 'Causal confusion in imitation learning', NeurIPS 2019; Wen et al., 'Fighting copycat agents', 2020. Spurious-correlation and copycat failure modes of history-conditioned diffusion policies that the proposal's history baselines and writers must control for.

Han et al., 'ViT^3: Unlocking test-time training in vision', arXiv 2512.01643, 2025. The example RoboTTT gives of task-specific TTT objectives, supporting the proposal's association or learned-loss writer as a 'robotics-oriented objective'.
Feng et al., 'In-place test-time training', ICLR 2026. Integrating TTT into existing pretrained layers; relevant to adding fast weights to a pretrained FM backbone without retraining it.

errors_found.reader_claim: Summary: "Context scaling: performance rises monotonically from 128 to 8K pretraining context (71.5% at 8K)"
errors_found.problem: The curve is not monotonic. The reader's own estimates (0.31, then 0.29) show a dip. At 128 and 256 context, RoboTTT also sits below the single-step GR00T baseline.
errors_found.evidence: The project page draws Fig. 8 as an SVG with gridlines at 0 to 100 (y = 330 to 26). Converting the RoboTTT polyline gives 30.8, 29.0, 39.3, 43.9, 54.3, 60.3 and 71.5 for 128 to 8K. The single-step dashed line is at 37.6. The paper itself says only "improves steadily".
errors_found.corrected: RoboTTT's score is roughly flat or dips from 128 to 256 (30.8 to 29.0), then rises steadily from 512 to 8K. It beats the single-step baseline only from 512 on, and beats both baselines only from 2K on.

errors_found.reader_claim: "an MLP fast model beats a linear one by 27%" (Results). This is repeated as "MLP about 27% better" (relevance) and "TTT-MLP beats TTT-Linear by 27%" (novelty threats).
errors_found.problem: The relative change is inverted. The paper says the linear model is 27% worse than the MLP. Measured the other way, the MLP is about 36% better than linear.
errors_found.evidence: Sec. 4: "The TTT-linear variant outperforms the GR00T N1.7 baseline but remains suboptimal, 27% worse than the MLP fast model". From Fig. 12, 0.48/0.655 = 0.73 and 0.655/0.48 = 1.36.
errors_found.corrected: TTT-Linear is about 27% worse than TTT-MLP (≈0.48 vs ≈0.655), so the MLP is about 36% better than linear.

errors_found.reader_claim: "DAgger Distillation on Pup Go Car: +36% for RoboTTT and +29% for GDN, vs about +9% for standard DAgger on average across the four models."
errors_found.problem: The two numbers use different baselines. The 36% and 29% gains are over no DAgger at all, for sequence models only. The 9% is averaged over four models, two of which gain little. So this overstates what DAgger Distillation adds beyond using the same data with standard DAgger.
errors_found.evidence: Sec. 4: "Standard DAgger ... improves the base policies by 9% on average across the four methods, and by 13% on the two sequence models ... DAgger Distillation ... yields a 33% average improvement: 36% for RoboTTT and 29% for GDN." Fig. 10 bars: RoboTTT 0.655 → 0.73 (standard) → 0.89 (Distillation); GDN 0.44 → 0.51 → 0.57. The introduction's "36% better than the same model not trained for this capability" is also measured against no DAgger.
errors_found.corrected: Against standard DAgger on the same model, DAgger Distillation gains about 22% relative for RoboTTT (0.73 → 0.89) and about 12% for GDN (0.51 → 0.57). The matched baseline for the 33% average is standard DAgger on the two sequence models (+13%).

errors_found.reader_claim: Claim check 6 and technical issue 2: "because of update-then-apply the fast state used within a denoising step also depends on the current noisy candidate"
errors_found.problem: This is stated as fact, but the paper never says how the k denoising forward passes interact with the fast-weight update. The reader's own core_mechanism section correctly lists this as "Not specified". The claim is a plausible inference from Eqs. 1–2 and Fig. 2, not something the paper states.
errors_found.evidence: Sec. 3.2 says only "updates the fast weights on the current observation, and propagates them to the next timestep. At each timestep, action chunks are generated with k-step denoising." Fig. 2's inference panel shows noised-action tokens in the mini-batch but does not say which denoising pass's W is propagated.
errors_found.corrected: Label this as inferred. If training-time update-then-apply is reproduced at each denoising pass, then the fast state inside a solve depends on the candidate. The paper does not confirm this, or say which pass's update persists.

errors_found.reader_claim: "at 512 context GDN (≈0.40) roughly equals RoboTTT (≈0.39), despite 'still outperforming GDN at matched lengths'"
errors_found.problem: This is correct but too weak. The exact plotted values show GDN above RoboTTT at 512, so the paper's claim is contradicted, not merely strained.
errors_found.evidence: Converting the project-page SVG gives GDN 40.2 vs RoboTTT 39.3 at 512. Sec. 4: "Below 1K, RoboTTT remains competitive (still outperforming GDN at matched lengths)".
errors_found.corrected: At 512 context, GDN scores slightly above RoboTTT (40.2 vs 39.3), which contradicts the paper's sentence.

errors_found.reader_claim: cited_works: GDN is "a delta-rule fast-weight memory without test-time gradient descent". Novelty threat: "nonlinear, gradient-written fast model over a delta-rule memory".
errors_found.problem: This repeats a questionable framing from the paper. The gated delta rule is one step of online gradient descent, with decay, on the linear key-value binding MSE ||S k − v||², so GDN is also gradient-written. RoboTTT's evidence isolates linear vs nonlinear fast models (plus gating and parameterization), not gradient descent vs none. The reader also accepts without comment the paper's claim that GDN "admits no such meta-learning", even though GDN's projections and gates are trained through the unrolled recurrence by the outer loss.
errors_found.evidence: Sec. 4 says the GDN "updates its state without test-time gradient descent" and "GDN's linear associative state admits no such meta-learning". RoboTTT itself cites Schlag et al. [58], "Linear transformers are secretly fast weight programmers". The TTT-Linear ablation (≈0.48 on Pup Go Car) is close to GDN before DAgger (≈0.44, Fig. 10).
errors_found.corrected: Describe GDN as a gated linear fast-weight memory written by a delta rule, which is itself a one-step gradient update. The robot evidence favours a nonlinear (MLP) fast model, not gradient descent as such.

errors_found.reader_claim: "The paper says TTT-Linear 'outperforms the GR00T N1.7 baseline', but its ≈0.48 in Fig. 12 is below GR00T N1.7's ≈0.53 before DAgger in Fig. 10" (listed as a statement that does not match the figures)
errors_found.problem: This is ambiguous rather than established. The paper's own GR00T scores on Pup Go Car are inconsistent between Fig. 8 and Fig. 10, so it is unclear which GR00T evaluation the ablation text refers to.
errors_found.evidence: Fig. 8's single-step line is 37.6%. Using the main-table Circuit (23) and Gear Bot (47) scores, this implies GR00T on Pup Go Car before DAgger ≈ 3×37.6 − 70 ≈ 43%, which is below TTT-Linear's 0.48. Fig. 10 shows ≈0.53 for the same condition.
errors_found.corrected: The claim holds against Fig. 10's GR00T bar but may hold against the evaluation behind Fig. 8. Report it as an unresolved inconsistency in the paper, not a clear misstatement.

errors_found.reader_claim: Relevance: "RoboTTT's learned V, trained only via the downstream task loss, did not collapse". Also: "RoboTTT's gains come mostly from history-dependent, non-context-identifiable information".
errors_found.problem: Both are interpretations presented as findings. The paper runs no collapse diagnostics and does not break down its gains by information type; its attributions are qualitative.
errors_found.evidence: Sec. 4 gives only qualitative explanations ("First, it tracks task progress ... Second, it exhibits strategic recovery ... Third, it is more precise"). No representation analysis is reported.
errors_found.corrected: Say that task performance is consistent with non-collapsed K/V, and that the qualitative analysis suggests the gains come from episodic, history-dependent information. Neither is measured.

claim_check_overrides.claim: Sec. 17 baseline row: "Internal TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP — Same writer data, meta-training targets, and lifecycle; compare both parameter and latency budgets."
claim_check_overrides.reason: This row makes no factual claim about RoboTTT. It is a design prescription, so accurate or inaccurate does not apply. The reader's critique is valid on substance and I would keep it as a technical issue. RoboTTT's ablation shows internal-TTT performance depends on writing action tokens (+23%), register tokens (+18%) and sequence action forcing (≈0.02 without it). A matched-writer internal-TTT arm should therefore be accompanied by RoboTTT-as-published.

missed_points: Fig. 8's baselines do not match the main results. From the project-page SVG, the dashed baselines in Fig. 8 are single-step 37.6% and short-context 45.7%. Averaging the main-table Circuit and Gear Bot scores with the before-DAgger Pup Go Car bars in Fig. 10 gives about 41% for GR00T and 49% for Hist. GDN is worse: at no pretraining context does it exceed 44.3% in Fig. 8, yet the main-result GDN averages about 52% before DAgger. Only RoboTTT-8K is consistent (implied Pup Go Car 65.5%, matching Fig. 10's 0.655). Two consequences follow. (i) The headline "57% higher than the best short-context baseline (45.6%)" would be about 46% against the main-table Hist (≈49%). (ii) Scores for the same method differ by several points between evaluation rounds, which is about the size of the step between adjacent points on the scaling curve.

With short pretraining context (128 and 256), RoboTTT (30.8% and 29.0%) is worse than the single-step GR00T baseline (37.6%). Adding a meta-trained fast memory to a pretrained flow-matching policy can hurt when the meta-training horizon is short. This is directly relevant to the proposal's short Stage B episodes (1–16 experiences) and to its claim that centering or reset preserves the base behaviour.

Statistical strength, from two-sided Fisher exact tests on the reported counts. Only one-shot imitation is clearly significant: 6/10 vs 0/10 gives p≈0.011. Roof perturbation 15/20 vs 13/20 for GDN gives p≈0.73, and vs 10/20 for GR00T p≈0.19. Full successes on Pup Go Car, 9/20 vs 3/20, give p≈0.08; Circuit 13/20 vs 8/20 gives p≈0.21; Gear Bot 2/10 vs 0/10 gives p≈0.47. The 'perturbation robustness' capability and the Gear Bot 'only method to fully complete' claim are therefore statistically weak.

The DAgger comparison is asymmetric. Of the 100 pooled DAgger trajectories, 50 were collected with RoboTTT, so they are on-policy for RoboTTT. None were collected with GDN or Hist. The main-table Pup Go Car numbers then compare RoboTTT with DAgger Distillation against GR00T with standard DAgger ("All evaluations in this figure predate the DAgger training used for Pup Go Car in the main results").

Every variant is post-trained at 1K context (App. A.2: "Post-training uses a 1K context length") and deployed on episodes of about 1.8K–9K steps. Yet pretraining length still produces large differences. So update dynamics meta-learned during pretraining survive a full-parameter fine-tune at a shorter window and extrapolate at deployment. This is a data point on the proposal's worry about memory interfaces continuing to work after the backbone changes, with the caveat that the TTT layers are co-fine-tuned here. The paper's 'rollout exceeds the training window' explanation for results below 1K sits awkwardly with the fact that every variant saw the same 1K post-training window.

RoboTTT's writer is generic and unconditional: self-supervised key-value binding on raw internal tokens at every decision, with no curated cue or content. It still extracts the goal from a single human video (6/10 vs 0/10). This challenges the need for the proposal's curated cue→content association writer (Eq. 7 with a fixed pretrained target encoder). The proposal should run a writer ablation with a generic KVB-on-stream writer. Granularity also differs: RoboTTT absorbs one 'experience' (a roughly one-minute video) through hundreds of per-chunk fast updates, while the proposal makes one write per discrete record. Saying RoboTTT 'meets Requirement 1' glosses over this difference in regime.

Notation inconsistency in the paper: Eqs. 4–5 sum over t=1..T with W_{t−1}, while Fig. 2 shows T/H mini-batch updates (W_0 … W_{T/H}), one per action chunk. The 8K 'timesteps' are control steps, so the number of fast-weight writes is 8K/H. H is unreported, so the actual write count per episode is unknown. This matters when comparing with the proposal's write counts and its write-count extrapolation sweeps.

The pretraining data is heavily weighted towards long trajectories (Fig. A.1: 41.4% of trajectories are 2K–4K steps and 17.1% exceed 4K). The long-context gains depend on this. A Stage E plan that expects memory benefits would need similarly long, history-dependent pretraining or meta-training data.
The paper's claim of constant inference latency comes with no latency measurement. Pretraining uses the gradual context curriculum and TBPTT, but the TBPTT segment length is unreported.
verification.novelty_threat_assessment:
Medium-high overall, split by component.

High threat to the 'fast memory used throughout action generation' half of the proposal. RoboTTT already places gradient-written fast weights (TTT-KVB, a two-layer GeLU MLP) inside every layer of a flow-matching action-chunk DiT on a VLA (GR00T N1.7). The fast weights act at every denoising pass with the noised action tokens among their inputs. They persist across decisions within a rollout, their W0 and projections are meta-learned with a causal sequence flow-matching loss using the same interpolant and target as the proposal's Eq. 11–12, and loss masking turns segments into pure-context writes. RoboTTT already shows on real robots that a goal identifiable only from context is recalled (one-shot imitation, 6/10 vs 0/10) and that failure-to-correction behaviour can be meta-trained into the fast-weight dynamics (DAgger Distillation). The proposal's Central question parts 1–2, Requirements 1–2, Eq. 1's 'history acts through updated weights', and the Sec. 6 sensitivity argument are therefore not novel in robotics. The Sec. 21 entry ('internal gated TTT in a diffusion transformer; fast weights persist across decisions') understates this overlap.

Low or no threat to the proposal's remaining contributions. RoboTTT has none of the following:
- a centered external velocity reader with exact reset,
- consolidation of fast-adapted behaviour into a memory-free slow policy,
- a memory-off test,
- retention bounds or replay,
- reset/refresh gates or repeated task arrivals,
- meta-training across backbone checkpoints,
- a comparison of endpoint vs path distillation.
It resets to W0 every rollout and post-trains separately for each task.

Practical threat. RoboTTT is the strong internal-TTT competitor the proposal's own falsification test ('if internal TTT matches or beats the external reader, abandon the superiority claim') will be run against, and its evidence (TTT-MLP ≫ linear or GDN) makes an external-reader win uncertain. The defensible novelty is the lifecycle: consolidation with retention, reset and renewed plasticity. RoboTTT's evidence base is thin, though: 10–20 trials per condition, only the one-shot result is significant, and baselines are inconsistent across figures. So it pre-empts the idea more firmly than it settles any effect size.

ref.title: Li, Alim & Azizan, HardFlow: Hard-Constrained Sampling for Flow-Matching Models via Trajectory Optimization (2025/2026, arXiv 2511.08425)
ref.role: Comparison for Sec 9-10 (whole-path energy, value/control reader). Proposal: "Constrained sampling through trajectory optimization of a pretrained FM model." Distinction: memory supplies experience-dependent information rather than only given constraints.
ref.focus: Exact formulation (control of FM ODE, terminal constraints, MPC / trajectory optimization, what is optimized — noise, controls, path?), guarantees, costs, experiments incl. robotics, relation to the proposal's eq 15 and eq 17-20.
