reading.summary:
Problem. Theory (Marr 1971; Hopfield 1982; McNaughton & Morris 1987; Rolls 1989; Hasselmo et al. 1995) proposed that the dense recurrent collaterals of hippocampal CA3 form an autoassociative network that does 'pattern completion'. The abstract defines this as "the ability to retrieve complete memories on the basis of incomplete sets of cues". The paper tests whether NMDA-receptor-dependent plasticity in CA3 is needed for this function at the behavioural and circuit levels.

Method. The authors built CA3-NR1 KO mice. Cre is driven by the KA-1 promoter (line G32-4) and crossed with floxed-NR1 mice, deleting the obligatory NMDA receptor subunit NR1 only in CA3 pyramidal cells, and only in adulthood. By in situ hybridisation, NR1 is intact until about 5 weeks, then deleted, "nearly completely deleted by 18 weeks". The deletion was checked for selectivity. Whole-cell recordings show the NMDA component is lost at the recurrent commissural/associational (C/A) synapse onto CA3, with a DNQX-insensitive component of 27.5±3% in controls vs 3.0±1% in mutants, P<0.0001. The MPP-DG and SC-CA1 NMDA currents are normal. C/A-CA3 LTP is absent (101±11% in mutants vs 202±28% in controls; nearly absent in 9 of 11 mutants), while mossy-fibre CA3 LTP and SC-CA1 LTP are normal. CA3 cytoarchitecture is normal.

Behaviour. Mice aged 18-24 weeks (44 mutants, 37 fNR1, 14 Cre, 11 wild-type) were trained on the hidden-platform Morris water maze with four extramaze cues. There were full-cue probes on days 2, 7 and 13. On day 14 came a partial-cue probe (P4) with "three out of the four extramaze cues ... removed", and on day 15 a no-cue probe (P5). Mutants did not differ in acquisition (escape latency, path length, swim speed, wall-hugging) or in full-cue probe recall. Under partial cues, controls searched "as much as they did in the full-cue probe trial", whereas mutants' search preference "was significantly reduced". Three controls rule out alternative explanations:
- faster forgetting: after P4, retraining with the cues restored gave equal latencies (P=0.32);
- the remaining cue being uninformative or unperceived: mice trained and probed with only one platform-distal cue learned normally;
- recall without any cue: in the no-cue probe, both genotypes were impaired.

Physiology. In CA1, full-cue place fields in mutants were normal in size, integrated firing and coactivity. Complex-spike bursting was reduced, and CA1 interneuron firing was reduced (30.96 vs 12.62 Hz), which suggests compensation. After a 4→1 cue removal with a 2-h delay, mutant CA1 cells showed smaller place fields, lower integrated firing and lower burst frequency. Field centres did not shift. Control cells were unchanged.

Conclusion and caveats. The authors conclude that CA3 NMDA receptors are needed for pattern completion. They interpret this as a deficit of NMDA-dependent storage in the CA3 recurrent network that shows up as a recall deficit under limited cues. The spatial memory itself can be formed and recalled with full cues without CA3 NMDA receptors, apparently through CA1 and EC→CA1 inputs. Caveats they state: perforant-path→CA3 synapses (also NMDA-dependent) may contribute; the knockout is present during both encoding and retrieval; the mutant deficit is a degradation, not a total loss.
reading.core_mechanism:
There are no equations; the mechanism is a conceptual circuit model (Fig. 7 and Discussion).

(1) Storage. During full-cue acquisition, inputs from DG mossy fibres and/or the EC perforant path produce a CA3 ensemble pattern. Recurrent synapses between coactive CA3 cells are strengthened through NMDA receptors: "recurrent fiber synapses are modified in an NR-dependent manner to reinforce this ensemble pattern by strengthening connections between coactive neurons within the ensemble." This is Hebbian autoassociation. In Hopfield terms, the conceptual form is W_rec += x x^T for the full-cue pattern x; this is my paraphrase, not the paper's notation. The CA3→CA1 Schaffer synapses and CA1 also store a trace.

(2) Full-cue recall. The full cue set reactivates the CA3 pattern, which reactivates CA1. In mutants, the CA3 recurrent trace is missing but the "CA1 memory trace is reactivated directly by the incoming cues", so full-cue recall is intact: "Reactivation of previously strengthened recurrent synapses is unnecessary for recall under full-cue conditions".

(3) Partial-cue recall (completion). A partial input activates only part of the CA3 pattern. In controls, "this limited output activates previously strengthened recurrent synapses onto CA3 neurons that had participated in the original full-cue pattern. These recurrently driven cells complete the output pattern of CA3". In mutants, "because of the lack of a memory trace in recurrent synapses, their activation is unable to drive neurons that had participated in the original full-cue pattern". The result is smaller CA1 place fields with reduced firing, and degraded behaviour.

(4) Where the deficit sits. The manipulation removes the plasticity, i.e. the write mechanism, of the recurrent store. CA3 cells still fire and project to CA1. The authors: "our results reflect a primary deficit in NR-dependent memory formation in CA3 that is then revealed as a deficit in recall under limited cue conditions" (supported by the AP5 literature, where blocking NMDA receptors affects acquisition but not retrieval). In the proposal's notation, the closest analogue is a writer switched off (eta_f = 0 in eq. 8, so W_k = W_0) with the readout path left intact. It is not removal of the reader.

(5) Behavioural index. The relative recall index (RRI) is the "averaged ratio of the target platform occupancy of the partial-cue (P4) or no-cue (P5) probe trial to that of the full-cue (P3) probe trial for each animal". The CA1 relative change index is RCI = (firing_A − firing_B)/(firing_A + firing_B) per cell.
key_results: The manipulation is selective and adult-onset. NR1 deletion occurs only in CA3 pyramidal cells: "intact until about 5 weeks of age, starts being deleted thereafter, and is nearly completely deleted by 18 weeks". "There was no indication of deletion of the NR1 gene elsewhere in the brain" by in situ hybridisation. The lacZ reporter did show Cre/loxP recombination in about 10% of DG and cerebellar granule cells and about 50% of facial-nucleus cells, which the authors attribute to differences in detection and substrate susceptibility.

NMDA currents: the DNQX-insensitive component at C/A-CA3 was 27.5±3% in controls (n=10) vs 3.0±1% in mutants (n=5), P<0.0001. It was unchanged at MPP-DG (15.8 vs 16.7%, P=0.96) and SC-CA1 (26.7 vs 29.3%, P=0.78).
LTP: C/A-CA3 was 202±28% in controls (n=5) vs 101±11% in mutants (n=11), nearly absent in 9 of 11 mutants. MF-CA3 LTP (265 vs 259%) and SC-CA1 LTP (232 vs 219%) were normal.

Full-cue water maze acquisition was normal in 18-24-week-old males (mutant n=44, fNR1 37, Cre 14, WT 11). There was no genotype effect on escape latency, distance, swim speed or wall time: F(3,102)<2.5, P>0.05, with no genotype×trial interaction. "There was no difference in the acquisition rate of spatial learning among the four genotypes."

Full-cue probe recall was normal. By day 13 (P3), all genotypes preferred the target quadrant (all P<0.0001). Authors: "no detectable effect on the animal's ability to form and retrieve spatial memory as determined by the standard hidden platform version".

Partial-cue probe (P4, day 14, 3 of 4 extramaze cues removed), target radial-quadrant occupancy from full cue to partial cue: Cre 63.0→55.8% (P>0.2), fNR1 65.9→58.8% (P>0.2), mutant 66.4→44.6% (paired t, P<0.002). Chance is 25%. On absolute platform occupancy, controls showed no change (P>0.9) and mutants were impaired (P<0.01). The RRI differed between fNR1 (n=18) and mutants (n=22) (Mann-Whitney P<0.009).
In the partial-cue condition, mutants "spent the majority of the time at or near the release site at the center of the pool" (Fig. 5H spatial histograms).
Faster forgetting is ruled out. After P4, retraining with the cues restored gave equal latencies for mutants and controls (P=0.32), and both had "reached the asymptotic level of learning by day 12".
No-cue probe (P5, day 15): "robust recall deficits in fNR1 control and mutant mice". The RRI did not differ between genotypes (P=0.9). Both then relearned efficiently with full cues (P>0.15).

Perception and information confound ruled out: when trained and probed with only one platform-distal cue, mutants acquired the memory as well as controls (mutant F(3,36)=5.5, P<0.005; fNR1 F(3,36)=17.7, P<0.005).

CA1 place cells in a familiar full-cue field (188 mutant cells from 5 mice vs 155 control cells from 3 mice): field size 133.1 vs 125.6 px, integrated firing 544.7 vs 549.5, covariance 0.041 vs 0.036 (all n.s.). Complex spike index was 16.84 vs 24.26 and burst frequency 42.18 vs 52.93% (both P<1e-4). CA1 interneuron rate was 12.62 vs 30.96 Hz (P<0.003), consistent with compensation.

CA1 after partial cue removal (4→1 cues, 2-h delay; controls 28/26 cells over 5+5 sessions, mutants 43/47 cells over 6+6 sessions): mutant cells showed reduced burst frequency, field size and integrated firing (post hoc P<0.05 vs all other conditions). Controls were unchanged. Field centres were not shifted in either genotype (P=0.097).

Interpretation: "a direct demonstration of a role for CA3 and CA3 NRs in pattern completion at the behavioral level". The deficit "reflects the degradation rather than the complete loss of spatial memory retrieval", and "this memory can be formed without CA3 NRs".

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Section 2 table: "CA3 manipulation impaired recall from partial cues in mice [8]."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Abstract: "The mutant mice normally acquired and retrieved spatial reference memory in the Morris water maze, but they were impaired in retrieving this memory when presented with a fraction of the original cues." Partial cue removal section: "three out of the four extramaze cues had been removed ... the search preference of the mutant mice for the phantom platform location was significantly reduced". The subjects were 18- to 24-week-old male mice.
proposal_claim_checks.correction:
The statement is true but under-specified, and it leaves out what makes the finding informative.
(a) "CA3 manipulation" was specifically an adult-onset, chronic knockout of the NMDA receptor subunit NR1 restricted to CA3 pyramidal cells. It removed NMDA currents and LTP at recurrent C/A synapses, spared MF-CA3 and SC-CA1 LTP, and left CA3 neurons and their output to CA1 in place. It is a plasticity (write) lesion, not a CA3 lesion or silencing.
(b) What was NOT impaired: acquisition, full-cue probe recall, full-cue CA1 place fields, and learning with a single cue.
(c) Recall with no cues was impaired equally in both genotypes.
(d) The partial-cue deficit was a degradation, not an abolition (66.4%→44.6% quadrant occupancy; chance 25%).
(e) The authors attribute it to missing storage in CA3 revealed at recall, not to a defective retrieval process.
Suggested wording: "Adult CA3-pyramidal-cell NMDA-receptor knockout left water-maze learning and full-cue recall intact but degraded recall when 3 of 4 distal cues were removed [8]."

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Design implication drawn from [8]: "Test cue-dependent association and completion. This does not determine an ANN architecture."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: The paper directly supports testing completion: "Pattern completion, the ability to retrieve complete memories on the basis of incomplete sets of cues". It frames CA3 as a recurrent autoassociative network: "Associative networks, in which memories are stored through modification of synaptic strength within the network, are capable of retrieving entire memory patterns from partial or degraded inputs". The hedge on architecture is appropriate.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: "Completion" is well supported. The paper, however, tests completion of a slowly acquired memory: 13 days of training to asymptote, retrieved from a degraded cue set. It does not test rapid or few-shot cue→content association. In [8], the association itself (cue→platform location) was acquired normally without CA3 NMDA receptors. The implication should say: test recall under degraded retrieval cues relative to the full encoding cues, with full-cue, partial-cue and no-cue probes. The proposal's experiment plan (Sec 16-17) never specifies such a partial-cue probe, even though Sec 8 makes the recurrent variant depend on 'partial-cue and distractor experiments'.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Reference list annotation: "Primary experimental evidence relevant to recall from incomplete cues. Open text."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: The paper is a primary experimental study (genetics, slice physiology, behaviour, in vivo tetrodes). The PMC author manuscript PMC2877140 is free to read.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: Minor point: it is freely readable but not in the licensed open-access subset (Europe PMC: "not open access"), and the supplementary Methods are not easily machine-retrievable.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 1 research position: "Hippocampal memory motivates rapid association, cue-dependent recall, and replay." Sec 2 opening: "The useful analogy is a rapidly learning associative system interacting with a slower system". [8] is the only CA3 evidence cited for this.
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: [8] supports cue-dependent recall and completion only. The water-maze memory was trained over many days: probes on days 2, 7 and 13, and "both the mutant and control animals had reached the asymptotic level of learning by day 12". Acquisition was normal without CA3 NMDA receptors: "this memory can be formed without CA3 NRs." Replay is not studied.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: [8] is not evidence for rapid or one-shot association. The follow-up by the same group, Nakazawa et al. 2003 (Neuron 38:305-315, "Hippocampal CA3 NMDA receptors are crucial for memory acquisition of one-time experience"; PubMed abstract checked), shows that CA3-NR1 KO mice are impaired in rapidly acquiring novel platform locations in a delayed matching-to-place task. That is the appropriate citation for 'rapidly learning associative system'. Replay needs [10]/[11].

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 2: "Calling the hippocampus simply a short-term buffer is misleading: encoding speed, retention duration, and working memory are different properties."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: In [8], the CA3 recurrent trace needed for completion supports a spatial reference memory built over 13 days and probed on day 14. The Discussion states that CA3 and CA1 both hold traces ("This reflects storage of the memory trace within CA3 ... storage of the memory trace within CA1"). The CA3 contribution is not a short-lived buffer.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: The paper supports the point even though the proposal does not cite it for this sentence. It also means the biological 'fast' store is not erased once the slower (CA1) trace exists; that bears on the proposal's reset-and-rebuild step (see technical issues).

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 8: the recurrent Hopfield-like retrieval (eq. 13) "is closer to an attractor-style computational analogy" and should be introduced only if partial-cue and distractor experiments show a benefit.
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: The mechanism [8] implicates is recurrent: "These recurrently driven cells complete the output pattern of CA3". The paper cites Marr 1971 and Hopfield 1982 as the associative-network theory it tests.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: Consistent with [8]. The proposal's recommended first memory (eqs. 6-8: a single-pass feedforward hetero-associative MLP f_W(q_e)≈y_e) is therefore not the mechanism [8] implicates. The proposal hedges correctly ('does not determine an ANN architecture'), but should state that [8] motivates the eq. (13) variant more than the default.

reading.relevance_to_proposal:
Sec 1 (research position) and Sec 2 (biological motivation table): [8] is the proposal's only evidence for cue-dependent associative recall. It supports "completion from partial cues" well. It does not support "rapid association" or "replay", which need other citations (e.g. Nakazawa 2003 Neuron for one-shot acquisition; [10], [11] for replay).

Sec 2 "Which option is closest to this analogy?": [8] supports an associative memory with cue-dependent recall. It says nothing about velocity readers versus attention, so the proposal is right that biology does not rank external correction above attention.

Sec 4 "Slow to fast" ("Slow encoders decide ... which partial cue is written") and Sec 5, eqs. (6)-(8). The writer keys a masked cue view q_e to content y_e with one gradient step per experience. [8]'s paradigm is encode with the full cue set, retrieve with a subset. To match it, the retrieval-time cue subset must differ from the write-time mask. Otherwise a 'partial-cue' success is exact-key lookup, not completion. Any generalisation across cue subsets may also come from the slow query encoder Q_phi, not the fast weights. [8]'s single-cue-training control shows how to separate a lack of completion from a lack of information.

Sec 6 and eq. (3): the query q_t is built from the partially denoised candidate z_t, so early-t queries are inherently degraded cues. My inference, not from [8]: recall quality as a function of t, or of the fraction of cue features removed, is a natural analogue of [8]'s cue-removal manipulation.

Sec 8, eq. (13): [8]'s circuit model (Fig. 7) is recurrent autoassociative completion, which directly motivates the optional Hopfield-like retrieval. The proposal gates that variant on "partial-cue and distractor experiments", but those experiments are not specified in Sec 16-17.

Sec 14 reset gate, criterion 1 ("retains the new reusable behavior on held-out contexts with fast memory removed"): [8] is a clean case where removing the recurrent associative store leaves full-cue performance intact while partial-cue recall degrades. A gate evaluated only under full context would pass while cue robustness is lost.

Sec 16 benchmark B (delayed cue → action-distribution associations, distractors): this tests information absent from the present input. [8] tests information present in degraded form. These are different tests, and the proposal needs both.

Sec 17 metrics: add a paired, per-episode relative recall index (partial-cue / full-cue success) and no-cue floors.

Sec 18 "Recall: A relevant past cue changes the correct later action": [8] suggests a stronger criterion, recall from a subset of the cues present at write time.

Sec 21 related-work table and references: bibliographic entry correct.
novelty_threats: None for the ML contributions. [8] is a 2002 mouse genetics and physiology study and does not anticipate any flow-matching, fast-weight, velocity-reader or consolidation mechanism.

It weakens the motivational narrative, not novelty. [8] shows the CA3 NMDA-dependent store is NOT needed to learn or to recall with full cues ("this memory can be formed without CA3 NRs"). Its measured contribution is robustness to degraded cues. Readers could take the proposal's framing (fast associative memory as the route by which new experience changes behaviour) as biologically grounded by [8], but [8] shows a different division of labour: a parallel direct EC→CA1 pathway acquires the memory, and the recurrent store only adds completion.

The mechanism [8] supports is recurrent autoassociative completion (Marr/Hopfield), which is closer to the proposal's optional eq. (13) and to modern Hopfield or attention retrieval [12] than to the recommended single-pass feedforward velocity reader. Biologically inspired arguments therefore do not favour the recommended design over attention or Hopfield-style baselines; the proposal already concedes this.
ideas_to_borrow: Full/partial/no-cue probe protocol. Write associations with the full cue set, then query with (i) the full set, (ii) a subset (e.g. 1 of 4 cue feature groups, and graded fractions), and (iii) no cue. [8]'s P3/P4/P5 design separates completion from memory presence (P3) and from cue-free guessing (P5).

A per-episode, paired 'relative recall index' (RRI = partial-cue recall / full-cue recall for the same memory state), analysed with paired statistics across seeds and episodes. This separates a completion deficit from overall weaker memory.

Restore-and-retest control. After a partial-cue query, re-query with the full cue to show the association is still present. This rules out forgetting, or memory corruption by reads or by the eq. (13) iterative retrieval, as the cause of partial-cue failure.

Information-sufficiency control, analogous to [8]'s single-cue training. Write AND query with only the reduced cue subset. If that succeeds but full-write/partial-query fails, the failure is lack of completion, not lack of information in the remaining cue.

Dissociation ablation. Disable only the fast writer (eta_f=0, i.e. W_k=W_0; with the eq. 4 centring this returns the base sampler) while keeping the reader, and also build a 'memory without completion' baseline (exact-key lookup or retrieval over history tokens with no generalisation across cue subsets). The diagnostic signature from [8] is no deficit under full cues and a deficit under partial cues.

Graded, distributional readouts instead of binary success: occupancy-style metrics (probability mass of generated 2D actions near the correct mode) and spatial histograms under full vs partial cues (cf. Fig. 5H). In [8], mutant search collapsed toward the release site; the analogue in the proposal is reversion toward the base policy's mode.

Internal analogue of the CA1 place-field analysis. Under partial cues, measure the magnitude and the direction of the velocity correction r (the proposal already plans an integrated velocity-difference measure in Sec 18). [8] found weaker output with preserved location ('degradation rather than complete loss'); the same split (weaker magnitude, same direction) can show a degraded but correctly directed recall.
Add partial-cue probes to Sec 14 reset-gate criterion 1 and to the Sec 17 retention matrix, so that consolidation followed by reset is not accepted when only full-context behaviour survives.

Methodological rigour in [8] worth copying: several control groups, not only the unmanipulated model (fNR1, Cre-only, wild-type littermates; the analogue is controls matched on implementation side effects), experimenters blind to genotype, and confirmation that the ablation hit its intended target (NMDA currents and LTP measured). The ML analogue is confirming that an ablation removes exactly the intended write pathway and nothing else.
technical_issues_in_proposal: The partial-cue experiment is missing from the plan. Sec 8 conditions the recurrent retrieval variant (eq. 13) on 'partial-cue and distractor experiments', and Sec 2 draws 'Test cue-dependent association and completion' from [8]. Yet the Sec 16 benchmark B and the Sec 17 baselines and metrics never define a retrieval-time cue-degradation probe, a no-cue floor, or a completion metric. Benchmark B ('Hold the current query context fixed while changing the prefix') tests information absent from the present input, which is a different property from completion from a degraded cue.

The write/read cue mismatch is unspecified. Eq. (7) writes f_W(q_e)≈sg(y_e) with q_e 'a partially masked view'. If retrieval uses the same masked features, a partial-cue success does not show completion. With a single gradient step per experience (eq. 8) and one mask, the fast MLP is trained only on that key; any generalisation to other subsets comes from Q_phi (a slow parameter) or from MLP smoothness. The proposal needs held-out masks at query time and an ablation that separates slow-encoder completion from fast-memory completion.

Mismatch between the analogy and the ablation. In [8], the associative store is not needed for acquisition or full-cue recall, because a parallel path (EC→CA1, NMDA-dependent CA1 storage) learns the association. In the proposal's strict fast-only protocol (theta frozen), turning off the fast writer removes acquisition entirely. The proposal therefore has no counterpart of the parallel slow-acquisition path during immediate adaptation, and the 'no memory' baseline is not the analogue of the CA3-NR1 KO. A 'memory without completion' baseline (exact-key or non-generalising store) is the missing analogue.

Blind spot in the reset gate (Sec 14). Criterion 1 checks that new behaviour survives fast-memory removal on held-out contexts, presumably with the full context. [8] shows a system can keep full-cue behaviour yet lose robustness to degraded cues when its associative store is removed. A consolidated student can pass the gate and still have lost completion. Criterion 4 only protects facts 'that cannot be inferred from the current context', so skills that are context-identifiable under full cues but need completion under partial cues fall through.

Hidden assumption behind reset-and-rebuild. The proposal assumes that once the slow model reproduces behaviour, the fast store's information is redundant. In [8]'s model, CA3 and CA1 traces coexist at recall and the CA3 trace keeps contributing (completion, and possibly 'a more robust input to CA1 from CA3'). Consolidation in the biological analogue is not copy-then-erase, a point the proposal itself makes for [9] and should apply consistently to the fast-store reset.

Overreach in the motivation. Sec 1 and Sec 2 motivate a 'rapidly learning associative system' with [8], which studied an incrementally trained (13-day) reference memory. Rapid acquisition needs Nakazawa et al. 2003 (Neuron 38:305) or a similar source.

Graded vs binary outcomes: [8]'s effect is a degradation (quadrant occupancy 66.4%→44.6%, chance 25%). Success-rate thresholds alone (Sec 17 targets such as 90% of teacher gain and 2 pp old-task loss) may miss partial-cue degradation. Report cue-fraction curves and distributional metrics under degraded cues.
stated_limitations: Perforant-path contribution not excluded: "plasticity at perforant path-CA3 synapses is NR-dependent (14). Therefore, we cannot exclude the possibility that the feed-forward input to CA3 via the perforant path contributes to the observed pattern completion effects." The authors argue recurrent inputs dominate because they are stronger.

Encoding vs retrieval confound: "Because CA3 NR function is absent during both memory formation and retrieval in CA3-NR1 KO mice, retrieval itself may be affected by NR manipulation." Citing AP5 infusion studies, they favour a primary deficit in CA3 memory formation revealed at recall.

Residual recall: the mutant deficit "reflects the degradation rather than the complete loss of spatial memory retrieval ... may also reflect the existence of additional recall mechanisms independent of CA3 NR function."

Possible compensation: CA1 interneuron firing is reduced in mutants, suggesting "homeostatic reduction of feedback or feedforward inhibitory drive" even under full cues. "Direct measurement of CA3 output may clarify some of these issues."
Recordings were made in CA1 rather than CA3 (justified as the hippocampal output and for comparability). The CA3 completion mechanism is inferred, not observed directly.

Implicit limitations, not emphasised by the authors: the place-cell samples are small (3 control and 5 mutant mice); the knockout is chronic; the reporter showed off-target recombination (about 10% of DG and cerebellar granule cells, about 50% of facial nuclei), although NR1 mRNA appeared intact outside CA3; the study used males only and a single task family (spatial water maze and open field).
cited_works_worth_adding: Marr D. 1971, Philos Trans R Soc B 262:23 ('Simple memory: a theory for archicortex'; title from background knowledge). The original recurrent-autoassociation and completion theory that [8] tests; the natural citation for the eq. (13) attractor variant.

Hopfield JJ. 1982, PNAS 79:2554 ('Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities'). The classic energy-based associative memory; the proposal cites modern Hopfield [12] but not the original, which [8] uses as its model class.
McNaughton BL & Morris RGM. 1987, Trends Neurosci 10:408. Hippocampal synaptic enhancement as a distributed associative memory; the conceptual bridge between plasticity and completion.

Hasselmo ME, Schnell E, Barkai E. 1995, J Neurosci 15:5249 (learning vs recall dynamics at CA3 recurrent synapses, with cholinergic modulation). Directly relevant to separating write and read modes so that retrieval does not overwrite storage, which the proposal handles by updating W only between decisions.

Tsien JZ, Huerta PT, Tonegawa S. 1996, Cell 87:1327, and McHugh TJ et al. 1996, Cell 87:1339. CA1-NR1 KO impairs spatial learning and place-cell coordination. Together with [8] this forms a double dissociation (CA1 plasticity is needed for acquisition, CA3 plasticity for completion), a useful template for the proposal's 'change one axis at a time' ablations.

Morris RGM. 1989, J Neurosci 9:3040. The AP5 (NMDA-antagonist) study showing that blocking NMDA receptors impairs acquisition, not retrieval; [8] uses it to argue that its deficit is at storage (write) rather than readout.

Not cited by [8]; later work by the same group, verified on PubMed. Nakazawa K et al. 2003, Neuron 38:305-315, 'Hippocampal CA3 NMDA receptors are crucial for memory acquisition of one-time experience': the correct citation for the proposal's 'rapidly learning associative system'.

Not cited by [8]; verified on PubMed. McHugh TJ et al. 2007, Science 317:94-99, 'Dentate gyrus NMDA receptors mediate rapid pattern separation in the hippocampal network'. Relevant to the proposal's distractor and interference tests (pattern separation is the counterpart of completion).

Not cited by [8]; verified on PubMed. Nakazawa K, McHugh TJ, Wilson MA, Tonegawa S. 2004, Nat Rev Neurosci 5:361-372, 'NMDA receptors, place cells and hippocampal spatial memory'. A review consolidating the CA1, CA3 and DG knockout results for a more careful Sec 2.

errors_found.reader_claim: core_mechanism (4): the manipulation 'removes the plasticity, i.e. the write mechanism' and leaves the readout intact. 'In the proposal's notation, the closest analogue is a writer switched off (eta_f = 0 in eq. 8, so W_k = W_0) with the readout path left intact. It is not removal of the reader.' Claim-check 1 correction (a) likewise states: 'It is a plasticity (write) lesion'.
errors_found.problem: This is presented as established fact, but it is only the authors' preferred reading, and they explicitly leave the alternative open. NMDA receptors also carry part of the synaptic current at recall time: the DNQX-insensitive component at C/A-CA3 was 27.5% in controls vs 3.0% in mutants. CA1 also shows signs of weaker CA3 drive even under full cues. The eta_f=0 analogy also fails on its own terms. In the proposal, eta_f=0 gives W_k=W_0, so r=0 exactly and every memory effect disappears, including full-cue recall. In [8], full-cue recall survives. The reader makes this same point in technical issue #3, so core_mechanism (4) contradicts the reader's own later analysis.
errors_found.evidence: Discussion: "Because CA3 NR function is absent during both memory formation and retrieval in CA3-NR1 KO mice, retrieval itself may be affected by NR manipulation." Spatial coding in CA1: "pyramidal cells from mutant animals showed a significant decrease in complex spike bursting properties ... This reduction may reflect a decrease in excitatory input from CA3 (27, 28) where NR1 is ablated." Discussion: "even under full-cue conditions, the strength of input from CA3 might be diminished and compensated for through homeostatic reduction of feedback or feedforward inhibitory drive ... Direct measurement of CA3 output may clarify some of these issues." Proposal Sec 4: "Resetting the fast weights then recovers the current base sampler".
errors_found.corrected: The knockout is chronic and adult-onset. It removes NMDA-dependent plasticity at recurrent synapses, and the authors favour a storage deficit on the basis of the AP5 literature (their ref. 37). It also removes the NMDA component of recurrent transmission during recall, and CA3→CA1 drive looks weaker. It is therefore mainly a write lesion with a possible read component, not a clean 'eta_f=0 with the reader intact'. The better ML analogue is ablating the auto-associative component of a two-component memory while keeping a hetero-associative path. Setting eta_f=0 in the proposal's single fast store is not that analogue.

errors_found.reader_claim: Claim-check 5 correction: "the biological 'fast' store is not erased once the slower (CA1) trace exists". Technical issue #5 builds on this: "CA3 and CA1 traces coexist ... Consolidation in the biological analogue is not copy-then-erase". Technical issue #3 and novelty_threat #2 call EC→CA1/CA1 storage a 'parallel slow-acquisition path'.
errors_found.problem: This maps the wrong brain regions onto the fast/slow split. In [8], CA1 and CA3 are both hippocampal sites with NMDA-dependent storage. The paper says nothing about CA1 learning more slowly, and it studies no neocortex, no time course of systems consolidation, and no erasure. The proposal's reset is about fast weights after distillation into the slow backbone θ, which corresponds to hippocampus→neocortex. [8] cannot inform that step. The 'not copy-then-erase' point comes from [9], which the proposal already cites for exactly that.
errors_found.evidence: Discussion: "NRs in area CA1 are critical for the formation of spatial reference memory ... Thus, area CA1 is a major site involved in the storage of spatial reference memory and that this memory can be formed without CA3 NRs." Fig. 7 legend: the model covers only CA3 and CA1 wiring ('Basic wiring of CA3 and CA1'). There is no cortical component and no consolidation interval.
errors_found.corrected: [8] shows a division of labour inside the hippocampus: CA3 recurrent (auto-associative) storage contributes completion, and CA1 NMDA-dependent (hetero-associative) storage supports acquisition and full-cue recall. It is not evidence about fast→slow consolidation or about whether a fast store should be reset. The critique of reset-and-rebuild should rest on [9], not [8].

errors_found.reader_claim: Claim-check 5 evidence: "the CA3 recurrent trace needed for completion supports a spatial reference memory built over 13 days and probed on day 14 ... The CA3 contribution is not a short-lived buffer."
errors_found.problem: [8] does not measure how long the CA3 trace is retained. Training continued daily, and there was an extra training block 1 h after P3 on day 13. The CA3 trace used at P4 on day 14 could therefore be less than a day old. The paper cannot tell a long-lived CA3 trace apart from one that is rewritten every day.
errors_found.evidence: Supplementary Materials and Methods (retrieved from the Wayback Machine copy of the PMC supplement): "The training was carried out in blocks of four trials per day ... for 12 days." Main text: "one more block (4 trials) of training 1 hour after the day 13 probe trial (P3) in order to counteract any extinction ... On day 14, we subjected these animals to a fourth probe trial (P4)".
errors_found.corrected: With respect to [8], the proposal's 'short-term buffer' sentence cannot be checked. It is not attributed to [8], and [8] has no retention-interval manipulation.

errors_found.reader_claim: Claim-check 6 correction and novelty_threat #3: the recommended single-pass hetero-associative MLP "is therefore not the mechanism [8] implicates", and "[8] motivates the eq. (13) variant more than the default".
errors_found.problem: This is overstated. [8] implicates recurrent CA3 synapses (auto-association). It says nothing about whether completion needs iterative attractor dynamics, which is what eq. (13) adds, or whether one recurrent pass is enough; Fig. 7 is compatible with one-step completion. Eq. (7) also trains f_W(masked cue q_e) ≈ content y_e. That is itself a partial-cue→content completion objective for the mask used at write time. The open question is whether it generalises to other masks, not whether it is completion at all. The proposal itself describes eq. (13) as "a finite recurrent retrieval procedure, not a guarantee of global pattern completion".
errors_found.evidence: Discussion: "These recurrently driven cells complete the output pattern of CA3 (red lines, Fig. 7C), which can then drive the full output pattern in CA1." Iterative convergence is not discussed. Proposal Sec 5: "Encode a partially masked view as [q_e] and the content to retain as [y_e]. The full view must already be available when writing."
errors_found.corrected: [8] favours an auto-associative (recurrent) store over a purely hetero-associative one. It does not decide between single-step and iterative (eq. 13) retrieval. Whether the default design completes from partial cues is an empirical question, to be tested with held-out masks at query time.

errors_found.reader_claim: cited_works_worth_adding: Tsien 1996 / McHugh 1996 CA1-NR1 KO "Together with [8] this forms a double dissociation (CA1 plasticity is needed for acquisition, CA3 plasticity for completion)".
errors_found.problem: This is not a double dissociation. Completion was never tested in CA1-NR1 KO mice, and it could not be tested because they fail acquisition. The paper claims 'distinct roles', not a double dissociation.
errors_found.evidence: Discussion: "The same neurotransmitter receptors (i.e., NMDA receptors) can play distinct roles in the mnemonic process depending on where and in which neural circuitry in the hippocampus they are expressed."
errors_found.corrected: Call it a dissociation of roles: CA1 NMDA receptors are needed for acquisition and full-cue place coding, while CA3 NMDA receptors are not needed for these but are needed for partial-cue recall.

errors_found.reader_claim: accessed: "NOT accessed: ... the Supplementary Materials and Methods ... the exact training schedule (trials per day), the cue geometry and the exact RRI formula are known only from the main text".
errors_found.problem: This is not a factual error, but it leaves out details that matter. The supplement can be retrieved (Wayback copy of the PMC supplement PDF, 5 pp.). It shows that the RRI was computed only for a selected subset of animals, and it specifies the cue geometry of P4.
errors_found.evidence: Supplement: "we defined a relative recall index (RRI) as the ratio of the target platform occupancy of the fourth (P4) or fifth (P5) probe trial to that of the third (P3) probe trial for each animal that exhibited significant target platform occupancy (more than 0.23 sec) in P3." Supplement: "For the partial-cue probe trial ... only one of the two cues that were located more distant from the platform during the training session was kept ... mice of each genotype were tested in six different combinations". Supplemental Fig. 1 legend: "The latencies differed significantly between mutant and fNR1 control mice in the P4 partial-cue probe trials (t test, P < 0.003), while no such latency difference was observed in the P3 full-cue trials or P5 no-cue trials."
errors_found.corrected: Training was 4 trials per day for 12 days, with 90 s probes starting from the pool centre. The remaining P4 cue was one of the two platform-distal cues, balanced over 6 of 8 cue/platform combinations. The RRI was restricted to animals with P3 occupancy above 0.23 s, which explains the n=18/22 in Fig. 5I versus 20/23 in Fig. 5F/G. First-crossing latency (Fig. S1) differed only at P4.

claim_check_overrides.claim: Design implication drawn from [8]: "Test cue-dependent association and completion. This does not determine an ANN architecture."
claim_check_overrides.reason: The implication follows directly from [8]'s own framing: the title is 'Requirement for Hippocampal CA3 NMDA Receptors in Associative Memory Recall', and the abstract says "Pattern completion, the ability to retrieve complete memories on the basis of incomplete sets of cues". The architecture hedge is appropriate. The reader's objections are that [8] does not test rapid association and that the proposal's Sec 16-17 plan contains no partial-cue probe. Both are valid, but they criticise the proposal's follow-through, not the accuracy of this sentence, which only recommends what to test.

claim_check_overrides.claim: Sec 2: "Calling the hippocampus simply a short-term buffer is misleading: encoding speed, retention duration, and working memory are different properties."
claim_check_overrides.reason: The proposal does not attribute this sentence to [8], and [8] contains no retention-interval manipulation. Training ran 4 trials/day through day 12, with an extra block 1 h after P3 on day 13, before P4 on day 14. The CA3 trace tested at P4 may therefore be less than a day old. [8] neither supports nor refutes the claim about retention duration. The reader's evidence ('The CA3 contribution is not a short-lived buffer') goes beyond the paper.

missed_points: NMDA receptors in the knockout affect recall-time transmission, not only plasticity. The KO removes nearly all of the NMDA current at C/A-CA3 (27.5% vs 3.0%). CA1 complex-spike bursting and interneuron firing are reduced even under full cues, which the authors attribute to 'a decrease in excitatory input from CA3'. The manipulation is therefore not a pure write lesion. The authors state: 'retrieval itself may be affected by NR manipulation.' For the proposal, an ablation that 'disables only the writer' is not the analogue [8] actually provides.

Selection criterion on the RRI (supplement): it was computed only for animals with P3 platform occupancy above 0.23 s, so animals that did not show full-cue recall were excluded. The partial-cue test was also run on 'randomly selected subsets' after an anti-extinction training block. For the proposal, a paired partial/full recall ratio is only meaningful for memories that pass a full-cue criterion first, and that conditioning and its exclusions should be reported.

The probe order was fixed (P3 full → P4 partial → P5 none, on consecutive days, with retraining in between). It was not counterbalanced, so order and extinction effects are not fully separated from cue condition. Retraining after P4 and P5 was normal, which partly addresses this. For the proposal, randomise or counterbalance the order of cue-degradation probes within an evaluation.

The P4 remaining cue was specifically platform-distal and was balanced over 6 of the 8 cue/platform combinations (supplement). Controls also fell numerically under partial cues (63.0→55.8%, 65.9→58.8%; n.s., P>0.2). 'Same level of recall' is therefore the authors' reading of a non-significant drop. The between-genotype evidence is the RRI Mann-Whitney test (P<0.009), plus the Fig. S1 first-crossing latency (P<0.003 at P4 only). Within-group paired tests that differ in significance are not by themselves a test of an interaction. The proposal should test differences between conditions directly.

Follow-up evidence that directly bears on the proposal's 'few recent experiences' premise (verified via PubMed abstracts). Nakazawa et al. 2003, Neuron 38:305: CA3-NR1 KO mice 'are impaired in rapidly acquiring the memory of novel hidden platform locations ... but are normal when tested with previously experienced platform locations'. Cravens et al. 2006, Eur J Neurosci 24:1771 (not mentioned by the reader): CA3 NMDA receptors are needed for one-trial context discrimination at 3 h but not at 24 h, or after multi-trial training, and 'support contextual pattern separation'. Together these, not [8], are the evidence for a rapid, one-shot CA3 associative store, and they bear on the proposal's distractor and interference tests.

The proposal's plan does contain near-misses that the reader did not mention: Sec 7 'ambiguous present observations' and Sec 18 'noisy or misleading memory'. Neither is a retrieval-time partial-cue probe. The first concerns information missing from the present input; the second concerns corrupted memory, not degraded cues. The reader's conclusion that no completion test is specified still holds, but it should be stated against these items.

In [8], full-cue performance is redundant with the CA3 store: an intact store produces no full-cue advantage at the behavioural or CA1 level. The ML consequence goes beyond the reset gate. Any benchmark scored only under full context will score a memory with completion ability the same as one without it. This is a direct reason for the proposal's Stage B 'advance only when' criteria to include a degraded-cue condition.
verification.novelty_threat_assessment:
None. [8] is a 2002 mouse genetics, slice-physiology, behaviour and tetrode study. It proposes no computational method and anticipates nothing in the proposal's ML contributions: centred velocity residual fast memory, readers applied at every denoising step, meta-trained writers, endpoint vs path FM distillation, and the retention bound or reset gate. Its effect is on motivation and evaluation, and it is modest.
(1) It supports only the 'cue-dependent recall / completion' part of the proposal's biological motivation. It does not support 'rapid association' (the memory was trained 4 trials/day for 12 days and was acquired normally without CA3 NMDA receptors) or 'replay'. The proposal should add Nakazawa 2003 (Neuron) and possibly Cravens 2006 for rapid encoding.
(2) It implies that evaluations run only under full cues cannot detect whether a memory completes from partial cues. That argues for adding partial-cue, no-cue and restore probes to Stage B and to the reset gate.
(3) It favours auto-associative storage but does not settle whether retrieval must be iterative (eq. 13) or single-pass, so it gives no ranking among the proposal's readers. It also does not inform the fast→slow reset step: CA1 and CA3 are both hippocampal, and [8] contains no neocortex and no consolidation time course.

ref.title: Kitamura et al., Engrams and circuits crucial for systems consolidation of a memory, Science 2017
ref.role: Motivation: "Cortical engram cells formed during initial learning and matured with hippocampal support in a mouse fear-memory study" -> consolidation need not be copy-then-erase.
ref.focus: Silent vs active engrams in PFC, role of hippocampus/BLA, time course of maturation and hippocampal engram silencing. Try the PubMed abstract, PMC, or other open copies. Is the proposal's characterization accurate and appropriately scoped? Relevance to the proposal's design (fast memory and slow policy both learn from early on?).
