reading.bibliographic_check:
The citation matches the real paper. Proposal: 'Kitamura, T., et al. Engrams and circuits crucial for systems consolidation of a memory. Science 356:73-78, 2017.'

PubMed record:
- Science 2017 Apr 7; 356(6333):73-78.
- doi:10.1126/science.aam6808; PMID 28386011; PMCID PMC5493329.
- Authors: Kitamura T, Ogawa SK, Roy DS, Okuyama T, Morrissey MD, Smith LM, Redondo RL, Tonegawa S. Kitamura, Ogawa, Roy and Okuyama are marked 'contributed equally'; Tonegawa is the corresponding author.
- Title, volume, pages and year all match. The URL given (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28386011/) is the correct record.

Minor points:
- The PMC author manuscript uses title case ('Engrams and Circuits Crucial for Systems Consolidation of a Memory').
- Its abstract differs trivially from the published one ('remain unknown' vs 'have thus far been unknown'; 'via inputs from both hippocampal-entorhinal cortex' vs 'through inputs from both the hippocampal-entorhinal cortex network').
- The proposal's note ('Mouse contextual-fear experiment; the scope should not be generalized to every memory system. Paper record.') is correct.
reading.summary:
Problem. Systems-consolidation theories hold that memories are first stored in the hippocampal-entorhinal cortex (HPC-EC) and later become cortex-dependent. The paper states the gap: 'little is known regarding specific neural circuit mechanisms underlying the formation and maturation of neocortical memories through interactions with the HPC-EC network.' Using contextual fear conditioning (CFC) in mice, the authors combine several methods:
- activity-dependent engram labelling (c-fos:tTA with TRE-driven ChR2, ArchT, H2B-GFP or TeTX, gated by doxycycline);
- pathway-specific optogenetic inhibition of axon terminals, at encoding or at recall;
- retrograde and trans-synaptic rabies tracing;
- dendritic-spine counts;
- in vivo microendoscopic Ca2+ imaging in medial prefrontal cortex (PFC).
They track three engrams over time: PFC, hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG), and basolateral amygdala (BLA).

Main findings.
(1) The PFC engram is created during Day-1 training and needs inputs from both medial entorhinal cortex layer Va (MEC-Va) and BLA. Blocking MEC-Va terminals in PFC only during conditioning left recall intact at Day 2 and Day 8 but abolished it at Day 15 and Day 22. Blocking BLA-to-PFC terminals during conditioning prevented PFC engram generation and remote memory. At Day 2 the PFC engram is 'immature': natural cues do not reactivate it and inhibiting it does not affect recall. Yet 4 Hz optogenetic stimulation of it already evokes freezing on Day 2.
(2) Over about 12-15 days the PFC engram matures. Natural-cue reactivation appears by Day 13, spine density rises by Day 12, inhibiting it impairs remote recall at Day 12, and Ca2+ context selectivity of shock-responsive cells appears at Day 15.
(3) Maturation needs output from hippocampal DG engram cells. Silencing DG engram output with TeTX blocked all three maturation markers.
(4) The DG engram becomes 'silent'. Natural cues reactivate it at Day 2 but not Day 13, and its spine density falls from Day 5 to Day 15. Optogenetic activation still evokes freezing at Day 15.
(5) The BLA engram formed on Day 1 is maintained, but the input that drives recall through BLA switches: MEC-Va carries recent recall (Days 2 and 8) and the PFC engram carries remote recall (Day 12). The authors summarise this in a new model (Fig. 4L).

Framing. The authors contrast their model with the 'standard model', which holds that 'remote memory is formed in the cortex by a slow transfer of hippocampal memory.' In their account, the hippocampus acts 'for the rapid generation of immature engram cells in the PFC during training and for the subsequent functional maturation of these preexisting engram cells.' They say the lasting but silent hippocampal engram is 'consistent with multiple trace theory'. They also leave open whether it eventually loses the information or still supports recall of episodic details.

Relation to the proposal. The proposal cites [9] only as biological motivation (Sec. 2 table). The description, 'Cortical engram cells formed during initial learning and matured with hippocampal support in a mouse fear-memory study', is accurate, though imprecise: 'cortical' means medial PFC specifically, and formation also needed BLA. The stated design implication ('Both systems can participate early; consolidation need not mean literal copying followed by erasure') is a fair reading of the authors' model, with two caveats:
- 'participate early' holds for encoding, not for expression;
- the paper shows necessity, not mere possibility.
The main issue is that the proposal's own lifecycle does not implement this implication. θ is frozen while experiences are written. Slow learning happens only at periodic consolidation, by distilling the behavior of the adapted teacher. Fast weights are then reset to W_0. That is behavioral copying followed by erasure, closer to the 'standard model' the paper argues against, plus a multiple-trace-like episodic store B. It is a legitimate engineering choice, but the citation points to an untested design alternative: an early, gated slow trace matured with fast-memory support.
reading.core_mechanism:
This is an experimental neuroscience paper with no equations. Below is the circuit model (Fig. 4L) as a plain-text timeline, with the manipulations that establish each link.

ENCODING (Day 1, CFC = context A + footshock):
- HPC-EC (MEC-Va) -> PFC and BLA -> PFC inputs together generate PFC engram E_PFC, in an 'immature' state.
  - Evidence: CFC raises PFC c-Fos+ cells but context-only exposure does not. Blocking MEC-Va terminals in PFC during CFC blocks both this c-Fos rise and the light-evoked freezing from the labelled PFC cells. Blocking BLA terminals in PFC during CFC blocks E_PFC generation and remote memory. Rabies tracing shows monosynaptic MEC-Va -> E_PFC input (n = 212 mCherry+ MEC cells).
- In parallel, DG engram E_DG and BLA engram E_BLA are formed. MEC-Va -> BLA input during CFC is required for memory at every time point.

RECENT RECALL (Day 2-8):
- Route: context -> HPC-EC -> MEC-Va -> BLA (E_BLA) -> freezing.
  - MEC-Va -> BLA terminal inhibition at retrieval impairs Day 2 and Day 8.
  - PFC-engram -> BLA terminal inhibition at Day 2 has no effect.
  - ArchT inhibition of E_PFC at Day 2 has no effect.
- E_PFC is not reactivated by natural cues on Day 2 (H2B-GFP/c-Fos overlap), but 4 Hz optogenetic drive (not 20 Hz) evokes freezing on Day 2. The trace is present but not accessible through natural cues.

MATURATION (Day 2 -> ~Day 12-15), requiring E_DG output:
- E_PFC changes: natural-cue reactivation appears in context A at Day 13; spine density is higher at Day 12 than Day 2; shock-responsive (SR) cells (~11% of imaged cells) become context-selective (A > B) at Day 15 but not Day 1 or 2.
- TeTX in E_DG (VAMP2 lost in CA3 stratum lucidum; ChR2 activation of DG fails to raise CA3 c-Fos) blocks all three maturation markers. The route is 'presumably through MEC-Va'.

REMOTE RECALL (Day 12-22):
- Route: context -> (unknown route, perhaps thalamus) -> mature E_PFC -> BLA (E_BLA) -> freezing.
  - E_PFC inhibition impairs Day 12.
  - E_PFC -> BLA terminal inhibition impairs Day 12.
  - MEC-Va -> BLA inhibition at retrieval has no effect on Day 15 or 22.
  - MEC-Va -> PFC inhibition at retrieval has no effect at any time.
- E_BLA is reactivated equally at recent and remote time points, so it is maintained.
- E_DG becomes 'silent': natural-cue reactivation is lost by Day 13, spine density is lower at Day 15 than Day 5, but optogenetic activation still evokes freezing at Day 5 and Day 15.

Functional abstraction, in ML terms:
- slow trace S (PFC) is written at t=0 but gated out of behavior;
- fast trace F (HPC) drives behavior early;
- S becomes accessible over time with F's support;
- F loses natural-cue accessibility but is retained;
- a shared downstream readout (BLA) is stable, and its input source switches from F to S.

Statistics: unpaired and paired t-tests, one-way ANOVA with Tukey-Kramer, KS tests on spine-density distributions, P < 0.05. Sample sizes are in the supplement, which I did not access.
key_results: MEC-Va -> PFC terminal inhibition only during Day-1 conditioning 'disrupted memory at Day-15 and Day-22, but not at Day-2 or Day-8' (Fig. 1F). The same inhibition during recall 'did not affect memory retrieval' (Fig. 1G). MEC-Va input to caudal ACC or retrosplenial cortex was dispensable, both during conditioning and at recall (Fig. 1J-L).
CFC raised PFC c-Fos+ cells relative to homecage, while context-only exposure did not. MEC-Va terminal inhibition during CFC 'inhibited the observed increase of c-Fos+ cells in the PFC' (Fig. 1O).

PFC engram cells labelled with ChR2 during CFC: 'Blue light stimulation at 4 Hz, but not the conventional 20 Hz ... induced freezing behavior on Day-2 and Day-12 in an unconditioned context' (Fig. 1S). This freezing was prevented by MEC-Va -> PFC inhibition during CFC (Fig. 1T, U).

Trans-synaptic retrograde tracing: PFC engram cells 'receive monosynaptic input from MEC-Va cells' (Fig. 1V-X; n=212 mCherry+ cells in MEC). The paper also reports input from medial-dorsal and anteromedial thalamus (fig. S5).

Natural-cue reactivation of PFC engram (H2B-GFP+ cells, c-Fos): 'preferentially reactivated in Context-A on Day-13 but not Day-2' (Fig. 2C). Spine density of PFC engram cells was higher at Day 12 than Day 2 (Fig. 2E).
ArchT inhibition of PFC engram cells at retrieval 'did not affect recent memory (Day-2), however at the remote time-point (Day-12) memory retrieval was disrupted' (Fig. 2F).

Ca2+ imaging in PFC: about 11% of cells were shock-responding (SR) and about 89% were not (SNR). SR-cell activity was higher in context A than context B 'on Day-15 but not on Day-1 or Day-2'. Population average event rates did not change, and the rate-difference-index distribution showed only 'a small but significant difference' (fig. S9).
BLA -> PFC terminal inhibition during CFC 'disrupted the generation of PFC engram cells' and 'inhibited remote memory formation' (Fig. 2Q, R).

TeTX in DG engram cells (VAMP2 lost in CA3 stratum lucidum; ChR2 fails to raise CA3 c-Fos) blocked three things: natural-cue reactivation of PFC engram at Day 12, the spine-density increase, and the rise in SR-cell context discrimination (Fig. 3B-H). The main text does not report the behavioral effect of TeTX on remote recall.

DG engram: 'preferentially reactivated in Context-A on Day-2 but not Day-13' (Fig. 3L). Spine density at Day 15 was lower than at Day 5 (Fig. 3O). 'On both Day-5 and Day-15, optogenetic activation of DG engram cells induced freezing' (Fig. 3Q). The paper frames this as silent, not erased.

MEC-Va -> BLA: inhibition during CFC impaired retrieval 'at all time-points'. Inhibition during retrieval impaired Day 2 and Day 8 but left Day 15 and Day 22 intact. PFC-engram -> BLA terminal inhibition left Day 2 intact but impaired Day 12 (Fig. 4B-E). BLA engram cells were 'reactivated equally well by the conditioned context at both recent and remote time-points' (Fig. 4H, K).

Authors' model: 'the prefrontal memory engram is already generated, albeit in an immature form, on Day-1 of training via inputs from both HPC-EC and BLA'. It contrasts with the standard model's 'slow transfer of hippocampal memory'. 'HPC engram cells formed during training became silent with time; they are not retrieved on Day-14 by natural recall cues but are still re-activatable optogenetically for recall.' The text says Day-14 here, while the experiment used Day-13.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 2 table, evidence column: 'Cortical engram cells formed during initial learning and matured with hippocampal support in a mouse fear-memory study [9].'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Abstract: 'neocortical prefrontal memory engram cells, critical for remote contextual fear memory, were rapidly generated during initial learning via inputs from both hippocampal-entorhinal cortex and basolateral amygdala. After their generation, the prefrontal engram cells, with support from hippocampal memory engram cells, became functionally mature with time.' Discussion: 'The immature PFC engram cells functionally, structurally, and physiologically matured during the subsequent few weeks and this process required inputs from HPC engram cells presumably through MEC-Va.'
proposal_claim_checks.correction: The claim is accurate as a summary. For precision: 'cortical' here means medial PFC (prelimbic). MEC-Va input to caudal ACC and RSC was dispensable. Formation also needed BLA input (shock information), not only hippocampal input. 'Hippocampal support' was shown as the necessity of DG-engram output (TeTX) for cellular and physiological maturation markers. The route is only 'presumed' to run through MEC-Va, and the main text does not report the behavioral effect of TeTX. Suggested wording: 'Prefrontal engram cells were formed during initial learning (requiring entorhinal and amygdala input) and matured over ~2 weeks in a manner requiring hippocampal engram output, in mouse contextual fear conditioning [9].'

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 2 table, implication column: 'Both systems can participate early'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Encoding: 'PFC memory engram cells for CFC were rapidly formed during Day-1 training ... but they were not retrievable with natural recall cues.' Blocking MEC-Va -> PFC only during Day 1 abolished Day-15/22 memory while Day-2/8 memory survived (Fig. 1F). At Day 2, inhibiting the PFC engram 'did not affect recent memory' (Fig. 2F), and natural cues did not reactivate it (Fig. 2C). 4 Hz optogenetic drive did evoke freezing at Day 2 (Fig. 1S).
proposal_claim_checks.correction: 'Participate' holds for encoding and plasticity, not for expression. Early on, only the hippocampal-entorhinal route drives recall; the cortical trace is written but gated out of behavior until it matures. The paper also shows more than 'can': in this paradigm, early cortical encoding was necessary for remote memory, and a hippocampal trace alone plus later support did not produce it. The implication should read along the lines of 'both systems are written at encoding; the slow trace is initially not expressed and matures with fast-system support'.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 2 table, implication column: 'consolidation need not mean literal copying followed by erasure.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: 'The standard model ... hypothesized that remote memory is formed in the cortex by a slow transfer of hippocampal memory. In contrast, in our study the role of the hippocampus in cortical memory is for the rapid generation of immature engram cells in the PFC during training and for the subsequent functional maturation of these preexisting engram cells.' 'Our finding of the lasting hippocampal engrams (Fig. 3Q) is consistent with multiple trace theory ... at the post-consolidation stage, the hippocampal engrams were not activatable by natural recall cues, but with optogenetic stimulation.' 'Although we did not determine how long after encoding this "silent state" of the hippocampal engram lasts, we speculate that the hippocampal engram will eventually lose the original memory information.'
proposal_claim_checks.correction: This is supported as the authors' interpretation. 'No copying': the cortical trace predates the maturation phase. However, the paper does not identify what the hippocampal 'support' carries. TeTX blocks DG engram output wholesale, so the data cannot rule out that maturation relays content, e.g. by replay. 'No erasure': shown only up to about Day 15, which is at the limit of the ChR2 labelling ('unable to maintain labeled DG engram cells with ChR2 beyond 12 days', extended 'by a few days'). The authors themselves speculate eventual loss. Better: 'need not be a late transfer; the hippocampal trace became silent (inaccessible to natural cues) rather than demonstrably erased, within ~2 weeks'.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Reference list note for [9]: 'Mouse contextual-fear experiment; the scope should not be generalized to every memory system.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: All experiments use CFC in wild-type or c-fos:tTA transgenic mice. The authors themselves restrict region generality: 'MEC-Va input into the cACC or RSC is dispensable for this process. For remote memory, the PFC may thus have a distinctive role compared to other neocortical areas.'
proposal_claim_checks.correction: One could add that it is also a single-trial Pavlovian association on a days-to-weeks timescale. Its mapping to action or skill learning in robots is purely analogical.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 2 'What we will claim': 'We will not claim anatomical fidelity ... or that resetting fast weights reproduces biological forgetting.' Also Sec. 2 opening: 'Calling the hippocampus simply a short-term buffer is misleading.'
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: The DG engram persists and is sufficient to drive freezing at Day 15 even though it is no longer reactivated by natural cues (Fig. 3L, 3Q). The paper states 'Our finding of the lasting hippocampal engrams (Fig. 3Q) is consistent with multiple trace theory'.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: This is consistent with [9], and the disclaimer is appropriate: [9] shows silencing, not erasure, so a hard reset of W to W_0 is not a biological analogue. These statements are not attributed to [9] in the proposal; they are listed here because [9] directly bears on them.

reading.relevance_to_proposal:
Sec. 2 (biological motivation table). [9] is the only cited evidence for the proposal's claim about how the fast and slow systems relate over time. The evidence column is accurate. The implication column is roughly right, but it merges 'encoded early' with 'expressed early' and understates necessity (see claim checks).

Sec. 3 'What changes when' and Sec. 15 lifecycle. θ is updated only 'During accepted consolidation', using adapted teachers. During the online loop only W_k changes, and φ, θ are held fixed ('Detach fast state between deployment writes'). So on the question 'do fast memory and slow policy both learn from early on?', the answer for the proposal is NO: only the fast memory learns at encoding. In [9], the slow (cortical) system is plastic at encoding, and that early encoding is necessary for the remote memory. The only 'early slow participation' in the proposal is representational: slow encoders pick the cue and content that get written (Sec. 4 'Slow to fast'). That is not the same as forming a memory-specific slow trace.

Sec. 4 'Fast to slow learning' and Sec. 11 endpoint FM distillation (Eqs. 21-22), path distillation (Eq. 23). Transferring adapted samples into a memory-free student is behavioral copying. The later reset (Sec. 14) is erasure. The proposal therefore implements, in behavioral rather than parameter space, the copy-then-erase scheme that its [9] implication says is unnecessary. This is not an error, since Sec. 2 calls these 'explicit engineering choices', but the motivation and the design do not match.

Sec. 11 'Gradual rather than one-shot transfer ... Keep the accepted teacher and fast memory available until transfer passes its predefined gate. Failed transfer is a reason to retain the memory.' This fits [9] well: blocking DG-engram output (TeTX) during the consolidation period blocked PFC maturation. Likewise, the candidate student is not deployed until it passes the gate, just as the immature PFC engram does not drive natural recall until it matures.

Sec. 14 (reset gate, two stores) and App. B.4 (hidden episodic facts). [9]'s hippocampal engram becomes silent rather than erased, and the authors suggest it 'may still participate in the successful remote recall of discrete episodic details'. That matches the proposal's retained episodic store B for non-context-identifiable facts. The hard reset of W to W_0, however, has no counterpart in [9].

Sec. 14 'The slow model also changes the meaning of fast adaptation'. In [9], the downstream BLA engram stays stable while its driving input switches from MEC-Va (recent) to the PFC engram (remote). This suggests a stable shared readout during handover, which could ease the writer/reader miscalibration the proposal flags after backbone changes.

Eqs. (4)-(5). The additive, centered residual works for post-hoc consolidation followed by reset and rebuild. It is not directly compatible with a [9]-style variant where θ also learns early: the correction would be counted twice unless r is gated or re-written against the updated backbone.

Sec. 16-17 experiments and baselines. [9]'s design offers a protocol for the proposal's lifecycle experiments (Stage C/D):
- time-window-specific lesions (block a pathway only at encoding, only during consolidation, or only at retrieval);
- measurement at both recent and remote time points;
- natural-cue versus direct-activation tests.
It also suggests missing arms: an early gated slow trace, a direct slow fine-tuning baseline, and an archived ('silent') fast-weight-snapshot baseline.
novelty_threats: No direct novelty threat. [9] is an experimental mouse neuroscience paper with no computational method, flow-matching, TTT, or consolidation algorithm. It pre-empts none of the proposal's technical contributions (the external velocity reader, centered residual, endpoint/path distillation, reset gate).

Indirect weakening of the biological framing. Taken literally as a template, [9]'s key result argues against a pure 'fast-write now, transfer later' lifecycle, which is what the proposal implements. Blocking cortical encoding only at training left recent memory intact but abolished remote memory, so delayed support from the hippocampal trace was not enough. A reviewer could say the proposal cites [9] for an implication that its own design contradicts.

[9]'s account is one of several and is contested. It sets itself against the standard model and calls its findings consistent with multiple trace theory. Later work (DeNardo et al. 2019, Nat Neurosci; I read the abstract only) reports that 'PL neurons TRAPed during later memory retrievals are more likely to be reactivated and make larger behavioral contributions to remote memory retrieval compared to those TRAPed during learning'. That suggests the remote cortical ensemble is not simply the matured encoding-time engram. The biological motivation should be presented as one account, not settled fact.
ideas_to_borrow: Add an 'early slow tag' arm, the analogue of PFC engram generation on Day 1. At each fast write, also make a small slow update: a low-rank slow adapter, or a few θ steps with replay, at a fixed and matched compute budget. Gate it out of behavior (e.g. expression weight 0) until a validation gate passes. During the consolidation cycle, 'mature' it using fast-memory-teacher targets. Compare against the current post-hoc distillation from scratch, at equal slow-update FLOPs and sample counts. This directly tests the design implication the proposal attributes to [9].

Add a 'support-blocking' ablation, the analogue of TeTX in DG engram cells. During the maturation/consolidation phase, deny the student the adapted fast-memory teacher, e.g. train only on raw episodic records in B, or with the fast residual disabled. This tests whether fast memory is needed for slow maturation or only for immediate adaptation.

Borrow [9]'s time-window lesion design. Disable the fast write, fast read, or teacher (a) only at encoding, (b) only during the consolidation window, or (c) only at retrieval/deployment. Measure performance at a 'recent' point (before consolidation) and a 'remote' point (after one or more consolidation/reset cycles). This separates encoding-time from consolidation-time contributions far better than a single before/after comparison.

Borrow the 'availability vs accessibility' test, i.e. natural cue vs direct optogenetic drive (Fig. 1S vs Fig. 2C; Fig. 3L vs 3Q). For the memory-off student, compare performance given only the natural context with performance when the hidden task or fact embedding is supplied explicitly. For a reset fast memory, test whether an archived W can be re-activated. This makes App. B.4's distinction between context-identifiable and hidden facts measurable.

Add a 'silent archive' baseline. Instead of erasing W at reset, store pre-reset fast-weight snapshots, which are tiny (1,072 parameters each), keyed by a task cue. Retrieve them only on explicit cue. Compare against consolidation plus reset plus episodic replay under the same byte budget. This is the engineering analogue of a silent engram and a standard parameter-isolation continual-learning baseline.

Keep a stable downstream readout during handover, the analogue of the maintained BLA engram with its switching input. For example, freeze or strongly regularize the final velocity head and reader R_φ across consolidation checkpoints. Consider a graded handover, annealing the residual as the student matures, with the residual re-written against the new backbone, instead of a single accept-then-reset step.

Report specificity controls in the style of [9]'s context A vs context B tests. After consolidation, the new behavior should appear in the trained contexts but not leak into unrelated or held-out contexts. [9] notes the remote memory 'is conditioned-context specific'.

Report a time course across several consolidation cycles, as [9] tests recall at Days 2, 8, 12-15 and 22. Track when the slow student becomes sufficient with memory off, and when the fast memory stops being necessary, rather than a single transfer measurement.
technical_issues_in_proposal: The motivation and the design do not match. The Sec. 2 table pairs [9] with 'Both systems can participate early; consolidation need not mean literal copying followed by erasure'. The actual lifecycle (Sec. 3 'What changes when', Sec. 11, Sec. 14-15) is different: θ is frozen during all online writes; slow learning happens only in periodic consolidation by distilling the adapted teacher's behavior (a behavioral copy); the fast weights are then reset to W_0 (erasure). The proposal should either (a) add and test an early-slow-trace arm, or (b) say explicitly that its lifecycle is a standard-model-like 'transfer then reset' engineering choice, with an episodic store playing a multiple-trace-like role, and that [9] motivates an untested alternative.

The design implication understates [9]. Blocking MEC-Va -> PFC or BLA -> PFC only during encoding abolished remote memory while recent memory stayed intact (Figs. 1F, 2R). In that paradigm, early cortical encoding was necessary, not merely possible. Artificial networks do not share this constraint, since a student can be distilled at any time. The proposal should say so, rather than let [9] appear to support its delayed-transfer design.

'Participate early' conflates encoding with expression. The Day-2 PFC engram was neither reactivated by natural cues nor needed for recent recall (Figs. 2C, 2F), yet 4 Hz optogenetic drive already evoked freezing (Fig. 1S). Any early-slow-learning variant would therefore need a gate that keeps the immature slow trace out of behavior.

The additive centered residual (Eqs. 4-5) double-counts under early slow learning. If θ absorbs part of a correction that W_k also stores, v_θ' + r_{φ,W_k} over-corrects. The proposal avoids this only through reset and rebuild at consolidation boundaries (Sec. 14). A concurrent-learning variant would need gating, or re-writing and re-centering the residual against the updated backbone.

'Hippocampal support' in [9] is shown only as the necessity of DG-engram output (TeTX) for PFC maturation markers: c-Fos reactivation, spine density, and Ca2+ context discrimination in shock-responsive cells. The main text does not report a behavioral remote-memory test under TeTX. The paper cannot say whether the support carries content (replay/transfer) or is permissive, so '[9] shows consolidation is not copying' goes beyond the evidence.

Silencing is not erasure, and the paper shows no deletion. The DG engram stays optogenetically sufficient at Day 15. The authors 'did not determine how long ... this "silent state" ... lasts' and speculate eventual loss. The proposal's hard reset has no support in [9], which the proposal already concedes in 'What we will claim'. Given how cheap 1,072-parameter snapshots are, archiving the fast weights is an obvious missing baseline.

The two-system analogy leaves out a component that [9] shows is essential. The BLA engram is formed on Day 1, maintained throughout, and serves as the stable downstream node whose driving input switches from MEC-Va to PFC. The proposal's fast/slow/episodic-store decomposition has no explicit stable shared readout. That matters for its own concern that consolidation miscalibrates the writer and reader (Sec. 14).

Missing baseline in the Sec. 17 table: direct slow learning from the new experiences without fast memory, e.g. online fine-tuning of θ with old-behavior replay or EWC at a matched compute and memory budget. The 'no replay / no consolidation / no refresh' ablations remove components but never test the parallel slow-learning alternative that [9] motivates. Sec. 14 already warns against comparing with baselines 'forbidden from making equivalent slow updates'.

Scope and precision. 'Cortical' should read 'prefrontal (prelimbic)', since MEC-Va input to cACC and RSC was dispensable. The paradigm is a single-trial Pavlovian aversive association over days to weeks; robot skill or action-distribution learning is arguably closer to procedural learning, whose consolidation systems differ. The reference note partly acknowledges this. The Sec. 2 table implication is phrased more generally than the evidence allows.

The proposal's framing ('inspired by complementary memory roles', a 'rapidly learning associative system interacting with a slower system that captures reusable structure') is Complementary Learning Systems theory, which [9] cites (McClelland et al. 1995). The proposal cites no CLS source, and no schema-dependent rapid neocortical learning work (Tse et al. 2007; McClelland 2013). That is the computational literature most directly relevant to the replay-based retention in Eq. (26), and to when a slow policy may learn quickly.
cited_works_worth_adding: McClelland JL, McNaughton BL, O'Reilly RC. Why there are complementary learning systems in the hippocampus and neocortex. Psychol Rev 102:419 (1995) [ref 4 in [9]]. The canonical computational statement of fast hippocampal plus slow neocortical learning with interleaved replay to avoid catastrophic interference. It is the direct theoretical ancestor of the proposal's fast/slow lifecycle and of its replay-based retention term (Eq. 26), yet the proposal does not cite it.

McClelland JL. Incorporating rapid neocortical learning of new schema-consistent information into complementary learning systems theory. J Exp Psychol Gen 142:1190 (2013) [ref 7], and Tse D et al. Schemas and memory consolidation. Science 316:76 (2007) [ref 6]. Both show the slow system can learn quickly when new information fits prior structure. This bears on the proposal's split between context-identifiable skills (consolidable into θ) and arbitrary facts, and on whether slow learning should wait for consolidation cycles.

Lesburgueres E et al. (Bontempi lab), Science 331:924 (2011) [ref 14], on early tagging of cortical networks being required for enduring associative memory. [9] explicitly links its immature PFC engram to this cortical 'tagging'. It is the direct precedent for an 'early slow tag' design arm.

Nadel L, Moscovitch M. Memory consolidation, retrograde amnesia and the hippocampal complex. Curr Opin Neurobiol 7:217 (1997) [ref 5]. Multiple trace theory: the hippocampus keeps episodic detail. This is the biological counterpart of the proposal's retained episodic store for non-context-identifiable facts (Sec. 14, App. B.4).

Ryan TJ, Roy DS, Pignatelli M, Arons A, Tonegawa S. Engram cells retain memory under retrograde amnesia. Science 348:1007 (2015) [ref 24]. It establishes 'silent engrams' (information available but not accessible by natural cues), which motivates an availability-vs-accessibility evaluation of the memory-off student and of reset fast memory.

Kitamura T et al. Adult neurogenesis modulates the hippocampus-dependent period of associative fear memory. Cell 139:814 (2009) [ref 33]. A biological mechanism that clears hippocampal dependence and regulates how long the fast system is needed. It is the closest biological analogue to the proposal's Requirement 4 (renewed plasticity) and the reset/refresh timing in Sec. 14.

Frankland PW, Bontempi B. The organization of recent and remote memories. Nat Rev Neurosci 6:119 (2005) [ref 11]. A standard review of systems-consolidation models that frames the standard model vs alternatives debate the proposal invokes.

Kim JJ, Fanselow MS. Modality-specific retrograde amnesia of fear. Science 256:675 (1992) [ref 3], and Tayler KK et al. Reactivation of neural ensembles during the retrieval of recent and remote memory. Curr Biol 23:99 (2013) [ref 29]. Classic temporally graded hippocampal dependence and ensemble-reactivation time courses, useful if the proposal wants primary evidence for a shifting fast/slow dependence over time.
stated_limitations: The duration of the hippocampal 'silent state' was not determined: 'Although we did not determine how long after encoding this "silent state" of the hippocampal engram lasts, we speculate that the hippocampal engram will eventually lose the original memory information ... Alternatively, the silent engram cells may still participate in the successful remote recall of discrete episodic details.'

Technical limit on how long the DG engram could be labelled: 'We were unable to maintain labeled DG engram cells with ChR2 beyond 12 days with injection of AAV9-TRE:ChR2-mCherry.' The split-Cre strategy extended labelling only 'by a few days'.

The route to the mature PFC engram is unknown: 'The route through which contextual stimuli activate the mature PFC engram is unknown. Most likely the information processed in a variety of sensory cortices reaches the PFC via the thalamus.'
The pathway for hippocampal support is inferred, not shown: maturation 'required inputs from HPC engram cells presumably through MEC-Va.'

Identifying SR cells as engram cells is an inference: 'These results ... suggest that the SR cells may be the PFC memory engram cells.' Population Ca2+ effects were modest: 'a small but significant difference was revealed in the cumulative distribution curves of a rate difference index.'

The findings are region-specific: MEC-Va input into cACC and RSC was dispensable, and 'the PFC may thus have a distinctive role compared to other neocortical areas.' A single paradigm (contextual fear conditioning in mice) was studied.

Minor internal inconsistencies in the author manuscript: the text says HPC engrams 'are not retrieved on Day-14' while the experiment used Day-13; the MEC-Va -> BLA retrieval result is cited as 'Fig. 3C' but belongs to Fig. 4C. Sample sizes and methods are in the supplement, which I could not access.

errors_found.reader_claim: Summary and core_mechanism: blocking MEC-Va terminals in PFC only during conditioning 'abolished it [recall] at Day 15 and Day 22'. Technical issue 2: blocking MEC-Va->PFC or BLA->PFC only at encoding 'abolished remote memory'.
errors_found.problem: This overstates the effect. The paper says 'disrupted', and the plotted data show a partial reduction, not abolition. I read the values off the Fig. 1F plot in the published PDF (N=10 per group): at D15, eYFP ~51% vs eArchT ~27% freezing; at D22, ~42% vs ~23%. Substantial freezing remains.
errors_found.evidence: Text: 'Axon terminal inhibition with optogenetics of MEC-Va cells within the PFC during Day-1 of CFC disrupted memory at Day-15 and Day-22, but not at Day-2 or Day-8 (Fig. 1F).' Published Fig. 1F (ref09_figs/f-002.jpg) shows eArchT still at ~23-27% freezing at the remote points.
errors_found.corrected: Encoding-time inhibition of MEC-Va->PFC reduced remote freezing by roughly half (significant at D15 and D22). Recent memory was unaffected. Remote memory was impaired, not abolished.

errors_found.reader_claim: Summary: 'Blocking BLA-to-PFC terminals during conditioning prevented PFC engram generation and remote memory.' Technical issue 2 cites Fig. 2R as showing remote memory was abolished.
errors_found.problem: Two problems. (a) Fig. 2R (N=6 per group) is significant only at D22 (~52% vs ~36%). D15 (~57% vs ~44%) is not starred. So remote memory was reduced at one time point, not prevented or abolished. (b) 'Engram generation' was measured only as the CFC-induced rise in PFC c-Fos+ cells (Fig. 2Q, N=4 per group). No activity-dependent engram labelling was used in this manipulation.
errors_found.evidence: 'Optogenetic inhibition of BLA terminals in the PFC during CFC disrupted the generation of PFC engram cells (Fig. 2Q). The terminal inhibition during CFC also inhibited remote memory formation (Fig. 2R).' Published Fig. 2R: a star appears only above D22. Fig. 2Q is labelled 'each group N=4 mice' and plots c-Fos (%) in PFC.
errors_found.corrected: BLA->PFC terminal inhibition during CFC blocked the CFC-induced increase in PFC c-Fos+ cells (N=4 per group). It also reduced freezing at D22 (N=6 per group), but not significantly at D2, D8 or D15.

errors_found.reader_claim: Bibliographic check: 'Kitamura, Ogawa, Roy and Okuyama are marked contributed equally'.
errors_found.problem: Only Kitamura, Ogawa and Roy carry the equal-contribution asterisk. Okuyama does not.
errors_found.evidence: Published PDF byline: 'Takashi Kitamura,1* Sachie K. Ogawa,1* Dheeraj S. Roy,1* Teruhiro Okuyama,1 Mark D. Morrissey,1 ...' with '*These authors contributed equally to this work.' The PMC manuscript matches ('Dheeraj S Roy 1,*, Teruhiro Okuyama 1,').
errors_found.corrected: Kitamura, Ogawa and Roy are co-first authors (equal contribution). Tonegawa is the corresponding author.

errors_found.reader_claim: Relevance section: '[9]: blocking DG-engram output (TeTX) during the consolidation period blocked PFC maturation.' The reader treats this as analogous to a time-window-specific support block.
errors_found.problem: The TeTX manipulation is not restricted to a window. TeTX is expressed in DG engram cells tagged during Day-1 CFC and blocks their output chronically from then on, including at the Day-13 (or '12 days after CFC') natural-cue test. Unlike the optogenetic manipulations, it cannot separate a role during the consolidation window from a role at test time. The paper also never tests recent memory under TeTX.
errors_found.evidence: 'When the mice were subjected to CFC, DG engram cells were labeled with TeTX ... TeTX expression in HPC engram cells inhibited the reactivation of PFC engram cells ... during exposure to the conditioned context 12 days after CFC (Fig. 3E, F).' Fig. 3E schedule: CFC Day-1 OFF-Dox, then test at Day-13. No time-restricted silencing is reported.
errors_found.corrected: Chronic silencing of DG-engram output from encoding onward prevented the PFC maturation markers. The data do not isolate the consolidation window.

errors_found.reader_claim: Accessed/core_mechanism: 'Sample sizes are in the supplement, which I did not access' and 'I have not seen sample sizes per group'.
errors_found.problem: This is not a false statement, but it is a significant omission. Most sample sizes are printed in the figure panels, which are part of the main text in both the PMC page and the published PDF (freely available at the MIT lab site, which the reader thought was paywalled). They show that several key claims rest on very small samples.
errors_found.evidence:
From the published figures (ref09_pub.pdf):
- Fig. 1O and 2Q: 'each N=4 mice'.
- Fig. 1S: N=6.
- Fig. 1U: N=5.
- Fig. 1X: rabies tracing in N=3 mice.
- Fig. 2C: N=5 per group.
- Fig. 2F: N=10.
- Fig. 2G-O: Ca2+ imaging in N=3 mice, with SNR n=28 and SR n=26 cells analysed.
- Fig. 2R: N=6/6.
- Fig. 3F: N=5.
- Fig. 3H: TeTX imaging, SNR n=10 and SR n=8 cells.
- Fig. 3L: N=5-6.
- Fig. 3Q: N=4 mice.
- Fig. 4B: N=12/12.
- Fig. 4C: N=10/10.
- Fig. 4E: N=10.
- Fig. 4H, K: each N=5.
errors_found.corrected: Report the Ns. In particular, the claim that the DG engram is 'silent, not erased' (Fig. 3Q) rests on N=4 mice with an optogenetic freezing increase of about 5-6 percentage points (Day 5 ~9->14%, Day 15 ~14->20%). The Ca2+ maturation evidence comes from 3 mice.

errors_found.reader_claim: core_mechanism: TeTX in E_DG caused 'VAMP2 lost in CA3 stratum lucidum'.
errors_found.problem: Minor overstatement.
errors_found.evidence: 'greatly reduced immunoreactivity of vesicle-associated membrane protein 2 (VAMP2) ... within the stratum lucidum (s.l.) in hippocampal CA3'
errors_found.corrected: VAMP2 immunoreactivity was greatly reduced.

errors_found.reader_claim: Relevance section: 'During the online loop only W_k changes, and φ, θ are held fixed ("Detach fast state between deployment writes")'.
errors_found.problem: The conclusion is right, but the quoted phrase does not support it. 'Detach fast state' refers to stopping gradients through the fast state at deployment, not to freezing θ. The correct support is elsewhere in the proposal.
errors_found.evidence: Proposal Sec. 3 'What changes when?': θ is updated only 'During accepted consolidation'. The sanity-check table reads: 'Reset equality and frozen slow ... slow weights unchanged during writes.'
errors_found.corrected: Cite 'What changes when?' and the 'frozen slow' check as evidence that θ is fixed during writes.

claim_check_overrides.claim: Sec. 2 table, implication column: 'Both systems can participate early'
claim_check_overrides.reason: This is a permissive design implication ('can'), and [9] directly supports it. PFC, DG and BLA engrams are all formed on Day 1: 'the prefrontal memory engram is already generated, albeit in an immature form, on Day-1 of training via inputs from both HPC-EC and BLA'. 'Participate' does not claim early behavioral expression. The reader's split between encoding and expression, and the point that early encoding was necessary for normal remote memory, are useful caveats for the design. But understating what the evidence shows does not make the claim inaccurate. Downgrading it to partially_accurate reads 'participate' as 'drive recall', which the proposal does not say.

missed_points: At the remote time point, DG engram cells were not just 'not preferentially' reactivated. They were reactivated significantly LESS than non-engram DG cells. Published Fig. 3L 'Remote A→A' (N=6): GFP+ ~5% vs GFP− ~9%, with a significance star. The text says only 'preferentially reactivated in Context-A on Day-2 but not Day-13'. This makes the 'silent' state stronger: natural cues actively underrecruit the old trace.

Effect sizes in the key sufficiency tests are small. 4 Hz stimulation of the Day-2 PFC engram raised freezing from ~9% to ~14% (Fig. 1S, N=6). 20 Hz DG-engram stimulation raised it from ~9% to ~14% at Day 5 and from ~14% to ~20% at Day 15 (Fig. 3Q, N=4). The PFC and DG engrams were also stimulated at different frequencies (4 Hz vs 20 Hz). The 'available but not accessible' interpretation that the reader wants to borrow therefore rests on modest, small-N effects.

PFC engram formation is conjunctive, i.e. salience-gated. CFC raised PFC c-Fos, but neither context-only exposure (Fig. 1O) nor shock-only (Fig. 2Q) did. The authors: 'the generation of the PFC engram cells requires both context exposure and footshocks.' For the proposal, this means the biological slow system tags only experiences that coincide with a teaching or salience signal carried by BLA. It maps onto the proposal's gated, validation-filtered consolidation. It also argues against an ungated 'early slow tag' on every fast write, which is what the reader's first borrowable idea proposes.

The time course of maturation is not resolved. The paper samples only an early point (Day 2) and a remote point (Day 12, 13 or 15), so 'matures over ~12-15 days' is an interpolation. The Fig. 4L model itself labels maturation 'Day-2-11' and remote recall '> Day-12'. The model's maturation panel also draws an active BLA->PFC arrow, but BLA->PFC was manipulated only during CFC, so that part of the model is untested.

The TeTX experiment has no behavioral readout, recent or remote, and silencing is chronic from encoding onward. So 'hippocampal support' is established only for cellular and physiological markers, and is not tied to a consolidation window. The reader noted the missing behavioral test but not the lack of temporal specificity.

The published Science version is freely available (MIT lab site, ref09_pub.pdf). The reader's text-only reading missed all information carried in the figure images: Ns, effect magnitudes, and which time points reach significance. Two inconsistencies also persist in the published text: 'Fig. 3C' should be Fig. 4C, and the text says 'day 14' where the experiment used day 13. The published Discussion cites '(Fig. 2)' where the manuscript cites '(Fig. 3)' for the maturation role. The manuscript Fig. 2 legend says 'Day-1, Day-2 and Day-3' where the published version says day 15.

The reader quotes DeNardo et al. 2019 selectively. The same abstract says 'PL activity during learning is required to initiate this time-dependent reorganization in PL ensembles', which partly corroborates [9]'s point that early cortical encoding is necessary. It is not simply a contesting result. The quoted sentence is also truncated: the original reads 'compared to those TRAPed during learning or early memory retrieval'.

In the reader's framing, the proposal copies and then erases. That understates the proposal's own design. Sec. 11 already says 'Keep the accepted teacher and fast memory available until transfer passes its predefined gate'. Sec. 14 keeps a finite episodic store and says 'replay retained recent experiences through the writer when their information is still needed'. So information is not simply erased at reset; it stays available in B and can be rewritten. That is closer to [9]'s silent-but-retained trace than the reader allows. The motivation/design tension is real but mild, and the proposal explicitly declares these as 'explicit engineering choices'.

ref.title: Maingret et al., Hippocampo-cortical coupling mediates memory consolidation during sleep, Nature Neuroscience 2016
ref.role: Motivation: "Manipulating hippocampal-cortical sleep coordination affected rat memory consolidation" -> replay/coordinated slow learning.
ref.focus: The closed-loop ripple-delta-spindle coupling manipulation, direction of effect (enhanced memory?), task. Is the proposal's summary accurate? Implications for designing replay timing/coordination in an ML system.

This matches the paper. The authors are Nicolas Maingret, Gabrielle Girardeau, Ralitsa Todorova, Marie Goutierre and Michaël Zugaro. The article is Nat. Neurosci. 19, 959-964 (2016), doi:10.1038/nn.4304, PMID 27182818. Europe PMC confirms volume 19 and pages 959-964.
