It is rectification/reflow ([13] Sec. 5.3, Theorem 47; Liu et al. 2023b; Liu 2022), and [13] Remark 50 connects it to consistency-model distillation. Theorem 47 already shows that such distillation preserves the endpoint map while straightening paths. Any 'efficiency' advantage the proposal hopes to find for path distillation (Sec. 12, 'The experiment this enables') must be measured against reflow, which is designed for exactly that.

App. C's points (non-Gaussian and Gaussian-mixture priors, the expressivity limit of a deterministic start, the difference between fixed-interpolant FM and the SB, spurious intermediate modes from a poor source/coupling) are all treated in [13] (Sec. 2.3, 3.1, 3.4, 4.2, App. A). App. C adds no new mathematics beyond them; it should cite [13] and be presented as background.

[13] does not threaten the core contribution: persistent gradient-written fast memory read inside every denoising step, the centered residual reader, and the consolidation/refresh lifecycle. It contains no memory, test-time adaptation or continual-learning material.
ideas_to_borrow: Smoothed path distillation, a new arm for Sec. 12 and the endpoint-vs-path experiment. Train on x_t = Γ_t + γ(t)z with target V_t + γ̇(t)z, where z ~ N(0,I) is fresh and γ(0) = γ(1) = 0, γ > 0 on (0,1) (e.g. γ = √(a t(1−t)) or sin²(πt), [13] Table 2). The endpoint laws are unchanged. By the mechanism of Theorem 6 (|g| ≤ e^{−γ²|k|²/2}), the intermediate density is positive and C^∞ and the field is smooth, which removes the collapse in (33). This interpolates between faithful path distillation (γ → 0) and more regular fields.

Rectified (same-seed straight-line) distillation baseline from [13] Sec. 5.3 and Liu et al. 2023b: x_t = (1−t)ε + t a_T(ε), target a_T(ε) − ε, using the teacher's own seed ε with no selection. It keeps the teacher's noise-to-action map (Theorem 47: same map under Assumption 46) but discards the intermediate path. Comparing (a) fresh-noise endpoint FM, (b) same-seed rectified FM and (c) teacher-path distillation separates the effect of the coupling from the effect of the path shape. As proposed, the endpoint-vs-path comparison confounds the two.

Invertibility or crossing diagnostic, the analog of Assumption 46. Monitor det(∂Γ_t/∂ε), or check h·Lip_z(v_θ + r) < 1 for Euler teachers. When the path map is invertible, path distillation should reproduce per-seed trajectories, not just marginals. When it is not (hidden-history mixtures, path-energy refinement in Sec. 9, large steps), expect averaging. Report this alongside endpoint-vs-path results so they can be interpreted.

Metrics and error control. For ODE students, do not rely on L2 velocity loss or likelihood proxies ([13] Lemma 21). Report W2, energy distance or sliced W2 between student and teacher endpoint laws. Optionally also learn a denoiser η_z and sample the student as an SDE with ϵ tuned by [13] eq. (2.49), since Theorem 23 then bounds KL by the regression losses.

Quantitative path-distillation bound in the style of Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden 2023 (Prop. 3) and the proposal's own App. B.1. For a Lipschitz student with constant L and the same-seed coupling, W2²(student_1, teacher_1) ≤ C_L · L_path(θ), with C_L = (e^{2L}−1)/(2L). The proof: Gronwall on d/dt(X−Γ) = [b_s(X) − b_s(Γ)] + [b_s(Γ) − V_t], then Cauchy-Schwarz. It needs no regularity of b*, only a Lipschitz student, and it holds even with hidden-history mixtures, though loosely there because of the irreducible variance. This would strengthen App. A beyond an exact-minimizer statement.

Analytic multimodal sanity check. Extend Sec. 19 using [13] App. A eq. (A.4)-(A.5), the closed-form ρ(t) and b for Gaussian-mixture sources and targets. This gives exact teacher fields and exact b* for path-vs-endpoint comparisons, for multimodal adaptation, and for measuring the spurious intermediate modes of Gaussian-mixture priors (App. C).

For App. C deterministic or history-initialized starts: use a diffusive interpolant or SDE on an initial window [0,δ], then switch to an ODE ([13] Theorem 31 and its proof), or a full-rank conditional Gaussian base (Remark 34; Albergo et al. 2023, data-dependent couplings). This makes "another source of randomness" concrete.

Algorithmic tips from [13] Sec. 6, if score or denoiser objectives are used (e.g. for SDE students or the value reader): antithetic sampling (±z) for the terms with γ^{-1}, which the authors "found necessary for stable training"; learning the denoiser η_z rather than s; capping t0 and tf, or letting ϵ(t) vanish near the endpoints.
technical_issues_in_proposal: Misattribution of scope (Sec. 12, App. A). [13] proves the transport equation only for C^2-in-time interpolants I(t,x0,x1) + γ(t)z under Assumption 5 (positive C^2 endpoint densities with finite Fisher information; E|∂tI|^4 and E|∂t²I|² bounded). Piecewise-linear teacher paths have second time derivatives that are Dirac masses at the knots. Paths from an adapted sampler also depend on history or memory state (W_k), success selection, or path refinement, so they are not of the form I(t,x0,x1). The weak continuity equation for general absolutely continuous paths is true, but the citation should be Liu 2022 (Sec. 3, eq. 13-14, Def. 3.1, Thm 3.2) or Ambrosio-Gigli-Savaré 2008, with [13] cited for the smooth special case and the regularization mechanism.

"The argument does not require those marginals to have smooth densities [13]" gets [13] backwards. [13]'s density and regularity results come from the Gaussian latent variable, and without it the paper only says the results 'formally stand' (Remark 11). Rephrase, and cite [13] Sec. 4.2 for the collapse phenomenon, which [13] already describes for γ = 0.

Missing remedy. App. A concludes that endpoint distillation should be the first baseline because b* can be singular, but it never considers the standard stochastic-interpolant fix: adding γ(t)z to the teacher paths ([13] Remark 11, Sec. 4.2-4.3). Adding it guarantees a positive smooth ρ(t) and a smooth field on (0,1) while keeping both endpoint laws. The 'smoothed path distillation' option should be discussed or tested.

Missing positive condition for per-seed reproduction. "It does not generally reproduce each same-seed trajectory" is true only when paths cross. For one context, one history and a deterministic Euler teacher with h·Lip(v_θ + r) < 1, the map ε -> Γ_t is a bijection. Then b*(z,t) = v(ψ_t^{-1}(z), t_i), with ψ_t(y) = y + (t − t_i)v(y,t_i), is Lipschitz in z, and the student ODE reproduces each teacher polygon exactly (the analog of [13] Theorem 47 under Assumption 46). Averaging, and possible irregularity, come from hidden-history mixtures, trajectory crossings in path-energy refinement (Sec. 9), or large steps. The proposal should state this and measure it.

Confounded experiment. Endpoint FM (21) uses fresh independent noise (product coupling), while path distillation (23) uses the teacher's own noise-action coupling. A difference between the two cannot be attributed to 'preserving intermediate evolution' without a same-seed straight-line (rectified/reflow) baseline ([13] Sec. 5.3; Liu et al. 2023b). Reflow is also the natural baseline for any efficiency or straightness claim.

Stochastic or non-ODE teachers. If any adapted sampler injects noise (SDE sampling, stochastic refinement, dropout), piecewise-linear interpolation of the nodes gives a b* that varies strongly within each step. For example, one Euler-Maruyama step X1 = X0 + √(2ε)ξ with X0 ~ N(0,1) gives b*(z,t) = 2εt z/(1+2εt²), which is 0 at the knot t = 0. A student evaluated only on the knot grid then recovers the drift, not the marginal-preserving velocity, and under-disperses (variance 1 instead of 1+2ε). [13] Sec. 3.1 makes the same point in continuous time: the ODE velocity for a diffusive process is the drift minus a score correction (b = u − s in eq. 3.7-3.9). App. A should restrict the claim to deterministic teachers, or require solvers that resolve within-step variation, or target the probability-flow velocity explicitly.

Only exact minimizers are covered. App. A's reproduction claim holds at the population optimum only. [13] Lemma 21 and Remark 24 show that an L2 velocity error does not control KL for ODE models. Give an approximate guarantee instead: a W2 bound via a Lipschitz student and the same-seed coupling, as in the proposal's own B.1 and Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden 2023 Prop. 3. Otherwise evaluate with W2 or energy distance.

Prior art for the retention bound. Eq. (27)-(28) (Gronwall plus Cauchy-Schwarz with a same-noise coupling) is essentially Proposition 3 of Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, ICLR 2023 ("W2²(ρ1, ρ̂1) ≤ e^{1+2K̂} H(v̂)" for a K̂-Lipschitz v̂), the paper that [13] extends. The proposal's constant (e^{2L}−1)/(2L) is sharper, but the argument should be credited.

App. C cites [1,2] for non-Gaussian and Gaussian-mixture sources, but [2] (Lipman et al.) builds Gaussian-source paths. [13] (Sec. 2.3, Remark 2, App. A) is the appropriate citation. Its eq. (A.4) shows that an independent coupling between an N0-mode source and an N1-mode target creates N0·N1 intermediate modes ('spurious intermediate modes', Fig. 4). This quantitative fact supports App. C's caution and should be stated.

Sec. 11's "sufficiently regular target distributions" can be made precise with [13] Assumption 33 (ρ1 ∈ C^2, ρ1 > 0, ∫|∇log ρ1|²ρ1 < ∞). Nearly deterministic teacher action laws, or laws concentrated on a low-dimensional set, violate it near t = 1.
cited_works_worth_adding: Q. Liu, "Rectified Flow: A Marginal Preserving Approach to Optimal Transport", arXiv:2209.14577, 2022 (cited in [13]). This is the correct rigorous source for the weak continuity equation of general time-differentiable processes: eq. (14) ρt(h) − ρ0(h) − ∫ρs(∇h·v_s)ds = 0, the 'rectifiable' condition (locally bounded v^X and a unique ODE solution), and Theorem 3.2 on marginal preservation. It should back the proposal's eq. (32).

X. Liu, C. Gong, Q. Liu, "Flow Straight and Fast: Learning to Generate and Transfer Data with Rectified Flow", ICLR 2023 (cited in [13] as Liu et al. 2023b). Reflow, i.e. same-seed coupling distillation, is the missing baseline for path-vs-endpoint consolidation and for efficiency claims.

M. S. Albergo and E. Vanden-Eijnden, "Building Normalizing Flows with Stochastic Interpolants", ICLR 2023 (cited in [13]). Its Proposition 3, W2²(ρ1, ρ̂1) ≤ e^{1+2K̂}H(v̂) for a Lipschitz field, is prior art for the retention bound (27)-(28) and gives a template for a quantitative path-distillation guarantee.

M. S. Albergo, M. Goldstein, N. M. Boffi, R. Ranganath, E. Vanden-Eijnden, "Stochastic Interpolants with Data-Dependent Couplings", arXiv 2023 (cited in [13]). It covers conditional or history-dependent base distributions and couplings, and is directly relevant to App. C's history-initialized sources (A2A) and to a z0 = μ(H) + Σ(H)^{1/2}ε style source.

A. Tong et al., "Conditional Flow Matching: Simulation-free Dynamic Optimal Transport", arXiv:2302.00482, 2023 (cited in [13]). FM with non-Gaussian sources and OT couplings; relevant to App. C's source/coupling discussion.

C. Léonard, "A Survey of the Schrödinger Problem and Some of Its Connections with Optimal Transport", DCDS 2014 (cited in [13]). A standard reference for the relative-entropy and hydrodynamic Schrödinger-bridge formulations used in App. C alongside [18].

Y. Song, P. Dhariwal, M. Chen, I. Sutskever, "Consistency Models", ICML 2023 (cited in [13], Remark 50). Distillation of a flow into a one-step map; a related consolidation and distillation baseline if solver-step efficiency becomes a claim.

C. Lu et al., "Maximum Likelihood Training for Score-Based Diffusion ODEs by High Order Denoising Score Matching", ICML 2022 (cited in [13]). Background for why L2 velocity or score matching does not control likelihood of ODE models; relevant if the proposal evaluates students by likelihood.
stated_limitations: Remark 11: without the latent variable (γ = 0), "we cannot guarantee the spatial regularity of b(t,x) and s(t,x)".

Sec. 2.4 / Remark 24: for deterministic (ODE) models, minimizing the velocity objective alone "is insufficient in general to maximize the likelihood"; control needs the Fisher divergence as well. Taking ϵ → ∞ is not practical because "increasing ϵ increases the expense of the numerical integration".
Remark 29: the cross-entropy estimators for SDE models involve extra terms "we do not know how to estimate"; using ŝ as a proxy "is uncontrolled in general".

Theorem 41 (Schrödinger bridge through a max-min over I) depends on the strong Assumption 39 (a reversible map to a Gaussian), which "becomes more stringent" as ϵ → 0; "we leave the numerical investigation of this formulation to future work".

Sec. 6.1: the losses "can become high-variance near the endpoints t = 0 and t = 1" because of 1/γ(t); antithetic sampling was "necessary for stable training of objectives involving γ^{-1}(t)". Sec. 6.2: drifts built from s = −η/γ are singular at the endpoints and need capping or an ϵ(t) that vanishes near the endpoints.
Sec. 4.3: for finite ϵ, the SDE ensemble started from a fixed x0 "is not distributed according to ρ1"; initial conditions must still be sampled from ρ0.

Assumption (2.2) is "made for convenience". Theorem 31's assumption I(t,x0,x1) = x0 on [0,δ] "can probably be relaxed". Assumption 46 (invertibility in rectification) is described as "generic" but is assumed, not proved.

Sec. 7.3: image generation "is not the main focus of this work"; there is no FID or ImageNet benchmark ("we will leave a more thorough study ... for a future study"). The 128-D Gaussian-mixture evaluation uses KL between KDE estimates of 2-D marginals, chosen "for computational tractability and interpretability".

errors_found.reader_claim: Technical issue on stochastic teachers: "[13] Sec. 3.1 makes the same point in continuous time: the ODE velocity for a diffusive process is the drift minus a score correction (b = u − s in eq. 3.7-3.9)."
errors_found.problem: The relation is missing the factor a. The paper prints "u − s = b", which appears to be a typo in [13], and the reader copied it. Because ∂tρ + ∇·(uρ) = aΔρ and aΔρ = ∇·(a s ρ), the transport velocity is b = u − a s.
errors_found.evidence: [13] eq. (3.7): "∂t ρ + ∇ · (uρ) = a∆ρ". Computing u − b from (3.8)-(3.9) with γ = sqrt(2a t(1−t)) gives −(2at + a(1−2t))/sqrt(2at(1−t)) · E[z|x] = −a E[z|x]/sqrt(2at(1−t)) = a s.
errors_found.corrected: b = u − a·s. The qualitative point (probability-flow velocity = SDE drift minus a score term) stands.

errors_found.reader_claim: Claim check 10 and key result on Theorem 41: [13] "Sec. 3.4 ... says 'this additional optimization step is not necessary in practice, as our approach leads to bias-free generative models for any fixed interpolant'".
errors_found.problem: The quote is in the wrong section. It comes from Sec. 1.3 (Related work, 'Optimal Transport and Schrödinger Bridges'), not Sec. 3.4. Sec. 3.4 ends with "we leave the numerical investigation of this formulation to future work."
errors_found.evidence: ref13.txt Sec. 1.3: "However, we stress that this additional optimization step is not necessary in practice, as our approach leads to bias-free generative models for any fixed interpolant."
errors_found.corrected: Cite Sec. 1.3 for the bias-free remark and Sec. 3.4 / Theorem 41 for the max-min Schrödinger bridge.

errors_found.reader_claim: Relevance section: "Sec. 16-18 (experiments): [13] suggests measuring W2 or energy distance for ODE students".
errors_found.problem: [13] never suggests W2 or energy distance and has no W2 result. Its only 'W2' is a related-work mention ("such as KL, W2, or TV"). Its metrics are KL between KDE estimates of 2-D marginals (eq. 7.1) and the mean/variance of |log ρ1 − log ρ̂(1)| (Fig. 8). Recommending W2 is the reader's inference from Lemma 21, and the W2 bound itself is in Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden 2023 (Prop. 3), not in [13].
errors_found.evidence: grep over ref13.txt: 'W2', 'Wasserstein', 'Lipschitz' and 'Gronwall' occur only on line 415 (related work). Sec. 7.2: "we make use of an error metric given by a KL-divergence between kernel density estimates (KDE) of low-dimensional marginals".
errors_found.corrected: [13] Lemma 21 / Remark 24 imply that L2 velocity error does not control KL for ODE models. Recommending W2 or energy distance (with the Lipschitz W2 bound of AVE 2023 Prop. 3) is the reader's own suggestion, not [13]'s.

errors_found.reader_claim: Technical issue: "'The argument does not require those marginals to have smooth densities [13]' gets [13] backwards."
errors_found.problem: This overstates the problem and contradicts the reader's own verdict (partially_accurate) on the same claim. [13] Remark 11 says that without the latent "the results above formally stand except that we cannot guarantee the spatial regularity of b(t,x) and s(t,x)". [13] also sets up µ(t,dx) and the conditional expectation weakly, via test functions (eqs. 2.4-2.5). The proposal says the weak equation holds without smooth densities, then immediately adds "additional uniqueness and regularity conditions are needed". That is consistent in spirit with Remark 11, not a reversal. The real defect is that [13] never proves a weak-form statement for measure-valued marginals or non-C² paths, so it is an insufficient citation.
errors_found.evidence: [13] Remark 11 (quoted above); Definition 3 / eq. (2.5): "for any test function ϕ ∈ C0∞ ... ∫ϕ(x)E[f|xt = x]µ(t,dx) = E[ϕ(xt)f]". Proposal App. A: "To recover them by solving the student's deterministic ODE ... additional uniqueness and regularity conditions are needed."
errors_found.corrected: The citation is mis-targeted, not backwards. Cite Liu 2022 (eq. 14, Def. 3.1, Thm 3.2) or Ambrosio-Gigli-Savaré for the weak form. Cite [13] Remark 11 / Sec. 4.2 for why smooth densities and fields require the latent γ(t)z.

errors_found.reader_claim: Technical issue: "Its eq. (A.4) shows that an independent coupling between an N0-mode source and an N1-mode target creates N0·N1 intermediate modes ('spurious intermediate modes', Fig. 4)."
errors_found.problem: (A.4) gives N0·N1 Gaussian components, not necessarily N0·N1 distinct modes. [13] itself says the latent partially damps spurious modes, and that the encoding-decoding path forms none even though (A.4) still has N0·N1 components. The key_results wording ("N0·N1-component intermediate mixture") is correct; this technical issue overstates it.
errors_found.evidence: Fig. 4 caption: "In this case, the spurious modes are partially damped by the addition of the latent variable"; for enc-dec: "no intermediate modes form in ρ(t)".
errors_found.corrected: Up to N0·N1 mixture components. They show up as distinct spurious modes when γ is small and the components are well separated.

errors_found.reader_claim: Relevance section: "[13] Sec. 5.3 (Theorem 47, Assumption 46) supplies the missing positive statement: when the path map ε -> Γ_t is invertible at every t ..., path distillation reproduces the teacher's per-seed map exactly, not just its marginals."
errors_found.problem: 'Supplies' is too strong. Theorem 47 is proved only for the straight-line rectified interpolant α(t)x + β(t)X_{t=1}(x), built from a perfectly learned flow. Its proof also relies on uniqueness of the ODE solution. For general invertible teacher polygons this is an analogy, and it additionally needs b* regular enough for uniqueness (e.g. Lipschitz, which the reader's Euler h·Lip<1 argument does supply).
errors_found.evidence: Sec. 5.3: "Suppose that we have perfectly learned the velocity field b". B.8: "This implies that (5.23) solves (5.21), and since the solution of this ODE is unique, we are done."
errors_found.corrected: [13] Thm 47 and its proof (B.77-B.78) give a template. The per-seed result for teacher paths needs (i) invertibility of ε→Γ_t and (ii) uniqueness for the student ODE, e.g. b* Lipschitz.

errors_found.reader_claim: Summary and novelty threats: "Theorem 47: rectification with the learned flow map gives straight paths but the same map"; "Theorem 47 already shows that such distillation preserves the endpoint map while straightening paths."
errors_found.problem: This leaves out [13]'s premise that b is perfectly learned. [13] warns that rectification of an imperfectly learned field introduces bias. That matters for the proposal's repeated consolidation across ≥10 task arrivals, where each student is distilled from an imperfect teacher.
errors_found.evidence: Sec. 5.3: "Suppose that we have perfectly learned the velocity field b". Sec. 1.3: "The method proposed in Liu et al. (2023b); Liu (2022) allows one to sequentially lower the transport cost through rectification, at the cost of introducing a bias unless the velocity field is perfectly learned."
errors_found.corrected: The same map is guaranteed only for an exactly learned teacher field. With approximation error, repeated distillation accumulates bias.

errors_found.reader_claim: Technical issue: "Missing positive condition for per-seed reproduction ... The proposal should state this and measure it."
errors_found.problem: The proposal already partly concedes this. Sec. 12 says: "Exact continuous paths of a smooth direct-reader ODE are a better behaved special case; finite numerical paths and multi-history mixtures still require care." What is missing is an explicit condition. The reader's Euler condition is mathematically correct: b*(z,t) = v(ψ_t^{-1}(z), t_i) with Lip ≤ L/(1−hL).
errors_found.evidence: Proposal p.14 (rendered pg-14.png), 'What this does not guarantee', second paragraph.
errors_found.corrected: The proposal mentions the well-behaved special case but gives no condition. Add the h·Lip(v_θ+r) < 1 invertibility condition and a crossing diagnostic.

errors_found.reader_claim: Core mechanism: "C_ij = alpha^2 C0_i + beta^2 C1_j + gamma^2 I (eq. A.4)"; summary: "to denoisers and SURE (Theorem 45)".
errors_found.problem: Wrong labels. m_ij and C_ij are defined in (A.3); (A.4) is the mixture density. SURE is Lemma 44; Theorem 45 is the iterated-denoiser scheme that consistently integrates the probability flow.
errors_found.evidence: ref13.txt App. A: "mij(t) = ... Cij(t) = α²(t)Ci0 + β²(t)Cj1 + γ²(t)Id, (A.3)". Sec. 5.2: "Lemma 44 (SURE)", "Theorem 45 ... (5.14) is a consistent integration scheme for the probability flow equation".
errors_found.corrected: (A.3) for m_ij and C_ij, (A.4) for ρ(t). SURE is Lemma 44; the denoiser-to-ODE result is Theorem 45.

missed_points: The proposal's counterexample (33), Γ_t = (1−2t)ε, is literally [13]'s Gaussian encoding-decoding interpolant (4.11) with γ = 0, using a linear schedule and the deterministic antipodal coupling x1 = −x0 between identical Gaussians. [13] Sec. 4.2 also gives the constructive contrast: with γ > 0, the enc-dec path passes through pure noise at t = 1/2, yet "its solution Xt is a bijection between the initial and final conditions". So a regular deterministic flow through the midpoint does exist once the latent is added. The reader cites the Dirac-collapse sentence but not this positive statement.

[13] Sec. 1.3 says rectification "introduc[es] a bias unless the velocity field is perfectly learned". This bears directly on the proposal's repeated consolidation (Experiment D, ≥10 task arrivals) and on its B.1 remark that one-cycle errors can accumulate. Distilling from imperfect teachers compounds bias, and [13] flags this for the closest prior procedure.

[13] Sec. 4.2: "the elimination of spurious intermediate modes can also be implemented by use of a data-adapted coupling ν(dx0, dx1), as considered in Albergo et al. (2023)". This is directly relevant to App. C's caution about choosing the source mixture and coupling: [13] names a coupling-based remedy, not only a latent-noise one.

Theorem 7's uniqueness class is C^0 in time: "unique minimizer in C^0([0,1];(C^1(R^d))^d)". The b* of a piecewise-linear teacher is generally discontinuous in t at the knots, so it falls outside [13]'s uniqueness and regularity class even when it is spatially smooth. The reader mentions this only in passing.

Sec. 3.4 frames the Schrödinger bridge hydrodynamically: min ∫∫|u|²ρ subject to a Fokker-Planck equation with both endpoint marginals fixed, with Euler-Lagrange/HJB-type equations (3.35), and ϵ → 0 recovers OT under stronger assumptions. This is the precise link to the proposal's value/control reader (Sec. 10, HJB eq. 20). With a soft terminal cost Φ_W, no endpoint-marginal constraint and no diffusion, that reader is neither SB nor OT. This supports App. C's disclaimer that the quadratic departure cost is an engineering regularizer.

Remark 4: the Gaussian latent can be any zero-mean Gaussian process N_t with N_0 = N_1 = 0, since only single-time statistics matter; a Brownian bridge is the example given. A 'smoothed path distillation' arm could therefore perturb teacher paths with a Brownian bridge and get the same marginals as γ(t)z.

Remark 42 / Table 2: the choice of γ changes the velocity at the endpoints. γ = sqrt(a t(1−t)) injects ±(a/2) × score terms into b at t = 0 and t = 1, while C^1 choices such as sin²(πt) do not. A smoothed path-distillation arm needs this choice made deliberately, together with antithetic sampling for the γ̇ z target, which is singular at the endpoints when γ = sqrt(t(1−t)).

Liu 2022 (which [13] cites) defines Rectflow(X) for any time-differentiable process X, not only linear interpolations (eqs. 11-15, Thm 3.2). The proposal's path distillation (23)-(24) is exactly Rectflow of the teacher's piecewise-linear process, so this is a stronger prior-art match for Sec. 12 / App. A than [13] itself. The reader cites Liu 2022 but does not state that the match is exact.
verification.novelty_threat_assessment: Low for the proposal's core contribution. [13] contains no memory, test-time adaptation, continual-learning, distillation-for-retention or robotics material; a grep for distill/continual/memory/policy/adapt finds only a consistency-model remark and adaptive ODE solvers. The gradient-written fast memory read at every denoising step, the centered residual reader, and the consolidation/refresh lifecycle are untouched. The threat is medium for the 'qualified account of behavior/path transfer' (Sec. 12, App. A) and for App. C's background. [13] Theorem 6 (conditional-expectation velocity and transport equation), Theorem 7 with eq. (B.23) (the regression decomposition identical to the proposal's eq. 31), Remark 11 and Sec. 4.2 (loss of regularity and Dirac collapse without latent smoothing, i.e. the proposal's counterexample 33), Sec. 3.1 / Theorem 31 (an ODE cannot sample a spread-out law from a point mass) and Sec. 3.4 (SB as a max-min) already cover this mathematics. Combined with Liu 2022 Sec. 3, where Rectflow of an arbitrary time-differentiable process is exactly the proposal's path distillation, App. A has no new theory. The proposal already calls its derivations a 'synthesis', so this is a citation and framing risk, not an invalidation. [13] also exposes a gap the proposal should fix: it never considers the standard latent-smoothing remedy (γ(t)z) for singular path-distillation fields. And the endpoint-vs-path experiment confounds the coupling with the path shape unless a same-seed rectified (reflow) baseline is added.

ref.title: Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics — Dynamic Programming chapter
ref.focus: HJB statement and sufficiency theorem conditions; derivation of optimal control for quadratic control cost and control-affine dynamics u* = -R^{-1} B^T grad J; check the proposal's eq 19-20 signs/constants (for cost 1/2||u||^2, dynamics z' = v + u) are correct; conditions under which HJB solution is valid (viscosity solutions, differentiability).

reading.bibliographic_check:
The proposal's entry reads "[14] Tedrake, R. Underactuated Robotics, chapter on Dynamic Programming. HJB and optimal-control background. Online chapter." The author, book and chapter topic are correct.

Missing or imprecise details:
- It is Chapter 7, titled "Dynamic Programming".
- The full title is "Underactuated Robotics: Algorithms for Walking, Running, Swimming, Flying, and Manipulation (Course Notes for MIT 6.832)".
- No year or access date is given. The page says © 2024 and was last modified 12 Sep 2026.
- The notes are living course notes ("They will be updated throughout the Spring 2024 semester"). The author's requested citation (misc.html) is "Russ Tedrake. Underactuated Robotics: Algorithms for Walking, Running, Swimming, Flying, and Manipulation (Course Notes for MIT 6.832). Downloaded on [date] from https://underactuated.csail.mit.edu/". The proposal should add an access date because the content can change.

The URL the task gives, https://underactuated.mit.edu/dp.html, resolves to this chapter. The finite-horizon HJB with terminal cost h(x(t_f)), which the proposal actually uses, is written out in the LQR chapter ("Finite-horizon LQR"), not in the DP chapter. The DP chapter only sketches the time-varying HJB. Its sufficiency theorem is the infinite-horizon one, and it credits the finite-horizon version to Bertsekas (2005).
reading.core_mechanism:
Infinite-horizon HJB (dp.html): 0 = min_u [ ℓ(x,u) + (∂J*/∂x) f(x,u) ], with π*(x) = argmin_u [ ℓ(x,u) + (∂J*/∂x) f(x,u) ]. Here ∂J/∂x is a row vector.

Finite-horizon / time-varying version (dp.html, "Continuous-time systems"): dJ*/dt = (∂J*/∂x) f + ∂J*/∂t. The sufficiency condition is 0 = min_u [ ℓ + (∂J*/∂x) f + ∂J*/∂t ], and pulling ∂J*/∂t out of the min gives "the (true) HJB": −∂J*/∂t = min_u [ ℓ(x,u) + (∂J*/∂x) f(x,u) ]. The terminal condition J*(x,t_f)=h(x) is not written in the DP chapter. It appears in the LQR chapter as J = h(x(t_f)) + ∫ ℓ dt with S(t_f)=Q_f.

Sufficiency theorem, formal version (Megretski). Assumptions:
- Ω is open, U is a set, f and g are continuous, g ≥ 0, and V: Ω→[0,∞) is C¹.
- (a) g is strictly positive definite in a sequence sense: g(x_k,u_k)→0 implies x_k→x*.
- (b) g_V(x,u) = g + (dV/dx) f ≥ 0, with equality when u = μ(x).
- (c) The closed-loop system ẋ=f(x,μ(x)) has at least one piecewise-continuous solution from every x_0.

Conclusion: J(x,u)=∫_0^∞ g dt reaches its minimum V(x_0)−V(x*) at every closed-loop solution. The proof integrates the identity ∫_0^T g dt = V(x_0) − V(x(T)) + ∫_0^T g_V dt. The chapter adds that the assumptions were "chosen to ensure that J(x(0)) < ∞ implies that x(t) → x*… 'without something like this, all sorts of counter-examples emerge.'"

Closed-form minimizer: take f = f_1(x) + f_2(x)u and ℓ = ℓ_1(x) + uᵀRu with R = Rᵀ ≻ 0 and u unconstrained. Setting ∂/∂u = 2uᵀR + (∂J/∂x) f_2 = 0 gives u* = −½ R⁻¹ f_2ᵀ (∂J/∂x)ᵀ. With cost ½uᵀRu instead, the same algebra gives u* = −R⁻¹ f_2ᵀ ∇J. That is the form in the task prompt; the ½ is purely a convention.

Applied to the proposal: eq 17 is ż = v_θ(z,s,c) + u, so f_1 = v_θ and f_2 = I. The running cost is ½‖u‖² + C_W, so R = ½I. Tedrake's formula then gives u* = −½(½I)⁻¹∇V = −∇_zV, which is the proposal's eq 19 (CORRECT). Substituting into −∂_tV = min_u[½‖u‖² + C_W + ∇V·(v_θ+u)] gives −∂_tV = C_W + ∇V·v_θ − ½‖∇V‖². Rearranged, ∂_tV + ∇V·v_θ − ½‖∇V‖² + C_W = 0 with V(1,z)=Φ_W(z), which is the proposal's eq 20 (CORRECT: the signs, the ½ and the terminal condition all match).

Verification argument in the proposal's own Bolza setting. For any admissible u, d/ds V(s,z_s) = ∂_sV + ∇V·(v_θ+u). By eq 20 this equals ½‖∇V‖² − C_W + ∇V·u ≥ −C_W − ½‖u‖², with equality iff u = −∇V. Integrating over [t,1] gives V(t,z) ≤ ∫(½‖u‖² + C_W)ds + Φ_W(z_1), with equality for the feedback in eq 19. This needs V to be C¹ in (t,z) and the closed-loop ODE ż = v_θ − ∇V to have a solution.
key_results: The HJB equation is stated as a sufficient condition: "if we can produce a J* and π* which satisfy these equations, then π* must be an optimal controller" (for the discrete Bellman equations), with "an analogous set of conditions for the continuous systems."

Informal sufficiency theorem (infinite horizon): with f and ℓ continuous, ℓ strictly positive definite with zero only at x*, J C¹ and positive definite satisfying the HJB, and π the minimizer, "then, under some technical conditions on the existence and boundedness of solutions, we have that J(x) - J(x*) is the optimal cost-to-go and π is an optimal policy." The chapter says Bertsekas (2005) proves the finite-horizon version: "The treatment in Bertsekas05 is for the finite-horizon case; I have modified it to one particular form of an infinite-horizon case here."

Differentiability caveat, verbatim: "since ∂J/∂x is not defined everywhere, it does not actually satisfy the requirements of the sufficiency theorem as stated above. Since cusps are commonplace in optimal value functions, one could say that the assumption in the sufficiency theorem that ∂J/∂x is defined everywhere makes our current statement very weak." Also: "this function might need to be non-smooth for even very simple dynamics and objectives" and "our PDE may have discontinuities (or at least discontinuous gradients) at locations in the state space which are not known apriori."

Closed-form minimizer: "if the system does not have any constraints on u, then we can solve in closed-form … u* = -½ R^{-1} f_2^T(x) ∂J/∂x^T. If there are linear constraints on the input, such as torque limits, then more generally this could be solved (at any particular x) as a quadratic program." For non-quadratic control costs, DDP-style quadratic approximation is used (Jacobson & Mayne 1970).
Worked example: for ℓ = q² + q̇² + u² on the double integrator, J = √3q² + 2qq̇ + √3q̇² and u* = −q − √3q̇ satisfy the HJB. I re-derived the residual symbolically: it is 0.

Time-varying HJB: "−∂J*/∂t = min_u[ℓ(x,u) + ∂J*/∂x f(x,u)]". The numerical recipe integrates backward on a mesh, and "often some 'viscosity' terms are added to the right-hand side to provide additional numerical robustness; see the Lax-Friedrichs scheme." The chapter does NOT treat the theory of viscosity solutions.

Function approximation: "In general, the convergence and accuracy guarantees for value iteration with generic function approximators are quite weak." Fitted value iteration uses fixed targets J^d_k = min_u[ℓ(x_k,u) + Ĵ(f(x_k,u))] or a slowly updated target network. Value iteration converges only up to a constant (Ĵ → J* + c), which does not change ∇J.

Discounting "does change the optimal policy", and the discounted controller can be destabilizing. A discretization exercise shows that the discrete-time cost-to-go S_h depends on the step h, so the discretized problem's optimum differs from the continuous-time one.

My check 1 (not from the paper), eqs 19-20 on a 1D test: v_θ = 0.7z, C = 0, Φ = 1.5(z−1.5)², start (t,z) = (0.2, −0.4). V from the Riccati solution of eq 20 is 1.3386532; the closed-loop cost under u = −∂_zV is 1.3386532 (difference < 1e-11); the eq-20 residual at a test point is about 2e-9. Direct L-BFGS optimization of a 400-step Euler discretization gives cost 1.34035 (an O(dt) gap) and u_0 = 2.1294, versus −∂_zV = 2.1302. The alternatives u = −½∇V and u = −2∇V give 1.065 and 4.26, which rules out a constant error.

My check 2 (not from the paper), kinks under multimodal terminal cost: v_θ = 0, C = 0, Φ(y) = 2·min((y−1)², (y+1)²). By the Hopf-Lax formula, V(0.5,z) has left derivative +1.333 and right derivative −1.333 at z = 0. So V is not C¹, and u* = −∇V jumps from −1.33 to +1.33 exactly on the boundary between modes.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 10: "Under the differentiability and well-posedness conditions required by the classical Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman argument [14], minimizing over unconstrained additive control gives (19) u*(z,t,c) = −∇_z V_W(t,z,c) and (20) ∂_t V_W + ∇_z V_W·v_θ − ½‖∇_z V_W‖² + C_W = 0, V_W(1,z,c) = Φ_W(z,c)."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: dp.html gives the HJB and its time-varying form: "−∂J*/∂t = min_u[ℓ(x,u) + ∂J*/∂x f(x,u)]". For control-affine f = f_1 + f_2u with cost ℓ_1 + uᵀRu and no input constraints it gives "u* = −½R^{-1}f_2^T(x) ∂J/∂x^T". With f_1 = v_θ, f_2 = I and R = ½I this is exactly eq 19; substituting it yields eq 20 with the correct signs, the ½ constant and the terminal condition. I confirmed this numerically (closed-loop cost equals V to 1e-11; HJB residual about 2e-9). However, the chapter's stated sufficiency theorem is infinite-horizon and time-invariant: "Consider a system ẋ=f(x,u) and an infinite-horizon additive cost ∫_0^∞ ℓ(x,u)dt, with f and ℓ continuous functions, and ℓ a strictly-positive-definite function that obtains zero only at a unique state x*..." and it notes "The treatment in Bertsekas05 is for the finite-horizon case." The terminal-cost form J = h(x(t_f)) + ∫ℓ appears only in the LQR chapter.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: The math in eqs 17-20 is correct. Two things about the citation should be fixed. (1) The DP chapter formally states only an infinite-horizon verification theorem, under conditions (ℓ strictly positive definite and vanishing at a unique x*, J ≥ 0 and positive definite) that do not apply to the proposal's finite-horizon Bolza problem with possibly signed learned costs C_W and Φ_W. The finite-horizon verification theorem should be cited from Bertsekas (2005, Vol. I, Ch. 3), Fleming & Soner, or Tedrake's LQR chapter (finite-horizon section), and the actual conditions spelled out: V ∈ C¹([t,1]×R^d); v_θ locally Lipschitz; C_W and Φ_W continuous and bounded below (or with at most sub-quadratic negative growth); an admissible control class such as L²; existence of a solution to the closed-loop ODE ż = v_θ − ∇V. (2) The same chapter explicitly warns that the C¹ assumption makes the statement "very weak" because "cusps are commonplace in optimal value functions."

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 10: "With control constraints or a different control metric, the simple gradient formula changes."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: dp.html: u* = −½R^{-1}f_2^T ∂J/∂x^T, so the metric R enters the formula. "If there are linear constraints on the input, such as torque limits, then more generally this could be solved (at any particular x) as a quadratic program." Non-quadratic control costs lead to DDP-style approximations.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 10: "The value is a cost-to-go, including future effects along the denoising dynamics."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: dp.html defines "the optimal cost-to-go (the cost that will be accumulated when running the optimal controller)" and computes it recursively over future transitions.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 10: "An arbitrary learned compatibility score does not become a value function because we take its gradient. It must be learned from valid continuation targets, a justified Bellman/HJB objective, or a solved control problem."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: This is consistent with the chapter's sufficiency logic: a function is certified as the optimal cost-to-go only by satisfying the HJB, with its minimizer, under the theorem's conditions. It also matches fitted value iteration with continuation targets J^d_k = min_u[ℓ(x_k,u) + Ĵ(f(x_k,u))]. The chapter adds that "the convergence and accuracy guarantees for value iteration with generic function approximators are quite weak." [14] is not cited on this sentence itself, but the chapter supports it.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 10: "Nor does this formulation require a physical forward-dynamics model: the dynamics above describe candidate actions in generative time."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: DP in the chapter assumes known dynamics ẋ = f(x,u). Here f(z,u) = v_θ(z,s,c) + u is known exactly (it is the flow-matching network), so that requirement is met without a physics model. It is also control-affine with f_2 = I, which is precisely the case where the chapter's closed-form minimizer applies.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec 10: "Optimizing each noise seed can send many seeds to the same outcome; control optimality does not imply the desired distribution or preserved mode coverage."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: The chapter does not discuss distributions of controlled terminal states; it optimizes each initial condition deterministically. The statement is mathematically correct. My double-well example shows the optimal feedback contracting seeds toward the minima of Φ. It is established precisely in the reward fine-tuning literature (Domingo-Enrich et al. 2024, arXiv:2409.08861), which the proposal does not cite.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Reference list: "[14] Tedrake, R. Underactuated Robotics, chapter on Dynamic Programming. HJB and optimal-control background. Online chapter."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: The page title is "Ch. 7 - Dynamic Programming", © Russ Tedrake 2024, with HTTP Last-Modified 12 Sep 2026. The notes say they "will be updated". The author's requested citation includes "(Course Notes for MIT 6.832). Downloaded on [date]".
proposal_claim_checks.correction: Add the chapter number, the full book title and subtitle, "Course Notes for MIT 6.832", the URL and an access date. For the finite-horizon terminal-cost HJB actually used, also cite the LQR chapter's finite-horizon section or Bertsekas (2005).

reading.relevance_to_proposal:
Sec 10, eqs 17-20. [14] is the only formal support for the value/control reader. Eq 17 is control-affine with f_1 = v_θ and f_2 = I, and the ½‖u‖² cost corresponds to R = ½I in Tedrake's convention. His closed-form minimizer u* = −½R⁻¹f_2ᵀ∇J therefore reproduces eq 19 exactly, and eq 20 follows from his time-varying HJB. I verified the signs and constants both analytically and numerically. The verification argument carries over to the finite-horizon Bolza problem, but only if V is C¹. The chapter itself flags that assumption as weak, which matters because the proposal's targets are multimodal action distributions.

Sec 8 table ("Value/control reader … requires a grounded cost and a learned or solved cost-to-go"). The chapter's material on fitted, neural and mesh value iteration shows what "learned or solved cost-to-go" entails and how weak the guarantees are with function approximators.

Sec 9, eq 15. The first term, dt/2 Σ‖(z_{i+1}−z_i)/dt − v_θ(z_i,t_i,c)‖², is exactly the Euler discretization of ∫½‖u‖²ds with u_i = (z_{i+1}−z_i)/dt − v_θ. So if Ẽ decomposes into state costs, Sec 9 is an open-loop, per-seed, local trajectory-optimization solution (K gradient steps from the base path) of the same kind of Bolza problem. Sec 10 is the feedback/DP solution of that problem. In Tedrake's framework these are two solution methods (trajectory optimization vs DP), not two different objectives. Sec 9 actually uses an edge energy g_φ(z_i, z_{i+1}, …) that depends on u, so the two differ in cost class as well as solver.

Appendix B (exact reset proofs) and the factorial "same lifecycle" claim of Sec 8. Reset proofs exist for the direct reader (B.2) and path refinement (B.3), but there is none for the value reader. The HJB's quadratic Hamiltonian determines how centering must be done (see technical_issues).

Sec 16-18 (value reader as a baseline; "Direct velocity vs path-energy vs value reader"). The chapter's mesh-based HJB solvers and its verification-by-HJB-residual idea give ground-truth and diagnostic tools for low-dimensional action experiments such as Experiment B's 2D actions.

Sec 19, eqs 29-30. The analytic Gaussian field v_μ(z,t) = b_t z + κ_t μ is affine in z. With quadratic C_W and Φ_W, eq 20 is therefore a finite-horizon LQ problem solvable by a differential Riccati equation (Tedrake's LQR chapter). That would give an exact analytic sanity check for the value reader.

Appendix C and Sec 9 remarks on stochastic control and Schrödinger bridges. The chapter's MDP section notes that expected-cost DP extends to stochastic systems; the stochastic, viscous HJB is the route to the relative-entropy identities the proposal says require "additional probabilistic assumptions".
novelty_threats: None to the memory mechanism. The chapter is textbook background, and the proposal claims no novelty for eqs 17-20. It does establish that eqs 17-20 are a standard control-affine Bolza problem with quadratic control cost whose optimal feedback is −∇V. So the value/control reader's only novel element is making the running and terminal costs memory-dependent (C_W, Φ_W).

Not from Tedrake (external; titles verified on arXiv): additive control of a pretrained flow's velocity field under ½‖u‖² plus a terminal reward is exactly the stochastic-optimal-control formulation of reward fine-tuning. Examples are Uehara et al. 2024, 'Fine-Tuning of Continuous-Time Diffusion Models as Entropy-Regularized Control' (arXiv:2402.15194), and Domingo-Enrich, Drozdzal, Karrer, Chen 2024, 'Adjoint Matching: Fine-tuning Flow and Diffusion Generative Models with Memoryless Stochastic Optimal Control' (arXiv:2409.08861). Adjoint Matching's abstract: "we prove that a very specific memoryless noise schedule must be enforced during fine-tuning, in order to account for the dependency between the noise variable and the generated samples." This addresses the proposal's own concern that "control optimality does not imply the desired distribution." The value reader should be compared against, or built on, this line of work, not only HardFlow [7].

Continuous fitted value iteration with a closed-form optimal action for control-affine dynamics (Lutter et al. 2021, cited in the chapter) and neural HJB solvers (DeepReach, Bansal & Tomlin 2021, cited in the chapter) already provide learned-value controllers of the same form. A memory-conditioned value reader is an amortized variant of these.
ideas_to_borrow: Implement the value reader with the closed-form minimizer: at each solver step apply u = −∇_z V (one backward pass through V). For a different action metric R use u = −R⁻¹∇V under the ½uᵀRu convention (−½R⁻¹∇V under Tedrake's uᵀRu). For box or linear constraints solve a small QP per step, as the chapter suggests for torque limits. For general convex action costs, the convex-conjugate policy of Lutter et al. 2021 (cFVI) generalizes the formula.

Certify any learned V_W by checking the HJB residual of eq 20 on sampled (t,z,c) and by testing that the closed-loop cost of u = −∇V from (t_0,z_0) equals V(t_0,z_0). Tedrake: "we can verify optimality … without doing any integration; we simply have to check a derivative condition." I ran this consistency test numerically; it is cheap and catches sign and constant errors.

Extend the Sec 19 analytic sanity check to the value reader. Because v_μ(z,t) = b_t z + κ_t μ is affine in z, quadratic C_W and Φ_W make V quadratic, with P(t), p(t), r(t) solving a backward Riccati system (as in Tedrake's finite-horizon LQR). This gives exact ground truth for u*, for reset behavior, and for the distribution induced by optimal control.

Train V by finite-horizon backward fitted DP over the actual solver grid (e.g., 16 Euler steps): J_N = Φ_W, J_i(z) = min_u[dt(½‖u‖² + C_W) + J_{i+1}(z + dt(v_θ + u))]. Use fixed targets or a target network as in the chapter's neural fitted value iteration. The horizon is finite, so no discounting is needed; the chapter warns that discounting "does change the optimal policy".

For low-dimensional actions (Experiment B uses 2D actions), solve eq 20 on a mesh with a Lax-Friedrichs scheme, or with Mitchell's level-set toolbox cited in the chapter, to get a reference value function. Report the learned value reader's error against it, especially near mode boundaries where V has kinks.
Only ∇V matters: value iteration converges to J* + c. Anchor V with the terminal condition V(1) = Φ_W and do not interpret or penalize absolute levels of V.

Borrow the chapter's warning about ill-posed problems (the 'Ill-Posed Optimal Control Problem' exercise and the input-limit remark). Keep learned C_W and Φ_W bounded below, e.g., bounded outputs or at most linear growth, so the infimum in eq 18 is finite.
technical_issues_in_proposal: Differentiability generically fails in the proposal's own regime. For multimodal terminal or running costs, the case that motivates flow-matching policies, V_W develops kinks (shocks) on the sets where optimal trajectories to different modes tie. There ∇V does not exist and u* = −∇V is discontinuous. My double-well example: Φ = 2·min((y−1)², (y+1)²) gives ∂_zV(0.5, 0±) = ∓1.33. Even a smooth double well k(y²−1)² loses the classical solution before t = 0 when its negative curvature is large enough. The proposal hedges with "under the differentiability … conditions" but gives no fallback. The correct object is the viscosity solution, which is Lipschitz and semiconcave, so ∇V exists almost everywhere and optimal controls are non-unique on the kink set. Neither the proposal nor the chapter covers this; the chapter mentions viscosity only as a numerical stabilizer. A smooth neural V will blur these kinks, and near a mode boundary ∇V ≈ 0 hands control back to v_θ. This should be stated, or a stochastic (viscous) formulation adopted, which gives smooth V.

Wrong theorem scope in the citation. The chapter's formal sufficiency theorem is infinite-horizon and time-invariant. It requires g ≥ 0, strict positive definiteness with a unique zero-cost state x*, and V ≥ 0, none of which fit a finite-horizon Bolza problem with signed learned costs. The finite-horizon verification theorem (Bertsekas 2005; Fleming & Soner) is what the proposal needs, and its conditions should be listed: V ∈ C¹, Lipschitz v_θ, costs bounded below, admissible controls in L², and a closed-loop solution to ż = v_θ − ∇V.

The value reader has no exact-reset construction, yet Sec 8 claims all readers share the same lifecycle. Appendix B proves reset only for the direct reader (B.2) and path refinement (B.3). For the value reader, centering must be applied to the costs, not the value. Setting C̃_W = C_W − C_{W0} and Φ̃_W = Φ_W − Φ_{W0} makes V_{W0} ≡ 0 and hence u = 0 exactly. Centering the value (V_W − V_{W0}) is NOT valid. Because the Hamiltonian is quadratic, D = V_W − V_{W0} satisfies ∂_tD + ∇D·(v_θ − ∇V_{W0}) − ½‖∇D‖² + (C_W − C_{W0}) = 0. That is the value function for the base field v_θ − ∇V_{W0}, not for v_θ, so −∇D is not optimal when added to v_θ. An amortized network V_φ(t,z,c,memory) will also not satisfy V_{W0} ≡ const exactly unless this is built into the architecture.

Discrete versus continuous optimality. The sampler uses Euler with about 16 steps (dt = 1/16). The optimality condition for the discrete sampler is the discrete Bellman recursion. Its minimizer is implicit, u_i = −∇J_{i+1}(z_i + dt(v_θ + u_i)), evaluated at the next state, and differs from eq 19's explicit −∇V(t_i, z_i) by O(dt). The chapter's discretization exercise shows that the cost-to-go itself changes with h. Calling eq 19 applied inside a 16-step Euler solver "optimal" is therefore only first-order accurate. My test showed an O(dt) gap between the Euler direct optimum (1.34035 at N = 400) and the continuous V (1.33865).

V_W depends on W, which changes after every write, so eq 20 would have to be re-solved at every decision k. The proposal says memory "can store arbitrary associations that condition a slow cost or value model" but gives no loss for learning V (no HJB-residual or fitted-DP objective) and does not address generalization of an amortized V across the distribution of W. Given the chapter's warning that generic function-approximator guarantees are "quite weak", this is a substantial unspecified component. The proposal does label the value reader "not implemented or validated".

Sec 9 and Sec 10 are not independent readers. Eq 15's departure term is the Euler discretization of ∫½‖u‖², so path-energy refinement is local open-loop trajectory optimization of a Bolza-type objective, while the value reader is its DP/feedback counterpart. The planned comparison "Direct velocity vs path-energy vs value reader" confounds cost class (the edge energy g_φ(z_i, z_{i+1}, …) depends on u, whereas eq 18 uses a state-only C_W) with solution method (K local gradient steps versus an amortized global value). To attribute differences to the reader, use the same state cost in both variants.

Mode coverage is acknowledged but not resolved. Deterministic optimal control of each seed does not produce the reward-tilted distribution p_base·exp(−Φ). Obtaining it requires a stochastic formulation with a memoryless noise schedule (Adjoint Matching, arXiv:2409.08861), which the proposal does not cite. The stochastic HJB, ∂_tV + ∇V·v − ½‖∇V‖² + (σ²/2)ΔV + C = 0, can be linearized by the substitution V = −σ² log ψ and has smooth solutions, which also addresses the kink problem above.
stated_limitations: The C¹ assumption in the sufficiency theorem is "very weak" as stated, because "cusps are commonplace in optimal value functions". For example, the minimum-time time-to-go for the double integrator satisfies the HJB only where its gradient exists.

The sufficiency theorem is "stated informally" and holds "under some technical conditions on the existence and boundedness of solutions". The formal version needs strict positive definiteness so that finite cost implies x(t) → x*: "without something like this, all sorts of counter-examples emerge."
The closed-form minimizer requires control-affine dynamics, a running cost quadratic in u, and no constraints on u. Otherwise a QP or DDP-style approximation is needed.
The optimal cost-to-go may be non-smooth or discontinuous at locations not known a priori, so mesh and PDE methods are limited in dimension.
"In general, the convergence and accuracy guarantees for value iteration with generic function approximators are quite weak." Convergence results exist mainly for linear function approximators.

Value iteration converges only up to a constant, and infinite-horizon value iteration needs a bounded optimal cost-to-go. Discounting changes the optimal policy and can yield destabilizing controllers.
Discretization error: value-iteration policies differ from the true optimal (e.g., bang-bang) policy because of the mesh, and the discretized problem's cost-to-go depends on the time step.
cited_works_worth_adding: Bertsekas, D. P., Dynamic Programming & Optimal Control, Vol. I & II, Athena Scientific, 2005. The chapter attributes the HJB sufficiency theorem to it and notes it treats the finite-horizon case, which matches the proposal's eq 18.

Lutter, Mannor, Peters, Fox, Garg, 'Value Iteration in Continuous Actions, States and Time', ICML 2021 (arXiv:2105.04682). Continuous fitted value iteration with a closed-form optimal action for control-affine dynamics and separable costs. A direct template for training and reading out the value reader, and it generalizes u* = −∇V to non-quadratic action costs.

Bansal & Tomlin, 'DeepReach: A Deep Learning Approach to High-Dimensional Reachability', ICRA 2021 (arXiv:2011.02082). Neural solution of HJ PDEs by residual training, relevant if V_W is learned from the eq-20 residual.
Doya, K., 'Reinforcement Learning in Continuous Time and Space', Neural Computation 12(1), 2000. Continuous-time value learning and HJB-based temporal-difference methods.

Osher & Fedkiw, Level Set Methods and Dynamic Implicit Surfaces, Springer 2003 (Lax-Friedrichs schemes with numerical viscosity), and Mitchell & Templeton 2005 (Level Set Toolbox). Useful for ground-truth solutions of eq 20 in the 2D-action experiments.
Jacobson & Mayne, Differential Dynamic Programming, 1970. The route when the control cost is not quadratic or the dynamics are not control-affine.
Munos & Szepesvári, 'Finite-Time Bounds for Fitted Value Iteration', JMLR 2008. Error bounds for learned value functions.

(Not cited by Tedrake; external, verified on arXiv) Domingo-Enrich et al. 2024, 'Adjoint Matching' (arXiv:2409.08861), and Uehara et al. 2024, 'Fine-Tuning of Continuous-Time Diffusion Models as Entropy-Regularized Control' (arXiv:2402.15194). These are the closest prior work to the Sec 10 value/control reader applied to flow models.

errors_found.reader_claim: My check 1: "The alternatives u = −½∇V and u = −2∇V give 1.065 and 4.26, which rules out a constant error."
errors_found.problem: The sentence is ambiguous and could be read as describing costs. 1.065 and 4.26 are the initial controls u_0 = ½·2.1302 and 2·2.1302, not closed-loop costs. Read as costs, 1.065 would be below the optimum V = 1.3387, which is impossible. The true closed-loop costs under those feedbacks are 1.905 and 1.782. The conclusion still holds: u = −∇V is the only one of the three that matches the direct optimum.
errors_found.evidence: I re-ran the reader's setup (v = 0.7z, C = 0, Φ = 1.5(z−1.5)², start (0.2, −0.4)) and reproduced its core numbers: V = 1.3386532227, −∂_zV = 2.1302335, closed-loop cost under u = −∇V = 1.3386532227449, and the N = 400 Euler L-BFGS optimum = 1.340354 with u_0 = 2.129389. The closed-loop costs under u = −0.5∇V and u = −2∇V are 1.9045556 and 1.7820757.
errors_found.corrected: State that u_0 under −½∇V and −2∇V would be 1.065 and 4.26, compared with the direct optimum's 2.1294. Their closed-loop costs, 1.905 and 1.782, are both above V = 1.3387.

errors_found.reader_claim: accessed: "Draft notes hidden in HTML comments were stripped." The extensions are summarised as "(discounted cost, stochastic MDPs, LP and SOS dynamic programming)", and the chapter is said to only sketch "the time-varying HJB".
errors_found.problem: Visible <todo> notes (not HTML comments) are still in the reader's own ref14.txt. The first item under 'Extensions' is an unwritten placeholder: `<todo> finite-horizon / time-varying dynamics or cost.</todo>`. So the chapter explicitly defers the time-varying case. Its continuous-time HJB derivation uses time-invariant f(x,u) and ℓ(x,u) and has no terminal cost. Its discrete finite-horizon recursion also has no separate terminal cost: J*(x,N) = min_u ℓ(x,u). The proposal's eqs 17-18 use time-dependent v_θ(z,s,c) and C_W(z,s,c) plus a terminal Φ_W, so this weakens [14] as the formal citation more than the reader says.
errors_found.evidence: ref14.html line 942: "<todo> finite-horizon / time-varying dynamics or cost.</todo>". Continuous-time section: "$$\frac{dJ^*}{dt} = \pd{J^*}{\bx}f(\bx,\bu) + \pd{J^*}{t},$$" with f(x,u) and ℓ(x,u) independent of t. Discrete version: "J^*(\bx,N) = \min_\bu \ell(\bx, \bu)".
errors_found.corrected: [14] gives the time-invariant HJB and only a sketch of the time-dependent J*(x,t). Time-varying dynamics and costs are listed as an unwritten extension, and no terminal cost appears. The fix is standard: augment the state with s, or cite Bertsekas 2005 Vol. I Ch. 3. The page source has a hidden comment "<!-- chapter 3 -->" next to Bertsekas05.

errors_found.reader_claim: technical_issues: "Deterministic optimal control of each seed does not produce the reward-tilted distribution p_base·exp(−Φ). Obtaining it requires a stochastic formulation with a memoryless noise schedule (Adjoint Matching, arXiv:2409.08861)."
errors_found.problem: "Requires" is too strong. Adjoint Matching itself names another route (learning or tilting the initial distribution). Uehara et al. 2024, which the reader also cites, optimizes the drift and the initial distribution jointly to reach the target distribution.
errors_found.evidence: Adjoint Matching Sec 4.2: "Another direction that has been proposed is to learn the initial distribution p0 to cancel out the bias (Uehara et al., 2024b; Tang, 2024)". Uehara et al. (2402.15194): "we formally show that the fine-tuned SDE, optimized for both the drift term and initial distribution, can produce specific distributions with high diversity".
errors_found.corrected: A memoryless noise schedule (Adjoint Matching) is one sufficient route. Tilting the initial distribution (Uehara et al.) is another. Either is needed to reach the tilted distribution.

errors_found.reader_claim: novelty_threats: "additive control of a pretrained flow's velocity field under ½‖u‖² plus a terminal reward is exactly the stochastic-optimal-control formulation of reward fine-tuning."
errors_found.problem: The two are analogous, not the same. In Adjoint Matching the control enters as σ(t)u alongside noise σ(t)dB_t, so setting σ = 0 removes the control. Uehara et al. use an SDE with σ > 0 and a KL-regularization reading. The proposal's eq 17 is a deterministic ODE with the control added directly, so ½‖u‖² is not a KL term there. It is the zero-noise analogue.
errors_found.evidence: Adjoint Matching eq (13): "dX_t^u = (b(X_t^u,t) + σ(t)u(X_t^u,t))dt + σ(t)dB_t". Sec 4.2: "when the sampling procedure is noiseless, i.e., σ(t) = 0, fine-tuning naïvely will not have any effect because X0 completely determines X1." Uehara eq (1): "dx_t = f(t,x_t)dt + σ(t)dw_t".
errors_found.corrected: Eqs 17-18 are the deterministic counterpart of the SOC reward fine-tuning formulation (same running and terminal cost structure). The stochastic versions are the natural extension and comparison point.

errors_found.reader_claim: technical_issues: "The value reader has no exact-reset construction, yet Sec 8 claims all readers share the same lifecycle."
errors_found.problem: This overstates the proposal. Sec 8 only says the readers "can be tested with the same replay/consolidation lifecycle". The status table calls the value reader "Research alternatives; not implemented or validated." Appendix B does give reset proofs only for the direct reader (B.2) and path refinement (B.3). The reader's technical point is correct, and I checked the algebra: D = V_W − V_{W0} satisfies ∂_tD + ∇D·(v_θ − ∇V_{W0}) − ½‖∇D‖² + (C_W − C_{W0}) = 0, and centering the costs makes V_{W0} ≡ 0.
errors_found.evidence: Proposal Sec 8: "All four readers can receive information from the same fast associative network, and all can be tested with the same replay/consolidation lifecycle." Status table: "Associative recurrent retrieval / value reader — Research alternatives; not implemented or validated."
errors_found.corrected: The proposal plans to test all readers under the same lifecycle but gives no reset construction for the value reader. The reset has to come from centering the costs, not the value.

errors_found.reader_claim: technical_issues: "Calling eq 19 applied inside a 16-step Euler solver 'optimal' is therefore only first-order accurate."
errors_found.problem: This is a forward-looking caveat, not an error in the proposal. The proposal never applies eq 19 inside the 16-step solver or calls it optimal there. The value reader is unimplemented, and the 16-step grid belongs to Experiment B's direct reader. The O(dt) gap numbers are correct (1.34035 vs 1.33865).
errors_found.evidence: Proposal Sec 10: "Do not use the word optimal for the direct residual reader without specifying and solving an objective of this kind." I reproduced the Euler optimum of 1.340354.
errors_found.corrected: Treat it as a design caveat: if the value reader is later run on a coarse Euler grid, its optimality should be defined through the discrete Bellman recursion.

errors_found.reader_claim: claim check 1 correction: the "actual conditions" include "C_W and Φ_W continuous and bounded below (or with at most sub-quadratic negative growth)".
errors_found.problem: This is sufficient, not necessary. The finite-horizon verification argument only needs a C¹ solution of eq 20 and a closed-loop solution. Tedrake's LQR chapter says cost positivity is not needed in the finite-horizon case. The reader did not read that general-form section.
errors_found.evidence: LQR chapter, "Finite-horizon LQR derivation (general form)": "It's tempting to require that the cost is always positive ... but this is not actually necessary in the finite-horizon case."
errors_found.corrected: Bounded-below costs are a convenient sufficient condition for eq 18 to be finite. They are not a requirement of the verification theorem.

claim_check_overrides.claim: Sec 10: "Optimizing each noise seed can send many seeds to the same outcome; control optimality does not imply the desired distribution or preserved mode coverage."
claim_check_overrides.reason: [14] is not cited for this sentence and says nothing about it, but the claim is correct. The reader rated claims 4 and 5 "accurate" on logical grounds, so this one should be rated the same way. Support: the reader's own double-well example (checked: ∂_zV(0.5, 0±) = ∓1.333, so seeds split toward the minima of Φ), and Adjoint Matching Sec 4.2, which shows the optimally controlled law is "p*(X0,X1) = p_base(X0,X1) exp(r(X1) + V(X0,0))", not the tilted target. In the noiseless case, "X0 completely determines X1".

missed_points: The chapter's 'Extensions' section lists `<todo> finite-horizon / time-varying dynamics or cost.</todo>` as an unwritten item. The continuous-time HJB assumes time-invariant f(x,u) and ℓ(x,u), and no terminal cost appears anywhere in the DP chapter. The proposal's v_θ(z,s,c), C_W(z,s,c) and V(1) = Φ_W therefore go beyond what [14] writes down. The fix is standard (time-augmented state, or Bertsekas Vol. I Ch. 3), but it should be cited precisely.

Tedrake's LQR chapter has a section, 'Finite-horizon LQR derivation (general form)', for time-varying affine dynamics ẋ = A(t)x + B(t)u + c(t) with time-varying quadratic costs and a final cost Q_f. That is exactly the proposal's Sec 19 Gaussian field v_μ = b_t z + κ_t μ (A = b_t I, B = I, c = κ_t μ). It is the right citation for an analytic check of the value reader, and it notes that cost positivity "is not actually necessary in the finite-horizon case". The reader read only the LTI finite-horizon section.

[14] presents the HJB as a sufficient (verification) condition: "if we can produce a J* and π* which satisfy these equations, then π* must be an optimal controller". The proposal's sentence goes the other way: V defined as the infimum in eq 18 satisfies eq 20, with optimal control eq 19. That direction needs V ∈ C¹, and [14] covers it only informally ("Bertsekas05 gives an informal derivation of these equations as the limit of a discrete-time approximation"). The reader covered viscosity solutions but did not separate necessity from sufficiency.

Adding noise to get a smooth, viscous V is not free for a pretrained flow-matching ODE. A σ·dB term changes the uncontrolled (u = 0) distribution unless the drift gets a score correction; Adjoint Matching's memoryless schedule handles this for flow matching. A naive stochastic value reader would therefore break the proposal's reset-equals-base property.

Fitted value iteration: "Are errors in all states equally important?" The LP's "state-relevance weights" make the same point. For an amortized V_W, accuracy matters mainly on the states the controlled denoising flow visits, which bears on how V_W should be trained and evaluated.

'Stochastic interpretation of deterministic, continuous-state value iteration': mesh interpolation acts like an MDP, and "discretization error here will cause a sort of diffusion". This links the numerical-viscosity smoothing of kinks to the reader's stochastic-formulation suggestion.

External support for the proposal's point that the gradient of an arbitrary score is not a value function: Uehara et al. (2402.15194) report that their method "outperforms a guidance baseline that uses the gradients of the reward model to steer the pre-trained diffusion model". Value- or return-gradient guidance of denoising already exists in robot planning: Diffuser, Janner et al. 2022, arXiv:2205.09991, "classifier-guided sampling ... reinterpreted as coherent planning strategies" (I verified title and abstract only). It is a natural baseline for the value reader alongside HardFlow [7].

Minor bibliographic point: the author's BibTeX on misc.html gives year = 2023, while the page footer says © 2024, and the requested citation uses the underactuated.csail.mit.edu domain. The proposal should give an access date either way (the reader's recommendation stands).
verification.novelty_threat_assessment: Low. [14] is textbook course material: an infinite-horizon HJB sufficiency theorem, a sketch of the time-varying HJB, and the closed-form minimizer u* = −½R⁻¹f₂ᵀ∂J/∂xᵀ for control-affine systems with quadratic control cost. The proposal claims no novelty for eqs 17-20 and cites [14] only as background. [14] does show that eqs 17-20 are a standard control-affine, quadratic-cost HJB. With f₁ = v_θ, f₂ = I and R = ½I, eq 19 is Tedrake's formula, and eq 20 follows from the time-varying HJB; I verified the signs and constants analytically and numerically. So the value reader's only non-textbook element is that the running and terminal costs depend on memory. Closer prior art for the formulation lies outside [14]: SOC-based reward fine-tuning of diffusion and flow models (Adjoint Matching 2409.08861; Uehara et al. 2402.15194), whose deterministic zero-noise analogue is eqs 17-18, and value-gradient-guided diffusion planning (Diffuser 2205.09991). The proposal treats the value reader as a later, unimplemented alternative, not a core contribution, so none of this threatens its central fast-memory and consolidation claims. It does mean the value reader should be framed and benchmarked against that SOC and guidance literature. The main technical risks are the reader's valid points: V is generally not C¹ for multimodal costs, [14]'s theorem has the wrong scope for this problem, and there is no reset construction for the value reader. They are not novelty issues.

ref.title: Marcotte et al., Regions of Reliability in the Evaluation of Multivariate Probabilistic Forecasts (ICML 2023)
ref.role: Cited for eq 16 energy score: "Its conditional population objective is proper; a finite training set gives no calibration guarantee".
ref.focus: Energy score definition (beta, unbiased vs biased estimator), propriety, finite-sample discrimination failures they document. Check the proposal's estimator in eq 16 (normalization 1/(2S(S-1)) over s!=r) is correct/unbiased; whether using it as a TRAINING loss for multimodal action distributions is well supported; what the paper actually says about reliability regions.

reading.accessed: I read the full PMLR camera-ready PDF (47 pp: main text, Appendices A-D, and all figure pages 20-47), downloaded from https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/marcotte23a/marcotte23a.pdf. Saved copies: /tmp/claude-1001/-home-licho-workspace-Horsea/6362e6e4-1b6e-43f7-ba9b-09289d83a6f6/scratchpad/refs/ref15.pdf, ref15.txt (pdftotext -layout), ref15_flow.txt (plain pdftotext) and ref15.html (PMLR landing page). I rendered pages 2, 7, 8, 12, 19, 20, 38 and 39 as PNGs (ref15_p-*.png) so I could read the equations, the Fig. 6 column order and the mixture heatmaps (Figs. 27-28). I also fetched the authors' code from github.com/ServiceNow/regions-of-reliability (ror/metrics/energy.py, ror/experiments/distributions.py, saved under refs/ref15_code/) to confirm which estimator they use and how the mixture test is built. Values I read off heatmaps by eye are marked as approximate. I ran my own Monte-Carlo and closed-form checks of the proposal's eq. 16 (scratchpad/es_check*.py).
reading.bibliographic_check: The citation is correct. The PMLR page lists the title "Regions of Reliability in the Evaluation of Multivariate Probabilistic Forecasts", authors Étienne Marcotte, Valentina Zantedeschi, Alexandre Drouin and Nicolas Chapados (ServiceNow Research), Proceedings of the 40th ICML, PMLR 202:23958-24004, 2023 (publication date 2023/07/03). This matches proposal ref [15] exactly. The annotation "Includes energy-score definitions and finite-sample limitations" is fair. One typesetting defect in the paper itself: Appendix A.2 eq. (15), the ES definition, renders blank in the PMLR PDF. The definition is present as main-text eq. (3).
reading.summary:
Problem. Multivariate probabilistic time-series forecasts are usually scored with proper scoring rules such as CRPS, the Energy Score (ES), the Variogram (VG) and Dawid-Sebastiani (DS), because the NLL is often unavailable. Propriety is a statement about expectations. The paper asks whether these rules can actually tell a wrong forecast from the true distribution with realistic finite samples. In their words: "properness only holds in expectation, while in practice evaluation is conducted based on a few samples from Dgt ... in realistic experimental conditions, they fail to distinguish between the ground-truth distribution and forecasts with significant imperfections."

Method. The paper frames reliability as statistical power. For a pair (ground truth D_gt, forecast D_f) it defines the score gap Delta_m = S(y, X^f_m) - S(y, X^gt_m), where y ~ D_gt and each score is estimated from m samples. Mean and variance are estimated from K=1000 trials. By the CLT, the average of n replications is N(mu_m, sigma_m^2/n) under the alternative and N(0, sigma_m^2/n) under the null. Power = P[H_S(n,m) >= t_alpha] at alpha = 5%. A "Region of Reliability" RoR_(1-beta) is the subset of (d, n, m) where the rule reaches at least 1-beta power (Def. 4.2). The benchmark has 19 synthetic discrepancy types: marginal mean, variance, exponential mean, skewness; Full, Checker and Block covariance, each missing or extra; and Mixture Missing/Extra. For each, the effect size epsilon is tuned so that the exact NLL has 80% power at n=30. The sweep covers d = 2^4..2^12 and m = 2^6..2^14. Six estimators are compared: CRPS-Q, CRPS-E, ES-Full, ES-Partial, VG and DS, with ES at p in {0.5, 1, 1.5} and VG at p in {0.5, 1, 2}.

Findings. None of the sample-based proper scores matches the NLL. ES and CRPS detect errors in marginal means and variances when m > d, but lose power when m < d. The dependence structure is mostly missed. ES max power averaged over d is only 0.11-0.27 on the covariance tests and 0.09 on skewness. All rules fail on the mixture tests, in which a two-component mixture is compared with a moment-matched Gaussian: ES-Full reaches 0.10 (Missing) and 0.13 (Extra), against the NLL's 0.8 by construction, and the RoR_0.5 is empty. Power is not monotone in d, and detection is asymmetric between over- and under-estimation. Increasing m helps only up to an asymptote. On real data (TACTiS fitted to solar, kdd-cup and electricity, with d in the thousands) the NLL again dominates, and ES loses power on some perturbations. The practical recommendations are larger n and m, checking the benchmark before trusting a rule, and complementing scores with calibration/sharpness diagnostics and correlation plots.

Scope. This is an evaluation and hypothesis-testing paper about time series. It never trains a model with a scoring rule, never discusses training-set size, and explicitly separates its notion of reliability from calibration diagnostics.
reading.core_mechanism:
Energy score (main text eq. 3): ES(y, D_f) = E_{x~D_f} ||y - x||_2^p - (1/2) E_{x,x'~D_f} ||x - x'||_2^p, with p in (0,2). App. A.2: "Given a parameter 0 < p < 2 (commonly called β in the literature, which we changed to avoid confusion with the false negative rate of §4.1) ... The ES is a strictly proper scoring rule." The paper does not state the finite-p-th-moment condition; that comes from Gneiting & Raftery (2007).

Propriety (eq. 4): E_{y~D_gt}[S(y, D_gt)] <= E_{y~D_gt}[S(y, D_f)]; strictly proper if the minimum is unique.

Estimators:
- ES-Full (eq. 16): (1/m) sum_i ||y - x_i||^p - (1/(m(m-1))) sum_{i<i'} ||x_i - x_{i'}||^p. The second term averages over the m(m-1)/2 unordered pairs and multiplies by 1/2, so it is an unbiased U-statistic of (1/2) E||X - X'||^p. Cost O(d m^2).
- ES-Partial (eq. 17): (1/m) sum_i ||y - x_i||^p - (1/m) sum_{i=1}^{m/2} ||x_i - x_{i+m/2}||^p. Uses m/2 disjoint pairs; also unbiased, cost O(dm).
- Code (ror/metrics/energy.py) confirms both: `second_term = s / (num_samples * (num_samples - 1) / 2)`; `return first_term - 0.5 * second_term`, with the comment "we need two independant realizations of the distributions. So we do a sum ignoring the i == j terms".

Power analysis: Delta_m = S(y, X^f_m) - S(y, X^gt_m) (eq. 5); mu_m and sigma_m^2 estimated over K=1000 trials (eqs. 6-7); H0(n,m) = N(0, sigma_m^2/n); H_S(n,m) = N(mu_m, sigma_m^2/n); P[H0 >= t_alpha] = alpha = 0.05 (eq. 8); power = P[H_S >= t_alpha] = 1 - beta (eq. 9, Def. 4.1). RoR_(1-beta) is the set of (d, n, m) with at least 1-beta power (Def. 4.2). Heatmaps show power at n=30, which can equally be read as the minimal n needed for 80% power.

Mixture test (App. B.3 and code): D_gt = 0.5 N(eps·1, I) + 0.5 N(-eps·1, I) versus D_f = N(0, I + eps^2 11^T), which has the same mean and covariance ("Missing"), or the roles swapped ("Extra"). Tuned eps (Table 3) shrinks roughly as 1/sqrt(d), e.g. 0.59 at d=16 for Missing. So the Euclidean mode separation 2·eps·sqrt(d) stays about 4.7 while each marginal separation is only about 1.2 sd.

My check of proposal eq. 16. D = (1/S) sum_s ||a_s - a*|| - (1/(2S(S-1))) sum_{s != r} ||a_s - a_r||. The sum over ordered pairs s != r has S(S-1) terms, each unordered pair counted twice, so 1/(2S(S-1)) sum_{s != r} = (1/(S(S-1))) sum_{s<r}. This is identical to the paper's ES-Full with p = beta = 1, and E[D] = ES(P_theta, a*) exactly.
- Monte-Carlo check: 10^7 draws, 2-D bimodal target, Gaussian model, S=2. Eq.-16 mean is 1.31217 +/- 0.00032 against the analytic ES of 1.31233.
- Why the normalisation matters: the biased V-statistic 1/(2S^2) sum_{s,r} shrinks the diversity term by (S-1)/S, and the resulting loss is not proper. For a 1-D N(0,1) target and N(0, sigma^2) model, the expected V-statistic loss is minimised at sigma ≈ 0.38 (S=2), 0.63 (S=4) and 0.89 (S=16), always under-dispersed, while the unbiased form is minimised at sigma = 1.
- Identity: E_{Y~Q} ES(P, Y) - E_{Y~Q} ES(Q, Y) = (1/2) D_E(P, Q), with D_E the energy distance. So the training "signal" is half the energy distance; this is a standard identity, not stated in the paper.
key_results: Abstract: propriety "is not sufficient to guarantee good discrimination in the non-asymptotic regime"; the results "reveal critical shortcomings in the evaluation of multivariate probabilistic forecasts as commonly performed in the literature."

Fig. 6 (max power over m, averaged over d; NLL = 0.80 by construction). Columns are CRPS-Q, CRPS-E, ES-Full, ES-Partial, VG, DS. ES-Full / ES-Partial: Normal(Single, mu↑) 0.76/0.73; Normal(All, mu↑) 0.83/0.76; Skew Normal 0.09/0.09; Full Cov(Missing) 0.25/0.21; Full Cov(Extra) 0.18/0.15; Checker Cov(Missing) 0.27/0.20; Block Cov(Missing) 0.11/0.11; Mixture(Missing) 0.10/0.09; Mixture(Extra) 0.13/0.13.
Fig. 8 (share of m > d settings inside RoR_0.5): ES-Full and ES-Partial score 0.00 on both mixture tests and on skewness, and only 0.06/0.04 on Full Cov (Missing).
Summary bullet: "The only exceptions are the mixture test cases, where all scoring rules fail."

Missing correlations (Fig. 3): ES-Partial has "a small RoR0.5 (d = 2^4 ∩ m ≥ 2^13) and a larger RoR0.2 (d ≤ 2^6 ∩ m ≥ 2^9)"; "the ground-truth sample size (n) needed for ES-Partial and VG to perform on par with the NLL is of the order of hundreds or thousands, a setting that is highly impractical."
Skewness: ES-Partial "reaches power values close to the false positive rate (α = 5%), indicating that its scores are essentially random."

Extra mode: "ES-Partial is the only scoring rule that was found to achieve non-negligible power. The results indicate a small RoR0.2 spanning d ≤ 2^5 ∩ n ≥ 2^10 [the figure axis suggests m] and that an impractical n of the order of hundreds would be required to match NLL performance." Figs. 27-28, read approximately: ES with p = 0.5 and p = 1 reaches about 0.3-0.4 power only at d = 16 with m ≥ 2^9-2^10; p = 1.5 does worse; Mixture (Missing) sits near chance for every p.
Mean shift (Fig. 2): when m > d, CRPS-Q and ES-Partial have RoR0.8 spanning d ≤ 2^5 ∩ m ≥ 2^10; "when m < d ... their power drops below 20%", and n = 300 would be needed to match the NLL.
