Fig. 9 (d = 16, m = 2^12, n = 30, Full Cov Missing): ES-Partial needs a much larger correlation eps (about 0.4-0.5) than NLL, DS or VG (about 0.1-0.2) to reach high power; "DS and VG being significantly more reliable than the ES on the most difficult settings (ε ≤ 0.4)."

Power is non-monotone in d (Fig. 5, App. C.1) and asymmetric between under- and over-estimation (App. C.1). "increasing m is only guaranteed to increase power up to an asymptote that is not necessarily β = 0."

Real data (solar, TACTiS, d = 9864, n = 30, m = 100), Sec. 6 text: breaking correlations, "ES and VG achieve a perfect power of 1.0"; multiplying by 1.05, CRPS/ES/VG 0.85/0.75/0.75; adding 0.05, ES 0.19 and VG 0.05. Table 4 (App. D) gives different numbers for the last two perturbations (ES-Partial 0.30 and 0.10; CRPS-Q 0.37 for multiplication; VG 0.30), so the paper is internally inconsistent here. kdd-cup (Table 5): ES-Partial 0.34/0.24/0.08. electricity (Table 6): ES-Partial 0.35 on breaking correlations.

Discussion: "none of the considered proper scoring rules is a good surrogate for the NLL, across all test cases, in the small-sample regimes that are common in practice. What is more, none of these scoring rules is able to reliably detect errors in modeling the statistical dependencies across variables."

Robustness (App. C.5): the conclusions are unchanged when alpha and the NLL target power are varied (Figs. 30-37). The CLT/normality approximation is reasonable except for the highest-kurtosis 2% of experiments (App. C.4, Fig. 29).

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 9: "Its conditional population objective is proper" (the sample energy score of eq. 16) [15].
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Main text eq. (3) defines ES with p ∈ (0,2); eq. (4) defines propriety. App. A.2: "The ES is a strictly proper scoring rule." The paper's setting is conditional forecasting, estimating P(X_{t+1..T} | X_{1..t}) (eq. 1).
proposal_claim_checks.correction: This is correct and in fact understated: ES is strictly proper for beta in (0,2), relative to distributions with finite beta-th moment. The moment condition and the strictness theorem come from Gneiting & Raftery (2007), which [15] cites as the source; the proposal could cite that for the propriety statement. "Conditional population objective" is right only pointwise in the conditioning (c, W_k). With one target a* per context, the correct conditional law is reached only through generalization across contexts.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 9: "a finite training set gives no calibration guarantee [15]."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: [15] shows that "properness only holds in expectation, while in practice evaluation is conducted based on a few samples from Dgt", measured as statistical power to detect discrepancies. It never studies training, training-set size, or calibration guarantees. Footnote 1: "our regions of reliability are distinct from reliability diagrams, which are graphical tools for checking forecast calibration." Sec. 7 separately recommends "inspecting calibration and sharpness (Gneiting et al., 2007)".
proposal_claim_checks.correction: The general statement is true, but it is not what [15] shows. [15] is about the finite-sample discriminative power of scores used for evaluation. Suggested rewording: "propriety holds only in expectation; with finite ground-truth and model samples the ES has low power to detect dependence, higher-moment and mode-structure errors, especially when dimension is large relative to sample size [15]." A calibration statement should cite Gneiting, Balabdaoui & Raftery (2007) instead.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Eq. 16: D = 1/S Σ_s ||â_s − a*|| − 1/(2S(S−1)) Σ_{s≠r} ||â_s − â_r|| as the sample energy score.
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: [15] App. A.2 eq. (16): ES-Full_p ≈ (1/m) Σ_i ||y − x_i||^p − (1/(m(m−1))) Σ_{i<i'} ||x_i − x_{i'}||^p. The code normalises by the number of pairs, m(m−1)/2, and multiplies by 0.5. Summing over ordered pairs s≠r and dividing by 2S(S−1) is algebraically identical at p = 1. My Monte-Carlo check agrees with the analytic ES to within 0.5 standard errors.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: No correction needed; this is the unbiased (fair, U-statistic) estimator. Two points worth adding: (i) beta = 1 is implied by the unpowered norms but never stated or justified; [15] tests p ∈ {0.5, 1, 1.5}. (ii) The S samples must be conditionally independent given (c, W_k), i.e. independent initial noises with no cross-sample coupling in path refinement; otherwise unbiasedness is lost. The biased 1/(2S²) V-statistic would reward under-dispersion (1-D Gaussian optimum sigma ≈ 0.38 at S = 2).

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Sec. 9: "Use at least two independent samples and finite first moments."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: [15]'s estimators need m ≥ 2 (the m(m−1) denominator; ES-Partial needs even m). The code comment reads "we need two independant realizations of the distributions". [15] does not state any moment condition.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: S ≥ 2 follows from [15]. The finite-first-moment condition for beta = 1 is correct but comes from Gneiting & Raftery (2007), not [15]. Note that S = 2 is unbiased but high-variance; [15]'s power results worsen sharply at small m, and "increasing m is only guaranteed to increase power up to an asymptote".

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Reference list: [15] "Includes energy-score definitions and finite-sample limitations."
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: Main text eq. (3); App. A.2 eqs. (16)-(17), ES-Full and ES-Partial; Secs. 4-6 and App. C give the finite-sample power analysis.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: The finite-sample limitations are about evaluation (hypothesis-test power) in time-series forecasting with d ≥ 16. The paper does not cover training losses or d < 16.

proposal_claim_checks.claim: Implied by Sec. 9 (context of [15]): the sample energy score is a suitable training loss when "preserving multimodality matters", in contrast to independent-noise endpoint MSE.
proposal_claim_checks.evidence: [15] never trains with ES and never compares to MSE. On multimodality its evidence is negative for d ≥ 16. Mixture (Missing), a bimodal truth against a moment-matched unimodal forecast: ES-Full max power 0.10 and ES-Partial 0.09, versus NLL 0.80; RoR_0.5 share 0.00; "the mixture test cases, where all scoring rules fail." Mixture (Extra): 0.13/0.13.
proposal_claim_checks.correction: [15] supports neither ES-as-training-loss nor ES's ability to preserve modes. ES does penalise a collapsed point prediction, because the spread term vanishes, so it is better than MSE against total collapse. But [15] shows ES gives little finite-sample signal separating a multimodal law from a moment-matched unimodal one when d ≥ 16. Action chunks in Experiment E fall in that range. For 2-D actions (Experiment B), [15] has no data, since its smallest d is 16. The proposal should cite training-with-scoring-rules literature for this design choice and test mode recovery directly.

reading.relevance_to_proposal:
Sec. 9, eq. 16 (training the whole-path-energy reader). [15] is the only citation behind using the energy score as the future-action distribution loss. It confirms the definition, propriety, and the unbiased estimator, which matches eq. 16 exactly with beta = 1. It gives no support for using ES as a training objective, and its mixture and dependence results warn that ES produces a weak finite-sample signal for mode structure beyond mean and covariance in d ≥ 16. That weakness applies directly to action chunks in Experiment E and less clearly to the 2-D actions in Experiment B.

Sec. 16, Experiment B ("Include a multimodal target family so that merely predicting a mean is insufficient"). [15]'s Mixture Missing/Extra construction is a ready-made test: a mixture against a moment-matched Gaussian, with the effect size tuned by NLL power. A model trained with ES could plausibly converge to such moment-matched unimodal solutions, and the benchmark should include this case.

Sec. 17, "Distribution quality: mode coverage and a distributional score alongside task success". This is where [15] matters most. If the "distributional score" is ES, [15] implies it may not detect missing or extra modes or broken dependencies at the proposal's sample sizes. The proposal's own habit of reporting mode coverage separately is well founded. The NLL, which [15] shows is the strongest discriminator, is computable for flow-matching policies via the instantaneous change-of-variables integral and is cheap for 2-D actions. The ground-truth densities in the synthetic benchmark are known.

Sec. 17, statistical plan (seeds, repeated samples not being replications). [15]'s separation of n (ground-truth draws) from m (model samples), and its finding that more m saturates while more n keeps helping, maps onto the proposal's distinction between test episodes and contexts on one side and action samples per context on the other.

Sec. 9 ("The procedure changes the output distribution and may reduce diversity") and Sec. 10 ("control optimality does not imply the desired distribution or preserved mode coverage"). [15] shows detection is asymmetric and that ES power for single-dimension variance changes is low (ES-Full max power 0.11-0.28 on the Normal Single-sigma tests). A loss of diversity may therefore go undetected by an ES-based metric, and dedicated dispersion and mode checks are needed.
novelty_threats: No direct novelty threat. [15] is about evaluating time-series forecasts and has nothing on memory, test-time training or flow-matching policies.

Indirect weakening. The proposal suggests (Sec. 9) that the energy score is a reasonable distributional training loss that preserves multimodality better than endpoint MSE. [15]'s mixture results (ES power 0.09-0.13 vs NLL 0.80; empty RoR_0.5) undercut any unqualified claim that ES-trained path refinement preserves modes. Any future claim that the path-energy reader beats the direct reader on distribution quality, if measured by ES, is at risk because ES may lack the power to register the difference.
ideas_to_borrow: Adopt [15]'s power-analysis protocol for the proposal's own evaluation metric. In the synthetic cue-to-action-distribution benchmark, build controlled discrepancies (missing mode, extra mode, wrong mode weights, shrunken variance, broken within-chunk correlations). Tune their size so a reference test (exact NLL) has 80% power at the planned number of test episodes and samples per context. Then verify that the reported "distributional score" can detect them before trusting it to rank methods.

Report NLL as the primary distributional metric wherever possible. [15] shows NLL dominates every sample-based rule, and a flow-matching policy is a CNF with a log-likelihood available through the divergence integral along the ODE, which is exact and cheap for 2-D actions. Use held-out ground-truth actions under the model (forward-KL direction), which penalises missing modes.

Use [15]'s Mixture (Missing)/(Extra) construction (App. B.3: 0.5 N(±eps·1, I) against the moment-matched N(0, I + eps^2 11^T)) as a unit test for whether the ES training loss in eq. 16 recovers modes, and compare against CFM-trained and NLL-evaluated baselines.

Report more than one proper score, since [15] finds them complementary ("VG is complementary to the CRPS and ES"): ES together with the variogram score (dependence across chunk dimensions), DS or NLL, and explicit mode-coverage and calibration/sharpness diagnostics, as [15] recommends in Sec. 7.

Sweep the ES exponent beta instead of fixing beta = 1. In [15]'s extra-mode test p = 0.5 and 1 gave more power than p = 1.5 (Fig. 28, read approximately). Also consider a kernel score (MMD with a tuned bandwidth); the ror/metrics folder includes kernel.py.

Treat the number of ground-truth draws per context (n) as the bottleneck, not only the number of model samples (m): "increasing n always improves the statistical power ... increasing m is only guaranteed to increase power up to an asymptote." In the evaluation, use many test contexts with several ground-truth actions per context where the synthetic generator allows it.

If eq. 16 is kept as a loss, the O(dS) ES-Partial pairing (eq. 17 in [15]) is also unbiased and cheaper, at the cost of higher variance. With the small S used in training, the full U-statistic is affordable and preferable.
technical_issues_in_proposal: Misattribution and framing (Sec. 9). "a finite training set gives no calibration guarantee [15]" is not what [15] studies. [15] measures finite-sample power of scores as evaluation tests and explicitly separates this from calibration (footnote 1). Reword the sentence as a finite-sample discrimination limitation, and cite Gneiting & Raftery (2007) for propriety and Gneiting, Balabdaoui & Raftery (2007) for calibration.

Unsupported design choice. Using ES as the training loss for multimodal action distributions is justified only by propriety. [15] gives no training evidence, and its mixture results show ES barely separates a bimodal law from a moment-matched unimodal one in d ≥ 16 (max power 0.09-0.13 vs 0.80). An inference not tested in [15]: the expected ES gap equals half the energy distance, so a weak gap against its variance suggests a weak, noisy gradient toward correct mode structure. Moment-matched unimodal solutions may be near-flat directions of the loss. The proposal should state this risk and test it.

Dimensionality mismatch. Experiment B uses 2-D actions or short 2-D chunks, below [15]'s smallest d = 16, so [15]'s evidence neither validates nor invalidates ES there. [15] warns "we cannot guarantee their validity beyond the considered domains (especially for d and m)". Experiment E's transformer action-chunk policy is likely to operate in the tens-to-hundreds of dimensions where [15] finds ES unreliable for dependence and mode errors.

Minimum S = 2. The eq. 16 estimator is correctly unbiased (verified exactly and by Monte-Carlo) but has high variance at S = 2. [15] shows power degrades sharply at small m. The proposal should budget S, and correctly exclude the s = r diagonal: a biased 1/(2S^2) implementation would be improper and push toward under-dispersion (1-D Gaussian optimum sigma ≈ 0.38 at S = 2, 0.63 at S = 4).

Independence requirement not spelled out. Unbiasedness of eq. 16 and the propriety argument need the S samples to be i.i.d. given (c, W_k): independent initial noises and no joint optimisation or coupling across samples during the K-step path refinement. The proposal says "independent samples" but should state explicitly that path refinement is per-sample.
beta is unstated. Eq. 16 implicitly uses beta = 1. [15] shows the exponent changes power (p = 0.5/1 beat 1.5 on the extra-mode test), so beta should be a reported hyperparameter.

Evaluation metric risk (Sec. 17). "a distributional score alongside task success": if this is ES, [15] implies it may miss missing or extra modes and dependence errors and may be insensitive to diversity loss. Include NLL (available for FM policies), mode coverage, a dependence-sensitive score (variogram), and a power check of the chosen metric.

Missing baselines and references for ES-as-training-loss. These are not cited in [15]; they are my suggestions, to be verified before citing: Pacchiardi et al., 'Probabilistic Forecasting with Generative Networks via Scoring Rule Minimization' (JMLR 2024); Bellemare et al., 'The Cramér Distance as a Solution to Biased Wasserstein Gradients' (2017); Shen & Meinshausen, 'Engression' (2023); De Bortoli et al., 'Distributional Diffusion Models with Scoring Rules' (2025). These are the literature that actually supports training generators with the energy score, and a CFM-trained, NLL-evaluated baseline should accompany the path-energy variant.
stated_limitations: "Our results are of empirical nature. As such, we cannot guarantee their validity beyond the considered domains (especially for d and m), which are constrained for computational reasons. This is particularly true in light of the non-monotonic behavior of the statistical power on certain test cases."
"Deriving finite-sample theoretical guarantees would be key to characterizing the domains not studied in the current work."
The methodology needs a known ground-truth distribution, so it "cannot directly be applied to real-world datasets". The real-data experiments use a fitted TACTiS model as a proxy ground truth.

In the real-data experiments the ground-truth sample is reused to build forecast samples, so "we ignore the extra variance in the scoring rules due to the sampling process, thus our estimates of 1−β for them are biased toward higher values."
Test cases are tuned to NLL power 0.8, so results reflect a single difficulty level. Fig. 9 and App. C.5 vary this partially.
The normal (CLT) approximation for averaged Delta_m is visibly off for the highest-kurtosis roughly 2% of experiments (App. C.4).
Smallest dimension studied is d = 16 and largest m is 2^14. No results exist for the low-dimensional (d = 2) regime of the proposal's Experiment B.
cited_works_worth_adding: Gneiting, T. & Raftery, A. E. (2007), 'Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation', JASA. The primary source for the energy score's strict propriety for beta in (0,2) under finite beta-moments. The proposal's propriety claim should cite it directly.

Gneiting, T., Balabdaoui, F. & Raftery, A. E. (2007), 'Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness', JRSS-B. The right citation for any statement about calibration, which the proposal currently attributes to [15].

Gneiting, Stanberry, Grimit, Held & Johnson (2008), 'Assessing probabilistic forecasts of multivariate quantities...', Test. Multivariate ES with ensemble (sample) estimators and multivariate calibration diagnostics.

Pinson, P. & Tastu, J. (2013), 'Discrimination ability of the energy score', DTU technical report. Early evidence that ES is weakly sensitive to dependence structure, directly relevant to within-chunk correlations.

Scheuerer, M. & Hamill, T. M. (2015), 'Variogram-based proper scoring rules for probabilistic forecasts of multivariate quantities', Monthly Weather Review. A dependence-sensitive score complementary to ES, useful as an additional metric.
Alexander, Coulon, Han & Meng (2022), 'Evaluating the discrimination ability of proper multi-variate scoring rules', Annals of OR. Independent evidence on ES versus variogram discrimination.

Ziel, F. & Berk, K. (2019), 'Multivariate forecasting evaluation: On sensitive and strictly proper scoring rules', arXiv:1910.07325. Separate marginal and copula scoring, relevant for diagnosing whether errors are marginal or dependence errors in action chunks.
Hamill, T. M. (2001), 'Interpretation of rank histograms for verifying ensemble forecasts', Monthly Weather Review. A calibration diagnostic and its pitfalls, if the proposal reports calibration.

errors_found.reader_claim: Claim check 4 and technical issue 4: "S = 2 is unbiased but high-variance; [15]'s power results worsen sharply at small m"; "[15] shows power degrades sharply at small m. The proposal should budget S".
errors_found.problem: This extrapolates beyond what [15] measured. Every heatmap in [15] uses m from 2^6 = 64 to 2^14, so [15] has no data for the S = 2 to 16 range a training loss would use. [15]'s power measures an evaluation test over n = 30 replications, not training-gradient noise that is averaged over thousands of minibatch contexts. At S = 2, ES-Full and ES-Partial are the same estimator (one pair).
errors_found.evidence: All figure axes run from 2^6 to 2^14. Limitations: "we cannot guarantee their validity beyond the considered domains (especially for d and m)". The only statement about small m is qualitative (Sec. 4.1): "small values might inflate the variance estimated in Eq. (7), resulting in increased overlap between H0 and HS and reduced power."
errors_found.corrected: The variance concern about S = 2 follows from first principles (and from [15]'s qualitative remark), but [15] gives no empirical evidence about m < 64. Present it as the verifier's own concern, not as a finding of [15].

errors_found.reader_claim: Claim check 6, technical issue 2, novelty threat 2, relevance: "[15] shows ES gives little finite-sample signal separating a multimodal law from a moment-matched unimodal one when d ≥ 16"; "ES barely separates a bimodal law ... (max power 0.09-0.13 vs 0.80)"; if the distributional score is ES, "it may not detect missing or extra modes ... at the proposal's sample sizes."
errors_found.problem: The numbers are right but the scope is left out. The powers are at n = 30. Each effect size was tuned so that even the NLL has only 80% power at n = 30, so these are near-threshold discrepancies. [15] itself says the heatmap values can be read as the n needed for 80% power, and that the extra-mode case needs n 'of the order of hundreds'. Under [15]'s own normal model, 0.10 to 0.13 power at n = 30 corresponds to roughly n ≈ 700 to 1,400 (my calculation from Fig. 6 values, approximate). The proposal plans 1,000 final-test and 10,000 training episodes, which puts it in that range. Fig. 9 shows ES-Partial power rising to about 1 as the discrepancy grows (about 0.8 at ε ≈ 0.4 and about 1 at ε ≳ 0.6), so the result does not cover well-separated modes of arbitrary size.
errors_found.evidence: Sec. 5.2: "we fix ε such that the NLL has a statistical power of 1 − β = 0.8". Sec. 5.3: "the values of the heatmap can be interchangeably read as the statistical power at n = 30 ... or as the minimal n required to achieve 80% power". Extra mode: "an impractical n of the order of hundreds would be required to match NLL performance." Table 3 gives Mixture (Missing) ε = 0.5906 at d = 16, falling to 0.0367 at d = 4096.
errors_found.corrected: [15] shows that at n ≈ 30 and near-threshold effect sizes, ES has little power against a moment-matched unimodal forecast for d ≥ 16. At the proposal's n of about 10^3 the concern is weaker, and for d = 2 it is untested. The warning should be stated with those qualifiers, and the proposal should run its own power check.

errors_found.reader_claim: Relevance: "ES power for single-dimension variance changes is low (ES-Full max power 0.11-0.28 on the Normal Single-sigma tests). A loss of diversity may therefore go undetected by an ES-based metric."
errors_found.problem: The reader cites only the single-dimension variance rows. A diversity reduction across the whole action (every dimension) matches the All-σ rows, where ES does noticeably better. The direction labels are also ambiguous: in the code, ε is placed on the ground truth (`sigma_gt[0][0] = self.ratio`, forecast N(0,1)), while Table 1 says '↓ The parameter is decreased in the forecast', so it is unclear which row is the under-dispersed forecast.
errors_found.evidence: Fig. 6: Normal (All, σ↓) ES-Full 0.61 and ES-Partial 0.50; Normal (All, σ↑) 0.62 and 0.56; compared with Normal (Single, σ↓/σ↑) at 0.11/0.10 and 0.28/0.25. App. B.1 eqs. 23-24 put ε on D_gt.
errors_found.corrected: ES is weak for a variance error confined to one dimension, and only moderately powerful (about 0.5 to 0.6, still below the NLL's 0.8) for a global variance change. A dedicated dispersion check is still advisable.

errors_found.reader_claim: Ideas/relevance: the NLL "is computable for flow-matching policies via the instantaneous change-of-variables integral"; "a flow-matching policy is a CNF with a log-likelihood available through the divergence integral along the ODE, which is exact and cheap for 2-D actions."
errors_found.problem: This is not from [15], and it does not hold for the variant that eq. 16 actually trains. The Sec. 9 path-energy reader returns the endpoint after K gradient steps on the path Z with z_0 fixed. That output map is not an ODE flow, it may not be invertible, and its density would need the Jacobian of the whole refinement procedure, not a divergence integral. Even for the ODE readers, the deployed sampler is a 16-step Euler map. The continuous divergence integral gives the density of the continuous ODE, not of the discrete sampler (in 2-D, the exact log-determinant of the discrete map can be computed instead).
errors_found.evidence: Proposal Sec. 9: "apply a fixed number K of gradient steps to Z, never to z_0 = ε. Return the final node as the action." Brief eq. 9: Euler sampler with 16 solver steps.
errors_found.corrected: The NLL can be computed for the base and direct-residual (ODE) readers, preferably as the log-determinant of the discrete sampler in 2-D. It is not straightforwardly available for the path-energy reader. There, mode coverage or kernel/MMD-type metrics with a power check are needed.

errors_found.reader_claim: Summary: "ES and CRPS detect errors in marginal means and variances when m > d".
errors_found.problem: This overstates the variance result for ES.
errors_found.evidence: Fig. 6: ES-Full 0.11 and 0.28 on Normal (Single, σ↓/σ↑). Fig. 8: the ES-Full share of m > d settings in RoR0.5 is 0.00 and 0.08 for these rows.
errors_found.corrected: ES detects mean errors and all-dimension scale errors reasonably well when m > d, but not single-dimension variance errors.

errors_found.reader_claim: Core mechanism: "the Euclidean mode separation 2·eps·sqrt(d) stays about 4.7 while each marginal separation is only about 1.2 sd."
errors_found.problem: The marginal separation of 1.2 sd holds only at d = 16. Because ε shrinks like 1/√d, the per-coordinate separation falls to about 0.07 sd at d = 4096.
errors_found.evidence: Table 3, Mixture (Missing): 0.5906 at d = 16 and 0.0367 at d = 4096.
errors_found.corrected: The mode separation along the diagonal stays about 4.7 at every d, while the per-coordinate separation is 2ε, from about 1.18 sd at d = 16 down to about 0.07 sd at d = 4096.

errors_found.reader_claim: "Mixture (Missing) sits near chance for every p" (Figs. 27-28, read approximately).
errors_found.problem: Slightly overstated.
errors_found.evidence: In Fig. 27, the p = 0.5 panels of ES-Full and ES-Partial show a small dotted RoR0.2 contour in the corner at d = 16, m ≈ 2^13 to 2^14.
errors_found.corrected: Near chance for p = 1 and p = 1.5. For p = 0.5, about 0.2 power only at d = 16 with the largest m.

missed_points: The other sample-based scores do not solve the mode problem either. VG is "a proper scoring rule but is not strictly proper since it is invariant to translations in the forecast" (A.3). DS "is only defined for m > d" (A.5) and depends only on the first two moments. On the mixture tests DS scores 0.07/0.08 and VG 0.08/0.09 (Fig. 6), and the paper attributes DS's covariance strength to its Gaussian assumption, "a thesis supported by its failure in the mixture test cases." The reader's suggestion to report 'ES together with VG, DS or NLL' should say that only the NLL (or explicit mode coverage) addresses the multimodal case, which is the proposal's key one.

The most direct quote for the proposal's Sec. 9 sentence is Sec. 2.3: "being proper does not imply that a scoring rule will be able to detect any prediction flaw ... properness only holds in expectation, while in practice evaluation is conducted based on a few samples from Dgt." This is about evaluation. [15] mentions a training set only once, in a different sense: "reducing the training set in favor of the test set" to raise n (Sec. 7).

A one-sided power heuristic from [15]'s framework converts n = 30 power into the n needed. For example, 0.10 power at n = 30 implies about 1,400 replications for 80% power, and 0.13 implies about 700. The proposal's 1,000-episode test set is therefore at the edge where ES-based comparisons could become usable for NLL-threshold mode errors. Neither the reader nor the proposal uses this.

[15] reports that "The various implementations of CRPS and ES perform comparably. This indicates that the computational gain of CRPS-Q and ES-Partial does not negatively affect their reliability." At S = 2 the full and partial estimators are identical, since both use one pair.

The paper has internal inconsistencies the reader did not flag. (i) Sec. 5.2 says the forecast "has one more or one fewer mixture component ..., denoted by Mixture (Missing) and Mixture (Extra), respectively", the reverse of App. B.3 and the captions of Figs. 27-28. (ii) The Table 1 caption puts ε on the forecast, but eqs. 21-27 and the code put it on D_gt. (iii) In Fig. 9 the vertical line marking NLL 80% power sits at about ε ≈ 0.06, while Table 3 gives ε = 0.2055 for Full Cov (Missing) at d = 16; at that ε the NLL curve in Fig. 9 is about 0.97. The reader did correctly flag the mismatch between the Sec. 6 real-data numbers and Table 4, and the n/m typo.

Reading the mixture test: at d = 16 the bimodality lies along a single direction (projected means ±2.36 with unit sd) with 15 isotropic noise directions. ES's weakness here reflects Euclidean distances being dominated by the noise dimensions. That mechanism is weaker in the proposal's 2-D actions and stronger in high-dimensional action chunks. This supports the reader's point about dimension, but [15] does not state it; it is my interpretation.
verification.novelty_threat_assessment: None. [15] is an evaluation-methodology paper, a power analysis of proper scoring rules for multivariate time-series forecasts. It has no content on fast weights, test-time training, memory, flow-matching policies, path refinement or consolidation, so it pre-empts none of the proposal's contributions. What it does is methodological. (a) It supports the definition and propriety of the ES and the exact unbiased estimator that the proposal's eq. 16 reproduces. I verified this algebraically, against eq. 16 in [15], against the authors' code (`second_term = s / (num_samples * (num_samples - 1) / 2)`; `first_term - 0.5 * second_term`), and by my own Monte-Carlo: with S = 2 and S = 4 the U-statistic mean is 0.73077±0.0004 and 0.73112±0.00025 against a true ES of 0.73085; the V-statistic is biased, and its 1-D optimum is σ ≈ 0.378, 0.626 and 0.885 for S = 2, 4 and 16. (b) It gives no support for ES as a training loss, and it does not support the proposal's claim about a 'finite training set / calibration guarantee' (partially accurate at best, mis-framed). (c) It warns that ES-based evaluation is weak at detecting dependence and mode errors near the detection threshold with n ≈ 30 and d ≥ 16. The reader overstates that warning when applying it to the proposal: the proposal's test n of about 10^3 and 2-D actions (Experiment B) fall outside or at the edge of [15]'s conditions, and [15] has no data for m < 64. The practical impact is on the proposal's evaluation design (use NLL where it is defined, mode coverage, and a power check), not on novelty.

ref.title: Schwarz et al., Progress & Compress: A scalable framework for continual learning (ICML 2018)
ref.role: Closest continual-learning prior for the fast->slow lifecycle: active column learns task, distilled into knowledge base protected by online EWC, active column reinitialized; lateral connections from KB to active column.
ref.focus: Exact algorithm (progress phase, compress phase, online EWC, lateral adaptors, reset), assumptions (task boundaries), RL/ supervised experiments, results on forgetting and forward transfer. Map each step onto the proposal's lifecycle (Sec 11-15) and identify what the proposal adds beyond P&C. Verify the proposal's claim "Progress & Compress uses online EWC; our initial replay-based retention choice is not a claim that replay is required by that method."
